title: Quantum Computing, Information and Physics in qang Space
text:
Preface
This book gathers, in reading order, the results of a research programme built on a simple idea: describing the qubit by what is measured. The qang unit (qg) expresses a qubit’s state on the scale on which the experiment delivers it, the polar bias \(qg_Z=\langle\sigma_z\rangle\), and that choice yields a practical tool, the qg symmetry filter: when a circuit conserves a number (excitations, photons, neutrino flavour, mass), the shots that violate it can only come from noise and are discarded.
The book goes from the foundations (Parts I and II) to the applications: neutrinos (Part III), teleportation in optical networks (Part IV), information-theoretic models of time loops and black holes (Part V), cryptography (Part VI), quantum machine learning (Part VII), dynamics and chemistry (Part VIII), error correction and characterization (Part IX). Part X gathers the evidence: the method, the confirmed advantages, the limits and the negative results, and the first run on real hardware.

title: Quantum Computing, Information and Physics in qang Space
text:
How to read the results
Three conventions run through the book:

Predictions recorded before running. Every experiment cited fixed its predictions before it was run (a commit or a sha256 hash of the script), and is reported as passed or failed. Failures are not left out: many of the book’s lessons come from them.
Simulated noise unless stated. Whatever is described “on a device” refers to calibrated noise models of IBM or IonQ processors, except for the real-hardware results, which are marked explicitly (Chapter 31).
References to the notes. Citations such as (§151) point to the corresponding section of the project’s research notes (RESEARCH_NOTES.md), where the code, the tests and the data are.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.1 Definition of the qang
A qubit is designed with angles and observed with frequencies. Whoever writes a circuit chooses rotations \(R_y(\theta)\); whoever runs it receives counts of zeros and ones. Between the two descriptions sits a trigonometric function that is rarely named, and that is the source of several practical difficulties: gradients that diverge, error bars that shrink or swell with the state, and parameters that cannot be read directly from the experiment. This chapter builds the foundation of the book in three steps: the definition of the qang unit (qg), the theory of the milli-qang (its submultiple) and the probability equation that ties both to what is measured. Every result is backed by a figure computed with the package itself (qang.probability, §167), so the figures and the text quote the same numbers.
Every pure state of a qubit can be written, up to a global phase, as
\[
|\psi\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle ,
\qquad \theta\in[0,\pi],\ \varphi\in[0,2\pi).
\]
The pair \((\theta,\varphi)\) is a point on the Bloch sphere and is the natural way to prepare the state: a rotation \(R_y(\theta)\) followed by a phase \(R_z(\varphi)\). A measurement in the computational basis does not return \(\theta\): it returns, on each shot, the outcome 0 with probability
\[
p_0 = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad\text{(Born's rule).}
\]
Definition. The qang unit takes as its primary coordinate the expectation value of \(\sigma_z\), called the polar bias:
\[
\boxed{\;qg_Z = \langle\sigma_z\rangle = p_0 - p_1 = 2p_0 - 1 = \cos\theta\;}\qquad qg_Z\in[-1,1].
\]
The other two readings of the unit come from the same probability: the qang angle \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\in[0,\pi]\) and the superposition spread \(qg_S=H(p_0)\in[0,1]\), the Shannon entropy of the outcome (studied below). Figure 1.1 summarizes the definition: the point on the circle is the state, its projection on the vertical axis is \(qg_Z\), and the scale on the right gives the same reading in milli-qang and in probability.
Three properties make \(qg_Z\) a good working coordinate:
The sign and range have an immediate physical reading: \(qg_Z=+1\) is the pole \(|0\rangle\), \(qg_Z=-1\) the pole \(|1\rangle\), and \(qg_Z=0\) any point of the equator, where the measurement outcome is maximally uncertain.
An engineering unit. A useful unit does not need to be a new physical quantity; it needs to make what is measured legible. The decibel adds no physics to power: it expresses it on a scale that makes the gains of a chain of amplifiers additive. The qang plays an analogous role for the qubit: it expresses its state on the scale in which the experiment delivers it, so that preparation, noise and read-out are compared in the same units. It is an operational convention, and like every convention it is worth what it simplifies.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
Figure 1.1: The qang circle. The state at angle \(\theta=60^\circ\) has \(p_0=0.75\), \(qg_Z=\cos\theta=0.5\) and a reading of \(+500\) m-qg. The four equations on the right are the same probability read in four ways.





It is a bijection. On \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\), \(\cos\theta\) is strictly decreasing and covers \([-1,1]\): each value of \(qg_Z\) corresponds to a single latitude of the sphere.
It is directly measurable. \(\widehat{qg}_Z = (n_0-n_1)/N\) is the average of the \(\pm1\) outcomes of the shots; it needs no inversion and no fit.
It holds for any state. For a mixed state, \(qg_Z = \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\), which reduces to \(\cos\theta\) when \(\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) (§3).

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.2 Theory of the milli-qang

1.2.1 Definition and scale
The deviations that matter in a real qubit are small: calibration errors, drift, read-out noise. A submultiple is convenient to express them, the milli-qang (m-qg):
\[
1\ \text{qg} = 1000\ \text{m-qg},\qquad m = 1000\,qg_Z\ \in[-1000,\,+1000]\ \text{m-qg}.
\]
The scale runs from \(-1000\) m-qg at the pole \(|1\rangle\) to \(+1000\) m-qg at the pole \(|0\rangle\), with zero on the equator. A state with \(qg_Z=0.5018\) sits at \(501.8\) m-qg; its difference from the ideal \(0.5\) is \(1.8\) m-qg. The same definition holds for the other axes, \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\), so the whole Bloch vector can be expressed in m-qg.


1.2.2 Linear in probability, not linear in angle
Since \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\), the milli-qang is linear in probability: one m-qg is always \(\Delta p_0=0.0005\), that is, 0.05 percentage points, anywhere on the scale. It is not linear in angle:
\[
\frac{dm}{d\theta} = -1000\,\sin\theta
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\Delta\theta \approx \frac{1}{1000\,\sin\theta}\ \text{rad per m-qg}.
\]
On the equator (\(\theta=90^\circ\)) one m-qg is exactly one milliradian; at \(\theta=30^\circ\) it is two. Near a pole the linear relation fails and the exact one must be used: a state \(\delta\) m-qg below the pole \(|0\rangle\) makes with it the angle
\[
\theta_\delta = \arccos\!\left(1-\frac{\delta}{1000}\right)\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{1000}} .
\]
One m-qg from the pole is \(0.0447\) rad (\(2.56^\circ\)); ten m-qg, \(8.1^\circ\). Figure 1.2 shows the consequence: on the milli-qang ruler the probability marks are evenly spaced and the angle marks crowd at the poles. That is why the unit is defined on probability and not on angle: it is the scale in which the instrument delivers the data.






Figure 1.2: The milli-qang ruler. Top, the scale in m-qg; middle, the probability \(p_0\), aligned and linear; bottom, the qang angle, whose marks every \(15^\circ\) are compressed towards the poles.





1.2.3 Resolution from shots
With \(N\) shots, \(\widehat{qg}_Z\) has variance \(\sin^2\theta/N\) (derived in the arcsine section), so the standard deviation of the reading in milli-qang is
\[
\sigma_m = \frac{1000\,\sin\theta}{\sqrt N}\ \text{m-qg},
\qquad
N_\delta = \left(\frac{1000\,\sin\theta}{\delta}\right)^{2}
\]
where \(N_\delta\) is the number of shots needed to resolve \(\delta\) m-qg at one sigma. On the equator, resolving 10 m-qg takes \(10^4\) shots and resolving 1 m-qg, \(10^6\). At \(60^\circ\) and 1000 shots, \(\sigma_m=27.4\) m-qg; to get down to 5 m-qg at that point takes 30,000 shots. Figure 1.3 compares \(\sigma_m\) with the uncertainty of the angle, \(\sigma_\theta=1/\sqrt N\): the m-qg reading is more precise near the poles, and the angle’s is the same all around the circle. The two curves touch on the equator, where one m-qg is one milliradian.






Figure 1.3: Resolution from shots. Solid lines: standard deviation \(\sigma_m\) of the m-qg reading; dashed lines: \(\sigma_\theta\) of the qang angle in milliradians, which does not depend on the state. For each \(N\), the two coincide at \(\theta=90^\circ\).





1.2.4 Gate error budget
The scale lets a gate error be expressed in the same units as the read-out. If the amplitude of a pulse has a random relative error of standard deviation \(\sigma\), the expected polar bias after \(R_x(\theta)\) is
\[
\mathbb E[qg_Z] = \cos\theta\; e^{-\theta^2\sigma^2/2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\varepsilon_m = 1000\cos\theta\left(e^{-\theta^2\sigma^2/2}-1\right)\ \text{m-qg}
\]
(§160). The error pulls the reading towards the equator: with \(\sigma=0.05\), an \(X\) gate (\(\theta=\pi\)) delivers \(qg_Z=-0.988\) instead of \(-1\), a shift of \(12.3\) m-qg. At multiples of \(\pi\) the shift grows with the square of the angle, always towards the equator; in general it goes as \(\theta^2\cos\theta\) (Figure 1.4). A \(\pi/2\) rotation does not shift at all, because it already sits on the equator. Chapter 2 uses this formula to choose, among equivalent representations of the same gate, the one with the smallest pulse area.






Figure 1.4: Error budget in milli-qang: shift of the polar bias after \(R_x(\theta)\) for several relative amplitude errors \(\sigma\).

text:
1.3 The probability equation of the qang and the milli-qang
The previous sections lead to a single statement, which is the foundation of the whole book: every qang reading of a qubit is an exact function of a single probability, \(p_0\):
\[
\boxed{\;
\theta = 2\arccos\sqrt{p_0},\qquad
qg_Z = 2p_0-1,\qquad
qg_S = H(p_0),\qquad
m = 2000\,p_0-1000\ \text{m-qg}
\;}
\]
and, in the other direction, the probability equation of the milli-qang:
\[
p_0 = \frac{1000+m}{2000},\qquad \theta = \arccos\frac{m}{1000}.
\]
There are no approximations: they are four readings of one number. Figure 1.5 shows them together. \(qg_Z\) and the milli-qang are the same straight line on two scales; the angle is monotonic but steepens at the poles; the entropy rises up to the equator and falls again, which is why it needs a branch to be inverted. Table 1.1 gives the reference values.

1.3.1 More than two outcomes: the statistical distance
The equation generalizes to a measurement with several outcomes. For two distributions \(p=(p_k)\) and \(q=(q_k)\), Wootters’ statistical distance (1981), or Bhattacharyya angle (Bhattacharyya 1943), is
\[
d(p,q) = \arccos\sum_k\sqrt{p_k\,q_k}.
\]
For two outcomes, the distance between \((p_0,1-p_0)\) and the pole \((1,0)\) is \(\arccos\sqrt{p_0}=\theta/2\): up to the factor 2, the qang angle is the statistical distance between what is measured and the reference state. With three outcomes, for example, \(p=(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) and \(q=(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)\) are \(0.113\) rad apart. This is the door through which the unit leaves the qubit: Part II uses it for the Fisher information and the Fubini–Study metric, and the same geometry holds for any measured proportion, quantum or not.

section: 1.4 Why measure in qg: the geometry–probability gap
text:
1.4 Why measure in qg: the geometry–probability gap
The relation \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\) between the control parameter and the observed quantity is non-linear, and its derivative vanishes at the poles. This has concrete consequences. If a variational algorithm wants to adjust the state according to what it measures, the chain rule introduces the factor
\[
\frac{dE}{dq} = -\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\,\frac{dE}{d\theta},
\]
which diverges at \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\pi\) (research notes, §1). And if \(\theta\) is to be estimated from \(N\) shots, the variance of \(\hat p_0\) changes with the state, so the uncertainty of each reading depends on where the qubit is (§5). Neither problem is exotic: both appear as soon as one reasons in terms of what the experiment delivers, and the probability equation is the tool to handle them.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.5 Inversion and the branch sign
The angle is recovered with \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\). The inversion has a limit: \(\cos\theta\) is even, so \(qg_Z\) does not distinguish \(\theta\) from \(-\theta\). As long as one works on \([0,\pi]\) there is no problem, but an optimizer that needs to cross a pole gets stuck. The remedy is to measure the sign of the sine as well: the pair \((qg_Z, s)\) with \(s=\operatorname{sign}(qg_X)\) is one-to-one on the whole circle (§65). In the H₂ molecule the variational optimum is at \(\theta\approx-0.22\); every update that uses only \(qg_Z\) stops at the Hartree–Fock state, while the signed version reaches the exact energy.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.6 The outcome entropy: \(qg_S\)
The polar bias says where the qubit points; it does not say how unpredictable the measurement is. That is the role of the superposition spread, the Shannon entropy of the outcome:
\[
qg_S = H(p_0) = -p_0\log_2 p_0 - (1-p_0)\log_2(1-p_0) \in [0,1].
\]
Since \(qg_Z\) and \(qg_S\) depend on the same population \(p_0\), they are tied by an exact, branch-free identity (§7):
\[
qg_S = H\!\left(\frac{1+qg_Z}{2}\right),
\]
valid for every single-qubit state, pure or mixed, however it was prepared. Its derivative, \(\tfrac{d\,qg_S}{d\,qg_Z}=\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac{1-qg_Z}{1+qg_Z}\), diverges at the poles: it is the entropic counterpart of the gradient singularity. Near a pole, a minimal change of the bias produces an enormous relative change of the entropy.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
section: 1.7 Invertibility of \(qg_S\) and its error bars
text:
1.7 Invertibility of \(qg_S\) and its error bars
Unlike \(qg_Z\), the entropy is not invertible over the whole domain: \(qg_S(\theta)=qg_S(\pi-\theta)\). The population \(p_0\) decreases from 1 to 0 on \([0,\pi]\) and \(H\) rises up to \(p=\tfrac12\) and then falls, so \(qg_S\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\pi/2]\) and strictly decreasing on \([\pi/2,\pi]\) (Figure 1.5). Inversion requires choosing one of the two halves (§2).
Estimating \(qg_S\) from finite shots raises a further problem: the entropy is flat at its maximum, and the delta method gives a zero standard error exactly where \(qg_S\approx1\). The native qang solution is to build the Wilson interval for \(qg_Z\) and map it through the identity above; since \(H\) is unimodal, the image is a valid interval. Over 2000 repetitions that interval kept a coverage of 0.90–0.99 in every case tested, even where the Wald interval or the bootstrap fell below 0.40 (§51).

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
section: 1.8 The qang angle as the arcsine transformation
text:
1.8 The qang angle as the arcsine transformation
The central statistical property of the unit follows from propagating shot noise. With \(\widehat{qg}_Z = 2\hat
p_0-1\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{qg}_Z)=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{N},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\approx \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{qg}_Z)\left(\frac{d\theta}{d\,qg_Z}\right)^2
=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{N}\cdot\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}=\frac1N .
\]
The \(\sin^2\theta\) factors cancel exactly: the uncertainty of the qang angle does not depend on the state (§5), which is the horizontal dashed line of Figure 1.3. It is not a coincidence. Since \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\), the qang angle is, up to the reflection \(\theta\to\pi-\theta\), the classical arcsine transformation of a proportion, \(\phi=2\arcsin\sqrt p\), introduced by Bartlett (1947), Anscombe (1948) and Freeman and Tukey (1950) precisely to stabilize the variance (§125).
The claim was checked with exact binomial sums, without simulation: with \(n=100\), \((n+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Var}
(\hat\theta)\) lies between 1.000 and 1.001; the coverage of the interval \(\hat\theta\pm z/\sqrt{n+1/2}\) stays between 0.930 and 0.962 for \(n\in\{30,100,1000\}\). The prediction failed in one case, and it is worth saying: with \(np\approx2.5\) both the angular and the Wald intervals lose coverage. The stabilization is asymptotic, and the regime of very few events requires the exact intervals of chapter 4.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.9 Mixed states and multi-qubit registers
The definitions extend unchanged to mixed states and to registers:

Mixed states. \(qg_Z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_z)\) no longer determines the state. The classical mixture of \(|0\rangle\) with weight 0.2 and \(|1\rangle\) with weight 0.8 has \(qg_Z=-0.6\) and von Neumann entropy 0.72, a combination no pure state reproduces (§3). The qang angle \(\theta=\arccos qg_Z\) is still a function of \(p_0\), so it keeps \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)=1/N\) here too: the probability does not know whether the state is pure. What loses the stabilization is the estimate of the Bloch polar angle, \(\arccos(qg_Z/r)\), of a qubit of length \(r<1\): \(\operatorname{Var}=\big[1+\tfrac{1-r^2}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\big]/N\), equal to the quantum Cramér–Rao bound \(1/(Nr^2)\) on the equator (§45).
Registers. Each qubit has its local profile, obtained by partial trace, and the register has a joint entropy normalized by the number of qubits (§4). The Bell state illustrates it: each qubit has \(qg_Z=0\) and a local entropy of 1 bit, but the normalized joint Shannon entropy of the outcomes is 0.5 (the von Neumann entropy of the register is 0). The register is globally pure and locally mixed; the local profiles are not enough to describe it, and chapter 5 returns to this point with the Bloch radius.

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
section: 1.10 Scope and limits of the base
text:
1.10 Scope and limits of the base
It is worth stating precisely what this base brings and what it does not, before building the rest of the book on it.
What it is not. The qang unit is not new physics. The polar bias is the expectation value of \(\sigma_z\), the qang angle is the arcsine transformation of a proportion and the milli-qang is, mathematically, \(1000\,\langle\sigma_z\rangle\). None of these readings holds information that the probability \(p_0\) does not already have; the probability equation says so explicitly. Nor does it reduce the shots a given precision requires (Chapter 4).
What it is. A working scale, in the sense of the decibel: it puts preparation, gate error, shot noise and read-out in the same units, so that they add, compare and can be budgeted. The question that matters is then empirical: does reasoning in milli-qang predict what a real processor does?
First test on hardware (§168). It was answered with a pre-registered experiment on one qubit of IQM’s superconducting Garnet processor: 26 circuits of 4000 shots, with four predictions fixed before the run. The result was mixed, and it is reported in full:

The cost of a gate is measurable and budgetable in m-qg. Chaining 3 to 41 \(X\) gates, the shortfall of the reading (corrected for the readout errors measured at the poles) grows with a single slope: 1.64 m-qg per \(X\) gate, with a \(\chi^2\) per degree of freedom of 0.81. After 41 gates it is 63 m-qg, eight standard deviations above zero (Figure 1.6, left). Linear rather than quadratic growth points to incoherent error, relaxation during the pulses, and not to a coherent over-rotation.
The scale makes visible an error that the readout model hides. The affine readout predicted from the poles fits at the equator, but the four intermediate angles read between 16 and 55 m-qg low (Figure 1.6, right). The processor calibrates the angles \(0\), \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\) well; the others are over-rotated by \(1.3^\circ\) to \(3.9^\circ\). The prediction passed by the 4-of-5 rule, not cleanly.
One prediction failed. The ten copies of the equator circuit scattered half as much as binomial shot noise allows, something independent shots cannot produce and which happens by chance with probability 0.013. A single run does not decide whether it was a fluke or a property of how the device returns batched circuits.
Another prediction was badly designed. Fitting two parameters on four points left an extrapolation band so wide that any reading passed. It is recorded as a design flaw, not as a success.







Figure 1.6: First test of the milli-qang on hardware (§168, IQM Garnet, one qubit, 4000 shots per circuit). Left: shortfall of the reading after \(k\) \(X\) gates, readout-corrected, with the single-slope line. Right: difference between measured and predicted by the affine readout; the poles are zero by construction, because they define the calibration.



The balance: on a real chip, the milli-qang turned the error of a gate into a budgetable number and exposed an angle error that the usual model does not see. But it was tested on one qubit, once, and shot noise did not describe the scatter of repeated circuits. Replication on more qubits and on another day is pending, and the book treats this base as solid mathematically and promising, but not yet consolidated, experimentally.

text:
1.12 In code
The qang.probability module is this chapter’s analysis tool: it reads counts and returns every reading, each with its interval.
import math
from qang import probability as pb

pb.readings_from_p0(0.75)        # theta = 1.047 (60°), qg_Z = 0.5, qg_S = 0.811, 500 m-qg

# 750 zeros in 1000 shots, against a target qg_Z = 0.5
r = pb.analyze(750, 1000, target_qg_z=0.5)
r.milliqang                      # (500.0, 444.5, 551.7) m-qg: estimate and Wilson interval

title: 1  The qang unit: definition, milli-qang and the probability equation
text:
1.13 Summary

Definition. The polar bias \(qg_Z=\langle\sigma_z\rangle=2p_0-1=\cos\theta\) is bijective, directly measurable and valid for mixed states; the qang angle \(\theta=\arccos qg_Z\) and the entropy \(qg_S=H(p_0)\) complete the unit.
Milli-qang. \(1\ \text{qg}=1000\) m-qg; the scale is linear in probability (1 m-qg \(=\Delta p_0=0.0005\)) and not linear in angle (1 mrad on the equator, \(2.56^\circ\) next to the pole). Resolving \(\delta\) m-qg takes \((1000\sin\theta/\delta)^2\) shots, and gate errors are budgeted in the same units.
Probability equation. \(\theta\), \(qg_Z\), \(qg_S\) and \(m\) are exact functions of a single probability \(p_0\); with several outcomes, the qang angle generalizes to Wootters’ statistical distance.
Statistics. The qang angle is the arcsine transformation of a proportion: its variance is \(1/N\) for every state, pure or mixed; what needs a correction in a mixed state is the estimate of the Bloch angle.
Scope. The unit is not new physics but a working scale. On real hardware (§168) it measured a cost of 1.64 m-qg per \(X\) gate, linear in the number of gates, and exposed reading shifts of 16–55 m-qg (over-rotations of \(1.3^\circ\)–\(3.9^\circ\)); a prediction about shot noise failed and replication is pending.

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
text:
2.1 The elementary gate \(R_{qg}\)
Chapter 1 described the state of a qubit in qg units and reduced all its readings to a single probability, \(p_0\), with the milli-qang as the working scale. This chapter does the same for operations: how a state is prepared from its probability or its m-qg reading, how any single-qubit gate is written as an algebraic function of \(qg_Z\), why its action on the populations is the probability equation of Chapter 1, how the idea extends to systems with more levels, and which compilation rules follow when the error of a gate, measured in m-qg, depends on its angle.
The basic operation is to prepare, from \(|0\rangle\), the state with polar bias \(q\): a rotation \(R_y(\theta)\) with \(\theta=\arccos q\). qang provides it as a native gate in the three most widely used development kits (§6):
By the probability equation (Section 1.3), the gate parameter can be set from any of the readings: for a probability \(p_0\) use \(q=2p_0-1\), and for a reading of \(m\) m-qg, \(q=m/1000\). Asking for \(p_0=0.75\) or for \(+500\) m-qg is asking for the same gate, \(R_y(60^\circ)\).
All three prepare exactly the same state for the same qg value, which is checked both on the measured probabilities and on the state-vector fidelity. The gate accepts symbolic parameters (Qiskit Parameter, sympy symbols), so it can sit inside parameterized circuits.
A signed variant, SignedRQangGate, applies \(R_y(s\cdot\arccos q)\) with \(s=\pm1\): it is the gate form of the branch sign of Chapter 1, and prepares the same state as the full gate with \(\varphi=0\) or \(\pi\) (§68).

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
text:
2.2 The universal operator in qg
Every single-qubit gate is, up to a global phase, \(U(\theta,\varphi,\lambda)\). With \(q=\cos\theta\) the half-angles become algebraic,
\[
\cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{1+q}{2}},\qquad \sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{1-q}{2}},
\]
and the universal gate is written without trigonometric functions of \(q\):
\[
U_3^{qg}(q,\varphi,\lambda)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{\dfrac{1+q}{2}} & -e^{i\lambda}\sqrt{\dfrac{1-q}{2}}\\[2ex]
e^{i\varphi}\sqrt{\dfrac{1-q}{2}} & e^{i(\varphi+\lambda)}\sqrt{\dfrac{1+q}{2}}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The amplitudes depend on the polar bias only, and the phases are decoupled into the factors \(e^{i\varphi}\) and \(e^{i\lambda}\). An immediate consequence is the transition matrix, the probabilities \(|U_{ij}|^2\):
\[
T(q)=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1+q}{2}&\tfrac{1-q}{2}\\[0.5ex]\tfrac{1-q}{2}&\tfrac{1+q}{2}\end{pmatrix},
\]
doubly stochastic, rational in \(q\) and independent of the phases. Seen from a measurement in the computational basis, and for inputs without coherences, every single-qubit gate is a binary symmetric channel with parameter \((1-q)/2\).

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
section: 2.3 The gate as a probability equation
text:
2.3 The gate as a probability equation
The transition matrix is Chapter 1’s probability equation written for an operation. With \(p_0=(1+q)/2\),
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}p_0&1-p_0\\1-p_0&p_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad p_0=\frac{1000+m}{2000}:
\]
on an input without coherences (\(|0\rangle\), \(|1\rangle\) or a classical mixture of them), the action of any single-qubit gate on the populations is fixed by a single number, its reading in m-qg. The identity and \(Z\) sit at \(+1000\) m-qg (they do not move populations), \(X\) at \(-1000\) (it swaps them) and the Hadamard at \(0\) (it equalizes them). The phases \(\varphi\) and \(\lambda\) do not appear: they are invisible to a \(Z\) measurement and only show up when gates are composed, as Chapter 3 shows. On an input with coherences the full formula is \(p_0'=T(q)\,p-\sqrt{1-q^2}\,\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\lambda}\rho_{01})\): the Hadamard on \(|+\rangle\) gives \(p_0=1\), not the \(0.5\) that \(T(0)\) would give.
The entropic reading has its version for operations too. The capacity of the binary symmetric channel with parameter \((1-q)/2\) is \(1-H\big((1-q)/2\big)\), and since \(H\) is symmetric, \(H\big((1-q)/2\big)=H(p_0)=qg_S\):
\[
C = 1-qg_S .
\]
A gate at a pole (\(qg_S=0\)) carries one full bit per use; the Hadamard (\(qg_S=1\)) carries nothing from the computational basis to itself.

section: 2.5 Beyond the qubit: the Cartan subalgebra
text:
2.5 Beyond the qubit: the Cartan subalgebra
For a \(d\)-level system (a qudit), the analogue of \(\sigma_z\) is not one matrix but the Cartan subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{su}(d)\): the \(d-1\) diagonal generalized Gell-Mann matrices,
\[
\lambda_k=\sqrt{\frac{2}{k(k+1)}}\;\operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k},-k,0,\dots,0),\qquad k=1,\dots,d-1,
\]
normalized so that \(\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_j\lambda_k)=2\delta_{jk}\). Their expectation values are linear in the populations and determine them:
\[
p=\frac1d+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\langle\lambda_k\rangle\,\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_k).
\]
For \(d=2\) a single matrix remains, \(\lambda_1=\sigma_z\), its expectation value is \(qg_Z\) and the formula reduces to \(p_0=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\,qg_Z\): the probability equation of Chapter 1. This is the natural generalization of the unit: a vector of \(d-1\) qg values measurable in the computational basis, each expressible in m-qg, which fixes the \(d\) probabilities the way \(qg_Z\) fixes \(p_0\) (§166).
Definition and usefulness should be kept apart. Whether a three-level readout gives qang an advantage was asked on a concrete case, a transmon leaking to the level \(|2\rangle\) in a surface-code memory, and the answer was no: reading \(|2\rangle\) as 1 is usually right, and declaring the qubit erased discards that information (§70). qang remains a qubit construction; the qudit generalization is an identity, not a demonstrated advantage.

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
text:
2.6 The minimal pulse-area principle
On devices with fractional gates (rotations \(R_X(\theta)\) or \(R_{ZZ}(\theta)\) with a continuous angle), the pulse area grows with \(|\theta|\), and so do the amplitude-miscalibration error and the relaxation during the pulse. In qg units, a random amplitude error of standard deviation \(\sigma\) damps the read-out as
\[
qg_Z=\cos\theta\;e^{-\theta^2\sigma^2/2},
\]
and a fixed one \(\varepsilon\) gives \(\cos(\theta(1+\varepsilon))\), with first-order error \(-1000\,\varepsilon\,\theta\sin\theta\) m-qg. The sensitivity to an absolute angle error, \(d\,qg_Z/d\theta=-\sin\theta\), is largest at \(\pi/2\) and vanishes at \(0\) and \(\pi\); the fixed error is relative (\(\varepsilon\theta\)) and weighs most near \(116^\circ\) (§160). This is Chapter 1’s milli-qang error budget (Figure 1.4), and the scale makes the gate error comparable with the shot noise of the read-out: with \(\sigma=0.05\), the shift of an \(X\) (12.3 m-qg) is about eight times the resolution of \(10^4\) shots at its reading, \(-987.7\) m-qg, where \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N=1.6\) m-qg (on the equator it would be 10 m-qg).
Every gate has shorter representatives. \(R_X(\theta)=-R_X(\theta-2\pi)\) has period \(2\pi\) up to a global phase, and Figure 2.1 shows what is gained: asking for \(R_X(324^\circ)\) as is shifts the reading by \(-31.7\) m-qg, while its representative \(R_X(-36^\circ)\), the same gate, shifts it by \(-0.4\) m-qg.






Figure 2.1: Milli-qang error of \(R_x(\theta)\) under a random amplitude error \(\sigma=0.05\): the angle as requested against the minimal-area representative. Below \(180^\circ\) they coincide; above it, the short representative avoids the error that, at multiples of \(\pi\), grows with the square of the angle.



More interesting: \(R_{ZZ}(\theta+\pi)=R_{ZZ}(\theta)\,(-i\,Z\otimes Z)\), and \(Z\otimes Z\) is two virtual \(R_Z(\pi)\) rotations, free on superconducting processors. So \(R_{ZZ}\) has period \(\pi\) and its area never needs to exceed \(\pi/2\). The function minimal_area_circuit rewrites a circuit with those representatives and preserves the unitary exactly, global phase included.
On a 4-qubit QAOA model with errors proportional to the area (150 instances), reducing the angles modulo \(2\pi\) cut the total area 4.4× and the error (total variation distance) 4.1×; using the period \(\pi\) of \(R_{ZZ}\) as well cut it another 1.37× in the same ratio of medians. The recorded prediction was about the median of the per-instance ratios, which was 1.14× against 1.5×, and it failed: half of the area, that of the \(R_X\) rotations, was already minimal after the first reduction. The general result stands: the error follows the area. Two scope notes: on IBM processors ordinary single-qubit rotations are virtual \(R_Z\) plus fixed \(\sqrt X\) pulses, of duration independent of the angle, so the rule applies to fractional gates; and the benefit depends on how strongly the error scales with the area on each platform.

2.7 An exposure screen before running
The symmetry filter (Chapters 20–21) discards the shots that left the conserved Hamming-weight sector. But a decay that happens while part of the state is outside the sector can rotate back in and pass the filter. That suggests a prior measure, computable without noise: the exposure, the population outside the sector right after each two-qubit gate (qang.sectors.sector_exposure).
Over 16 compilations of one step of an XXZ chain, the rank correlation between exposure and T1 leak was exactly 0.80, the recorded threshold, and the zero-exposure compilations removed at least 98% of the T1 error (§68):

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
section: 2.8 One qubit order for every kit
text:
2.8 One qubit order for every kit
A practical detail that causes silent errors: Qiskit writes qubit 0 at the right of the bitstring, while Cirq, PennyLane, Braket and pytket put it first. qang.interop converts any result to \(\{(b_0,\dots,b_{n-1}):\text{count}\}\) and computes the qg read-outs on that form: per-qubit \(qg_Z\) with its error, the filter and the register entropy (§130). A 3-qubit W state sampled with 20 000 shots in each kit gave \(qg_Z\) between 0.316 and 0.343 (ideal \(1/3\)), all shots in weight 1 and register entropy 0.528 (ideal \(\log_2 3/3\)), alike in all three. In milli-qang the readings run from 316 to 343 m-qg against 333 ideal; with 20 000 shots the resolution is \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N=6.7\) m-qg, so the largest deviation (\(-17\) m-qg) sits at about 2.6σ: it is shot noise, not a difference between kits.

title: 2  Native gates, closed algebra and the universal operator
text:
2.11 Summary

Preparation by polar bias is native in Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane, with the same convention and a signed variant.
Every single-qubit gate is an algebraic function of \(q=qg_Z\) and two phases; its transition matrix is doubly stochastic, does not depend on the phases and is the probability equation of Chapter 1: a single m-qg number fixes its action on the populations of an input without coherences, and the channel capacity is \(1-qg_S\).
The Cartan subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{su}(d)\) generalizes \(qg_Z\) to qudits as an identity; no advantage of a multi-level readout was shown.
In fractional gates the error follows the pulse area; choosing the shortest representative reduces it (from \(-31.7\) to \(-0.4\) m-qg for \(R_X(324^\circ)\)), and the budget is stated in m-qg, the same scale as the shot noise.
The exposure outside the sector, computed without noise, ranks compilations by how much T1 the filter will let through.

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
text:
3.1 Transition matrices without transcendental functions
Grover’s algorithm is, at heart, a sequence of reflections. Written in qg units, each reflection is an algebraic matrix in the polar bias, the trajectory of the algorithm is a Chebyshev polynomial and the information each iteration brings has a closed form. Everything rests on the base of Chapter 1: the transition probability between two states is a probability like \(p_0\), with its own qang angle and m-qg reading, and the bias of Grover’s flag is read on the same scale. This chapter develops that reading and sets it against what happens when the gates are noisy, where the qg reading loses to the simplest tool.
Chapter 2 showed that every single-qubit gate has the transition matrix
\[
T(q)=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1+q}{2}&\tfrac{1-q}{2}\\[0.5ex]\tfrac{1-q}{2}&\tfrac{1+q}{2}\end{pmatrix},
\]
doubly stochastic and rational in \(q\). By construction it is unistochastic: it comes from a unitary. Its composition shows the difference between classical probability and quantum amplitude. Two classical channels with biases \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) compose by multiplication: \(T(q_1)T(q_2)=T(q_1q_2)\). Two successive quantum rotations instead give
\[
q_{12}=\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)=q_1q_2-\sqrt{(1-q_1^2)(1-q_2^2)} .
\]
The term \(-\sqrt{(1-q_1^2)(1-q_2^2)}\) is the interference: the transverse part of each state, invisible in \(T\), adding up in amplitude. With \(q_1=0.3\) and \(q_2=-0.5\), the classical composition gives \(-0.15\) and the quantum one \(-0.976\): in milli-qang, \(-150\) against \(-976\), an interference of 826 m-qg, close to half the scale. The transition matrix describes each gate on its own, but not the sequence: that needs the phases.

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
section: 3.2 The Householder reflector in qg space
text:
3.2 The Householder reflector in qg space
A reflection with respect to the state \(|\psi\rangle\) is the Householder operator \(I-2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\). For \(|\psi(q)\rangle=\sqrt{\tfrac{1+q}{2}}|0\rangle+\sqrt{\tfrac{1-q}{2}}|1\rangle\) it is
\[
H(q)=I-2|\psi(q)\rangle\langle\psi(q)|=-q\,\sigma_z-\sqrt{1-q^2}\;\sigma_x ,
\]
a Hermitian, unitary matrix with \(H(q)^2=I\), whose coefficients are the state’s own qg values: \(q\) on \(\sigma_z\) and its transverse part \(\sqrt{1-q^2}\) on \(\sigma_x\) (§166). On the Bloch sphere it is the rotation by \(\pi\) about the axis of the state, together with an overall sign change.
crumbs: I. Foundations: the angular–probabilistic metric (the qang unit)
3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
section: 3.3 The Grover diffuser as a qg reflection
text:
3.3 The Grover diffuser as a qg reflection
The Grover diffuser reflects about the initial state: \(D=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I\). Comparing with the previous section,
\[
D(q)=-H(q)=q\,\sigma_z+\sqrt{1-q^2}\;\sigma_x .
\]
In the two-dimensional plane of the algorithm (the “good” state being searched for and the “bad” one, its complement), the oracle is the reflection about the bad axis and the diffuser the reflection about the initial state. The product of two reflections is a rotation by twice the angle between their axes: that is the whole of Grover’s dynamics.
crumbs: I. Foundations: the angular–probabilistic metric (the qang unit)
3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
text:
3.4 Transition probability between qg states
The fidelity of two pure states is written with their qg vectors \(\mathbf r=(qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\):
\[
|\langle\psi_1|\psi_2\rangle|^2=\frac{1+\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf r_2}{2}.
\]
If the two states share a meridian (the same azimuthal phase), it depends on the polar biases alone:
\[
P(q_1\to q_2)=\frac{1+q_1q_2+\sqrt{(1-q_1^2)(1-q_2^2)}}{2}.
\]
The condition matters: with different azimuths the polar biases are not enough and the full transverse part is needed. The formula was checked against the inner product on 200 random pairs (§166).
The transition probability in the equation of Chapter 1. \(P\) is a probability, so it has its own qang readings. If \(\gamma\) is the angle between the two Bloch vectors, \(\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf r_2=\cos\gamma\) and \(P=\cos^2(\gamma/2)\): it is Born’s rule with \(\gamma\) in place of \(\theta\). Therefore
\[
2\arccos\sqrt P=\gamma,\qquad m_P = 2000\,P-1000 = 1000\;\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf r_2\ \text{m-qg}:
\]
the qang angle of the transition probability is the angle between the states, and its milli-qang reading is a thousand times the dot product of their qg vectors. It is Chapter 1’s Wootters statistical distance applied to two states (Section 1.3). With \(q_1=0.3\) and \(q_2=-0.5\) on the same meridian, \(P=0.838\), \(m_P=+676\) m-qg and \(\gamma=0.828\) rad, which is exactly \(|\theta_1-\theta_2|=|\arccos 0.3-\arccos(-0.5)|\).

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
section: 3.5 The Grover trajectory as a Chebyshev polynomial
text:
3.5 The Grover trajectory as a Chebyshev polynomial
Let \(a=\sin^2 t\) be the fraction of good states, read with a flag qubit whose initial bias is \(qg_0=1-2a=\cos 2t\). Each iteration advances the amplitude angle by \(2t\), so after \(k\) iterations the angle is \((2k+1)t\) and
\[
qg_k=\cos\big((2k+1)\,2t\big)=T_{2k+1}(qg_0),
\]
with \(T_m\) the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind, \(T_m(\cos x)=\cos mx\) (§37). By the probability equation, the success probability is \(P_k=(1-qg_k)/2\), and certain success is the pole at \(-1000\) m-qg. For instance, with \(a=0.1\), \(qg_0=0.8\) and the successive iterations give \(+800\), \(-352\), \(-997\) and \(-206\) m-qg: the bias crosses the pole at \(k=2\) (\(P_2=0.9986\)) and then moves away (Figure 3.1).






Figure 3.1: The Grover trajectory in milli-qang: the flag bias samples a cosine at the odd points \((2k+1)\,2t\). With \(a=0.1\) success arrives at \(k=2\); with \(a=0.3\) the angle is coarse, success arrives at \(k=1\) and by \(k=2\) the bias has overshot the pole.



The Chebyshev structure yields for free the one-shot Fisher information at depth \(m=2k+1\). Since \(T_m'=mU_{m-1}\) and \(1-T_m^2=(1-q^2)U_{m-1}^2\),
\[
F_m=\frac{m^2}{1-qg_0^2}:
\]
depth multiplies the qg information of Chapter 1 by \(m^2\), uniformly along the fringe. It is the qg form of the known factor \(4m^2\) for the angle (Suzuki et al. 2020). On the milli-qang scale, the resolution on \(qg_0\) with \(N\) shots at depth \(m\) is \(1000\sqrt{1-qg_0^2}/(m\sqrt N)\) m-qg: with \(a=0.1\) and 100 shots, 60 m-qg without iterating and 12 m-qg at depth \(m=5\).

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
section: 3.6 Analytic limits: coarse angles and overshoot
text:
3.6 Analytic limits: coarse angles and overshoot
The optimal number of iterations is \(k^\ast=\operatorname{round}\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{4t}-\tfrac12\big)\). When the searched fraction \(a=M/N\) is small, \(t\) is small, \(k^\ast\approx\tfrac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N/M}\) and the rounding hardly matters. When \(M/N\) is not negligible, the angle per iteration is coarse: the bias jumps in large steps along the curve \(\cos((2k+1)2t)\) and can overshoot the pole. Iterating more does not help; it hurts, because the rotation keeps going. The qg reading makes this behaviour visible: \(qg_k\) samples a cosine at odd points. With \(a=0.3\), \(k^\ast=1\) gives \(-944\) m-qg (\(P=0.972\)) and one more iteration jumps to \(+884\) m-qg (\(P=0.058\)), the orange curve of Figure 3.1.

3.6.1 Grover with noise
With noisy gates the picture changes, and it is worth recording as it came out (§63). In searches on 4 to 6 qubits, with each multi-controlled Z compiled to 14, 36 and 84 CNOTs and depolarizing noise on every CNOT:

Noise moves the best iteration earlier and eats the speed-up. With \(n=6\) and \(p_2=0.005\) the best iteration drops from 4 to 1 and the cost per verified success rises from 6.1 to 27.6 oracle calls, against 32 for classical search.
The qg formula fails under gate noise. If the unmarked outcomes were uniform, each qubit would have \(qg_{Z,i}=\pm(NP-1)/(N-1)\), and the signs would give the answer and the magnitude the success probability without knowing it. Depolarizing noise is not uniform after the diffuser, and the label-free estimate was worse than the frequency of the most common outcome in every case.
Reading the answer from signs loses. With \(n=5\), 100 shots find the marked item 66% of the time with the qg signs and 91% with the most frequent bitstring.

The honest balance: in Grover search the outcome histogram is a better estimator than the per-qubit qg reading. qg provides the Chebyshev picture and the information factor, not a better estimator.

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
text:
3.7 Amplitude estimation
Where the Chebyshev structure does pay off is in amplitude estimation: using increasing depths to estimate \(a\) with fewer oracle queries than direct sampling. With maximum-likelihood estimation (depths 0, 1, 2, 4, …, 100 shots each), without noise, the error falls as queries\(^{-0.93\ldots-1.12}\) against queries\(^{-0.5}\) for Monte Carlo, and is 8.4–9.3 times lower at 26 200 queries (§37).
Noise sets limits. With depolarization \(p=0.01\) per iteration, a likelihood that ignores the noise ends worse than Monte Carlo (\(6.8\cdot10^{-3}\) against \(2.7\cdot10^{-3}\)), while one that includes it keeps a 4× advantage. With \(p=0.05\), not even the noise-aware likelihood beats Monte Carlo: beyond a depth of order \(1/p\) the iterations carry almost no signal.
On IonQ’s calibrated noisy simulator (3 qubits, \(a=0.3\), 36 000 queries), the estimate was accurate, with an RMS error of 0.0005–0.0015 and a fitted visibility of 0.965–0.985 per iteration, and 7 to 30 times better than a realistic Monte Carlo, whose depth-zero circuit is biased by the device noise (§39).

title: 3  Reflections, Householder and Grover dynamics
text:
3.10 Summary

The transition matrix of a gate is rational in \(q\), but it does not compose like the gate: the difference between \(q_1q_2\) and \(\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\) is the interference.
The Householder reflector and the Grover diffuser are \(\mp(q\,\sigma_z+\sqrt{1-q^2}\,\sigma_x)\).
The transition probability between two states is \((1+\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf r_2)/2\); on a common meridian it depends on the polar biases alone. Read with the equation of Chapter 1, its qang angle is the angle between the states and its reading is \(1000\,\mathbf r_1\cdot\mathbf r_2\) m-qg.
The Grover trajectory is \(qg_k=T_{2k+1}(qg_0)\), with certain success at \(-1000\) m-qg, and the Fisher information at depth \(m\) is \(m^2/(1-qg_0^2)\): the m-qg resolution improves by a factor \(m\).
With noise, the per-qubit qg reading loses to the histogram in search; in amplitude estimation the advantage holds if the noise enters the likelihood, and ends near depth \(1/p\).

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.1 Propagating shot noise
Every number a quantum processor delivers is an estimate made from a finite number of shots. This chapter gathers the statistical tools of the qg unit: how shot noise propagates, which prior is the natural one for an unknown qubit, how to build intervals that do not collapse near the poles, how to correct the bias of quadratic quantities and how many shots to plan for. All of them rest on the base of Chapter 1: what is estimated is always the probability \(p_0\), and since the milli-qang is linear in it, every interval and every shot plan is stated directly in m-qg. It closes with the mathematical foundation that explains why \(qg_Z\) is the canonical read-out.
With \(N\) shots and \(k_0\) outcomes 0, the natural estimator is \(\widehat{qg}_Z=2k_0/N-1\). It is unbiased and its variance is exactly
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{qg}_Z)=\frac{1-qg_Z^2}{N}=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{N},
\]
which attains the Cramér–Rao bound for the parameter \(qg_Z\): no unbiased estimator does better with the same information. In milli-qang it is the resolution \(\sigma_m=1000\sqrt{1-qg_Z^2}/\sqrt N\) of Chapter 1 (Figure 1.3). Propagated to the angle by the delta method, the variance becomes constant, \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)
\approx1/N\), as seen in Chapter 1 (§5). The two statements are compatible: \(qg_Z\) is the curved coordinate, with Fisher information \(1/(1-qg_Z^2)\) per shot, and \(\theta\) the flat one, with information 1 (Chapter 23).
The delta method is a first-order approximation and fails where the derivative vanishes. Near a pole, \(\widehat{qg}_Z\) is exactly \(\pm1\) in a sizeable fraction of experiments, and the estimated standard error \(\sqrt{(1-\widehat{qg}_Z^2)/N}\) becomes zero: the interval collapses exactly where the state is most extreme.

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
section: 4.2 The Haar distribution in qg space
text:
4.2 The Haar distribution in qg space
What is known about a qubit before it is measured? If its state is “any state”, the natural distribution is the Haar measure, the only one invariant under rotations. In qg units it takes a remarkable form: \(qg_Z\) is uniform on \([-1,1]\). This is Archimedes’ hat-box theorem: the area of a band of the sphere between two latitudes is proportional to the difference of heights, not of angles. It was checked on 200 000 Haar states (§15).
The statistical consequence is direct. A uniform prior on \(qg_Z\) is equivalent to \(p_0\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\), and with \(k_0\) zeros in \(N\) shots the posterior is
\[
p_0\mid k_0\ \sim\ \mathrm{Beta}(k_0+1,\ N-k_0+1),
\]
from which a credible interval for \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\) follows with a beta function alone (bayes_qg_estimate, implemented without external dependencies and checked against scipy.stats.beta).
The probability equation of Chapter 1 explains why this prior is so simple. Since \(m=2000\,p_0-1000\) is linear, a distribution uniform in \(qg_Z\) is uniform in milli-qang and uniform in \(p_0\): the three statements are one. In the angle, by contrast, the same measure has density \(\tfrac12\sin\theta\) and piles up at the equator (Figure 4.1). The “uninformative” prior depends on the scale it is written in, and Haar’s is flat exactly on the scale that is measured.






Figure 4.1: Two hundred thousand Haar states read in milli-qang (left) and in angle (right). The dashed line is the theoretical density: \(1/2000\) per m-qg and \(\tfrac12\sin\theta\) in the angle.

Near the pole the delta method covers the true value in fewer than one experiment in ten; Wilson and the Haar posterior recover the nominal coverage. On Haar states the posterior mean has a 4% lower mean squared error than the raw frequency.
Figure 4.2 shows the cause in milli-qang. With 50 shots, the width of the delta-method interval drops to zero at the ends of the scale: with 50 zeros in 50 shots it gives \([+1000,+1000]\) m-qg, an interval with no width. With 48 zeros it gives \([+811,+1029]\) m-qg, which runs off the top of the scale. Wilson gives \([+731,+978]\) and Bayes–Haar \(+885\) \([+731,+975]\) m-qg: widths that do not collapse and stay inside \([-1000,+1000]\).






Figure 4.2: Width of the 95 % interval with 50 shots, in milli-qang, against the estimate. The delta method collapses at the poles; Wilson and Bayes–Haar do not.



The honest reading of the table has two parts. The Haar prior repairs the collapse of the delta method and has a clean geometric justification; but the Wilson interval, standard in statistics, achieves the same coverage, and the gain over good frequentist practice is in the point estimate and is modest. The qg unit does not reduce the number of shots a given precision requires; what it brings is making the cost explicit and choosing the interval well.

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.4 Second-order unbiased estimators
Quadratic quantities have a systematic bias. The plug-in estimator \(\widehat{qg}^{\,2}\) overestimates \(qg^2\) by \((1-qg^2)/N\), because shot noise always adds variance. The correction is exact:
\[
\widehat{qg^2}=\frac{N\,\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1}{N-1},\qquad \mathbb E\big[\widehat{qg^2}\big]=qg^2 ,
\]
valid for \(N\ge2\) (qg2_unbiased). It can go negative when \(qg\approx0\), the price of being unbiased. With \(N=20\) and \(qg=0.6\), the plug-in estimator averages 0.390 and the corrected one 0.358, against the true value 0.36.
It matters because the Bloch radius of Chapter 5, \(r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2\), is a sum of squares: without the correction each axis adds its bias, and an entangled state looks purer than it is (§97). The same correction enters the reading of the gravitational redshift with two clocks (§126, Chapter 8).

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.5 Planning the shots
The inverse relation, how many shots a given error needs, is the one used when preparing an experiment. plan_shots turns a target standard error of the filtered \(qg_Z\) into shots and estimated processor seconds, taking into account the fraction of shots the filter will keep (§143). For a target of 0.02 (20 m-qg) on two circuits per device it planned 3000–3400 shots, and over 30 repetitions the error of the worst qubit was 0.021–0.023 (21–23 m-qg): the plan held. For reference, Chapter 1’s formula without the filter gives \(N=(1000\sin\theta/\delta)^2=2500\) shots for 20 m-qg on the equator; the plan asks for more because it discounts the shots the filter will discard.
The per-qubit prediction, however, was 1.4–1.6 times optimistic on average, and its analysis is instructive: the qubits that missed were those near a pole (\(|qg|>0.8\), with ratios of 2.4–3.1), whose \(qg_Z\) the noise pulls away from \(\pm1\) and whose real variance is larger than the ideal one. The plan uses the worst qubit and therefore holds; the safe option, assuming no value of qg, is to plan for the worst case, \(qg=0\).

Would classical shadows (random Pauli measurements) do better than measuring the bases directly? For the quantities qang uses, no (§62). They only match direct measurement when the target is all one- and two-qubit quantities at once. And the shot-level filter does not exist with shadows: only \(3^{-6}=0.14\%\) of the random shots have every qubit measured in \(Z\).

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.7 The foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
A conceptual question remains: why \(qg_Z\) and not some other function of the populations? The operators of an \(n\)-qubit register form a finite-dimensional Hilbert space under the Hilbert–Schmidt product \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger B)\), and density matrices live in it. The Riesz–Fréchet representation theorem says that every continuous linear functional \(f\) on a Hilbert space has the form \(f(x)=\langle y_f,x\rangle\) for a unique \(y_f\); in finite dimension continuity is automatic and the theorem reduces to linear algebra (Appendix F).
The application is immediate. \(\rho\mapsto qg_Z(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\) is linear in \(\rho\), so it has a unique representative, \(\sigma_z\). Every linear read-out of a state (an expectation value, a population, a per-shot average) has that form, and \(qg_Z\) is the one whose representative is the \(Z\) observable. By contrast, \(qg_S(\rho)=H(\langle0|\rho|0\rangle)\) is strictly concave in \(\rho\): no operator represents it. Two properties already seen follow from this structural fact: linear functionals have unbiased sample-mean estimators and the entropy does not (Jensen’s inequality), and the identity \(qg_S=H((1+qg_Z)/2)\) shows that \(qg_S\) carries no information about the state beyond what the representative of \(qg_Z\) already extracts.
The milli-qang inherits this property: \(m(\rho)=1000\,\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\) is linear too, with representative \(1000\,\sigma_z\), which is why its estimator is the shot average, without bias. It is the underlying reason Chapter 1 defined the unit on probability and not on angle: \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\) is not linear in \(\rho\), has no representative and its direct estimator is biased.

title: 4  Sampling statistics, Bayesian inference and the Haar distribution
text:
4.10 Summary

\(\widehat{qg}_Z\) is unbiased and attains the Cramér–Rao bound; the delta method collapses near the poles, where its m-qg interval loses its width or runs off the scale.
Under the Haar measure \(qg_Z\) is uniform on \([-1,1]\), that is, uniform in milli-qang and in \(p_0\); the matching prior is \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) and gives exact intervals with a beta function.
Wilson and Bayes–Haar recover the nominal coverage where the delta method covers less than 10%; neither reduces the shots required.
Quadratic quantities need the correction \((N\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1)/(N-1)\); without it, Bloch radii are overestimated.
Planning on the worst qubit meets the target; the qubits near a pole are the ones the noise pulls away most.
For qang’s quantities, measuring directly in \(Z\) costs 3–41 times fewer shots than classical shadows.
\(qg_Z\), and with it the milli-qang, is the canonical linear read-out by the Riesz–Fréchet theorem; \(qg_S\) and the angle are not linear and have no representative.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.1 The probability equation with a radius
Part I treated the qubit as a point on the surface of the sphere: a pure state, a probability \(p_0\) and its four readings. A qubit that belongs to a register is almost never pure: it is mixed by noise or by its entanglement with the others, and it sits inside the sphere. This chapter adds to the base of Chapter 1 the missing quantity, the local radius \(r\), and shows that the probability equation still holds with a single change: the polar bias is no longer \(\cos\theta\) but \(r\cos\theta\). From the radius come an entanglement measure, a way to separate the direction of the state from its purity, and wave–particle duality, all read in qg units.
For a qubit in a mixed state, its Bloch vector \((qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\) has length \(r\le1\), and Born’s rule in the \(Z\) basis reads
\[
p_0=\frac{1+qg_Z}{2}=\frac{1+r\cos\theta}{2}.
\]
It is the probability equation of Chapter 1 with the radius inside: the readings \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\) and \(m=2000\,p_0-1000\) m-qg do not change, but they no longer fix the angle, because the same \(p_0\) can come from a tilted pure state or from a mixed one closer to the pole. Each axis has its own probability, \(p_0^{(a)}\) in the basis \(a\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), and the squared radius is the sum of the three readings squared (§97):
\[
r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2=\frac{m_X^2+m_Y^2+m_Z^2}{10^6}=2\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2-1 .
\]
The radius is linear in the purity \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2\): it is 1 on the surface (pure state) and 0 at the centre (maximally mixed state). The sphere of radius \(r\) has area \(4\pi r^2\), and the surface deficit \(4\pi(1-r^2)\) is the area the qubit has lost; the library works with \(1-r^2\), which carries the same information.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
section: 5.2 The deficit as an entanglement measure
text:
5.2 The deficit as an entanglement measure
If the whole register is in a pure state, all the radius a qubit lacks is due to its entanglement with the rest. Then \(1-r_q^2=4\det\rho_q\) is the one-tangle of qubit \(q\), which for two qubits is the squared concurrence (Coffman et al. 2000), and its mean over the qubits is the global entanglement of Meyer and Wallach (2002):
\[
Q=\frac1n\sum_q\left(1-r_q^2\right).
\]
Two examples set the scale. In the Bell state each qubit sits at the centre of its sphere, \(r=0\), and \(Q=1\). In the 3-qubit W state each has \(r^2=1/9\) and \(Q=0.889\). If the global state is mixed, the deficit mixes entanglement and noise and cannot separate them: the radius measures entanglement only when the register is known, or guaranteed, to be pure. Reading \(r^2\) takes three measurement settings for the whole register (every qubit in \(X\), in \(Y\) and in \(Z\)), not three per qubit.

5.3 The radius under gates and algorithms
A single-qubit gate rotates the sphere and preserves the radius, also for mixed qubits. SWAP exchanges the radii of two qubits. CNOT, CZ, iSWAP, Toffoli and Fredkin can take a qubit of a product input to the centre (\(r=0\), from inputs of the type \(|{+}0\rangle\) or \(|{+}{+}\rangle\)) and can also bring it back to the surface; on computational-basis states they create no deficit, because they act as classical permutations (§97). section: 5.4 Definite weight: the radius from the Z basis
text:
5.4 Definite weight: the radius from the Z basis
In a state of definite Hamming weight every local \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\) is zero, so \(r_q=|qg_Z^{(q)}|\) and the radius is read from \(Z\) shots alone. With the probability equation, the deficit becomes
\[
1-r^2=1-\left(\frac{m}{1000}\right)^2=4\,p_0\,(1-p_0):
\]
four times the binomial variance of the outcome, the same \(p_0(1-p_0)\) that governs the shot noise of Chapter 1. Figure 5.1 shows it on the milli-qang scale. The deficit is zero at the poles, largest on the equator and very sensitive near a pole: a qubit at 990 m-qg has a deficit of 0.02, and one at 800 m-qg, which is what 10 % of misplaced shots on a basis state gives, already reads 0.36.






Figure 5.1: The deficit of a definite-weight qubit against its milli-qang reading (bottom) and its probability (top). Near a pole, a few misplaced shots produce a large deficit.



This is where the symmetry filter (Chapters 20–21) and the radius meet. Under equal T1 on every qubit the filtered state is the noiseless pure state, so the filtered deficit is an exact entanglement measure. The predictions were committed before running (§98); on RBS circuits of 4 and 6 qubits:

On product states the filtered deficit is exactly 0 under all three noise models, while the raw read-out shows 0.60–0.95 on every excited qubit from decay alone: false entanglement. One prediction failed: the raw error was expected to be smaller at half filling, and it was larger (0.177 against 0.074), because the first-order cancellation holds only at exactly \(p=1/2\).
On noise models of real devices (three from IBM and two from IonQ, §100), the filter cut the error of the deficit 3.2–4.0× where the deficit is large, but it did not work as a test of “no entanglement”: on a product state it removed only 15–33 % of the false deficit. The cause is the one in Figure 5.1: errors inside the sector leave 10–21 % of misplaced shots, and near the pole that already reads as 0.36. A small deficit needs an echo calibration before it is interpreted.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.5 Direction and radius apart
The polar bias \(qg_Z=r\cos\theta\) mixes the direction of the vector with its length. The usual reading \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)\) drifts towards the equator whenever noise shortens the vector. With the radius the two separate (§102):
\[
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2},\,qg_Z\right)=\arccos\frac{qg_Z}{r}.
\]
A state at \(30^\circ\) shortened to \(r=0.8\) by depolarizing noise has \(qg_Z=0.693\): \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) reads \(46.1^\circ\), and the separated angle reads the true \(30^\circ\). Figure 5.2 shows the effect for several radii: the naive angle flattens towards \(90^\circ\), and the separated one does not depend on \(r\).






Figure 5.2: The angle read against the true direction. The dashed curves are \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) for shortened vectors; the straight line is the angle separated from the radius, exact for any \(r\) under depolarizing noise.



The separation has a cost and does not always win. With the same total number of shots split over three bases:

Depolarizing: the separated angle is exact and \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) errs by up to 0.70 rad near the poles; with shots, the root-mean-square error drops 5.8×.
Dephasing: this is where it loses. Dephasing does not shorten \(qg_Z\), so \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) is exact, and the separated angle is pulled 0.03–0.12 rad towards the poles.
No noise: measuring three bases costs 1.6× in root-mean-square error.
Devices: on the IBM models the vector shrinks almost uniformly and the separated angle is 5–9× more accurate. On IonQ, \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) won at first, because the compiler had removed pairs of identical CX gates; in the native gate set the separated angle wins there too, 8.7–9.0× (§103).

The practical rule: if the measured radius is close to 1, use \(\arccos(qg_Z)\) with all shots in \(Z\); if it is clearly below 1 and the noise is not pure dephasing, use the separated angle.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.6 Wave–particle duality and entropic uncertainty
The radius also orders a classical result of the foundations. The predictability \(P=|qg_Z|=|m|/1000\) measures how much is known about the path (particle) and the visibility \(V=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2}\) measures the contrast of the interference (wave). Their relation is exactly the radius (Greenberger and Yasin 1988; Englert 1996):
\[
P^2+V^2=r^2\le1 .
\]
The duality inequality is, in qg units, the statement that the state lies inside the sphere, and it is an equality for pure states (Figure 5.3). A state at \(60^\circ\) with \(r=0.9\) has \(P=0.45\), \(V=0.779\) and \(P^2+V^2=0.81\). It was checked on 2000 random states with a largest deviation of \(2.2\cdot10^{-16}\) (§127).






Figure 5.3: Wave–particle duality in qg units: each state is a point of the quarter disc, at distance \(r\) from the origin. Pure states lie on the arc \(r=1\).



The entropic version uses Chapter 1’s spread \(qg_S\) in two bases. The Maassen–Uffink relation, with the correction of Berta and co-workers for mixed states, says
\[
qg_S(Z)+qg_S(X)\ \ge\ 1+S(\rho),\qquad S(\rho)=H\!\left(\frac{1+r}{2}\right).
\]
For the state above the sum is 1.349 and the bound 1.286. The bound is tight: the state \(|0\rangle\) meets it with equality. That gives a practical warning. With plain (uncorrected) entropy estimates, a pure state seems to violate the relation in 93 % of runs at 100 shots, because the estimated entropy is biased downwards; with the Miller–Madow correction, in 37 %. A test of the bound needs corrected estimators or intervals, like those of Chapter 4.

text:
5.7 Estimating the radius from shots
Since \(r^2\) is a sum of squares, it inherits the bias of the quadratic estimators of Chapter 4 (Section 4.4): each axis adds \((1-qg^2)/N\), and an entangled state looks purer than it is. The exact correction \((N\widehat{qg}^{\,2}-1)/(N-1)\) is applied axis by axis (radius2_estimate), and in a definite-weight state the \(Z\) axis is enough.

title: 5  The local Bloch radius as a measure of purity and entanglement
text:
5.10 Summary

For a mixed state, Chapter 1’s probability equation still holds with \(qg_Z=r\cos\theta\); the local radius \(r^2=qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2=2\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2-1\) is the missing reading.
If the register is pure, the deficit \(1-r^2\) is the one-tangle and its mean is the Meyer–Wallach measure; with a mixed global state, it mixes entanglement and noise.
At definite weight, \(1-r^2=4p_0(1-p_0)\) is read in \(Z\) alone, and with the filter under equal T1 it is exact; near a pole a few misplaced shots inflate it, and on devices a small deficit needs calibration.
\(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z/r)\) separates direction from purity: it wins under depolarizing noise and loses under pure dephasing.
Wave–particle duality is \(P^2+V^2=r^2\), and entropic uncertainty bounds \(qg_S(Z)+qg_S(X)\) by \(1+S(\rho)\).

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.1 Malus’s law as a probability equation
The polarization of a photon is a qubit, and classical polarization optics is, unchanged, the physics of a qubit written with other names. This chapter reads that optics with the base of Chapter 1. The key piece is that a polarizer is a two-outcome measurement, pass or block, and its transmission is exactly the probability \(p_0\) of the qang equation. From there follow Malus’s law, the Stokes parameters, the degree of polarization and photon-counting polarimetry, all in qg and in milli-qang (§83).
Light linearly polarized at an angle \(\alpha\) goes through a polarizer set at \(\vartheta\). With \(\Delta=\vartheta-\alpha\), the transmitted fraction is Malus’s law, which for a single photon is a probability:
\[
p_0=\cos^2\Delta .
\]
The comparison with Born’s rule in Chapter 1, \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\), is immediate: the qang angle is twice the physical angle, \(\theta=2\Delta\), and the milli-qang reading is \(m=1000\cos2\Delta\). That is why two orthogonal polarizations, H and V, \(90^\circ\) apart in the laboratory, are opposite points of the sphere, \(180^\circ\) apart (Figure 6.1). An analyser turned \(30^\circ\) from the light transmits \(p_0=0.75\): it is the state at \(\theta=60^\circ\) and \(+500\) m-qg of Chapter 1’s qang circle (Figure 1.1).
For light with any polarization, pure or partial, the transmission through a linear polarizer at \(\vartheta\) is
\[
p_0=\frac{1+qg_Z\cos2\vartheta+qg_X\sin2\vartheta}{2}=\frac{1+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a}{2},
\qquad \mathbf a=(\sin2\vartheta,\,0,\,\cos2\vartheta),
\]
with \(\mathbf r=(qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\) the qg vector of the light and \(\mathbf a\) that of the state the analyser lets through. It is Chapter 3’s transition probability between two qg vectors (Section 3.4), and its milli-qang reading is \(m=1000\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a\). Figure 6.2 shows four cases: H light (\(\cos^2\vartheta\)), D light (the same curve shifted \(45^\circ\)), unpolarized light (always \(\tfrac12\), that is, 0 m-qg) and partially polarized light with \(qg_Z=0.6\) and \(qg_X=0.3\). The last transmits 0.80 at \(0^\circ\), a maximum of 0.835 at \(13.3^\circ\) and a minimum of 0.165 at \(103.3^\circ\); the difference between maximum and minimum, 0.671, is its degree of polarization.

The Poincaré sphere is the Bloch sphere. With \(|H\rangle=|0\rangle\) and \(|V\rangle=|1\rangle\), the normalized Stokes parameters are the three qg values, each the difference of the two probabilities of an analyser:

The convention for right circular light varies between texts; here \(R=(|H\rangle+i|V\rangle)/\sqrt2\), so \(S_3>0\) means \(qg_Y>0\) (the library takes the opposite convention with circular_sign=-1). Since each parameter is \(2p_0-1\) in its own basis, each is expressed in milli-qang with the equation of Chapter 1.
The polarization ellipse is read from the angles of the qg vector, halved: its orientation is \(\psi=\tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(qg_X,qg_Z)\) and its ellipticity \(\chi=\tfrac12\arcsin(qg_Y/P)\). For the partial light of the example, \(\psi=13.3^\circ\): the angle where Figure 6.2 has its maximum.

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.3 Degree of polarization and purity
Partially polarized light is a mixed state. Its degree of polarization is the length of the qg vector, the radius of Chapter 5 (Section 5.1):
\[
P=\sqrt{qg_X^2+qg_Y^2+qg_Z^2}=r,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=\frac{1+P^2}{2}.
\]
Unpolarized light sits at the centre of the sphere. An ideal depolarizer has Mueller matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,d,d,d)\): it shortens the vector by a factor \(d\) and does not change its direction. It is the case in which Chapter 5 separates direction and radius (Section 5.5): with \(d=0.7\), the light of the example goes from \(P=0.671\) to \(P=0.470\), and the orientation of its ellipse stays at \(13.3^\circ\).

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
section: 6.4 Lossless elements: the Mueller matrix is the gate rule
text:
6.4 Lossless elements: the Mueller matrix is the gate rule
A Mueller matrix acts on \((S_0,S_1,S_2,S_3)\); in the order \((I,Z,X,Y)\) it is the Pauli transfer matrix. For a lossless element, with a unitary Jones matrix \(U\), it is exactly qang’s gate rule:
\[
qg'_P=qg_{U^\dagger P U}.
\]
Wave plates are single-qubit gates, and Chapter 2 applies as is (Section 2.3): a half-wave plate with its axis at \(22.5^\circ\) takes H to D (\(qg_X=1\)), because it turns the physical polarization by \(45^\circ\) and the point on the sphere by \(90^\circ\); a quarter-wave plate at \(45^\circ\) takes H to a circular polarization (\(qg_Y=-1\) with the convention above). The polarizer, by contrast, is not unitary: it is the measurement. All these identities are checked numerically in tests/test_polarization.py.
crumbs: II. Local geometry, quantum optics and geometric phases
6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.5 Photon-counting polarimetry
With weak or single-photon sources, the Stokes parameters are estimated by counting: \(n_H,n_V\) in the H/V basis, \(n_D,n_A\) in the diagonal one and \(n_R,n_L\) in the circular one. Each pair gives a qg value with its interval, just like a qubit measurement (Chapter 4). With 1000 photons per basis and counts \((800,200)\), \((650,350)\) and \((500,500)\):
\[
qg_Z=0.599\ [0.548,\,0.647],\quad qg_X=0.299\ [0.240,\,0.358],\quad qg_Y=0.000\ [-0.062,\,0.062],
\]
95 % Bayes–Haar intervals. In milli-qang, \(qg_Z\) is \(+599\) m-qg with a resolution of \(\sigma_m=1000\sin\theta/\sqrt N=25\) m-qg.
The degree of polarization needs more care. \(P\) is the square root of a sum of squares, and each square inherits the bias \((1-qg^2)/N\) of Chapter 4 (Section 4.4): with few photons, unpolarized light looks polarized. Figure 6.3 quantifies it with a simulation from this chapter (4000 repetitions per point). With unpolarized light, the plug-in estimator averages \(\hat P\approx0.50\) with 10 photons per basis, \(0.16\) with 100 and \(0.05\) with 1000. Using the unbiased squares brings it down about three times (\(\approx0.18\), \(0.055\) and \(0.017\)), but does not remove it: the square root and the clipping at zero leave a residual bias. With light of \(P=0.5\), the plug-in estimator overestimates at few photons and the unbiased one slightly underestimates; from about 200 photons per basis both match the true value.






Figure 6.3: Bias of the degree of polarization estimated by counting, against the photons per basis. Solid lines: plug-in estimator; dashed: with the unbiased squares of Chapter 4. The horizontal dotted lines mark the true value.



The practical consequence: to claim that a source is polarized from few photons, one needs an interval for \(P\) or a threshold calibrated with unpolarized light, not the point value.

title: 6  Optical polarization and Stokes parameters in qg units
text:
6.8 Summary

A polarizer is a two-outcome measurement: its transmission is \(p_0=\cos^2\Delta\), Chapter 1’s probability equation with the qang angle equal to twice the physical one, \(\theta=2\Delta\).
For any light, Malus’s law is the transition probability \((1+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a)/2\) between the light and the analyser; its reading is \(1000\,\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf a\) m-qg.
The normalized Stokes parameters are \(qg_Z\), \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\); the ellipse is read from half the angles of the qg vector.
The degree of polarization is the radius of Chapter 5; a depolarizer shortens it without turning the ellipse.
Wave plates are gates: the lossless Mueller matrix is the rule \(qg'_P=qg_{U^\dagger PU}\).
From photon counts each parameter has its interval; the degree of polarization is biased upwards at few photons, and the unbiased squares cut that bias about three times without removing it.

title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
text:
7.1 The Berry connection and curvature
A phase is not a probability. Chapter 2 showed that the phases of a gate do not appear in its transition matrix: a \(Z\) measurement does not see them. This chapter deals with a phase that does carry physical meaning, the geometric phase a qubit picks up when carried around a closed loop, and shows that the base of Chapter 1 reaches it twice. First, its value: for a loop at constant height, the phase in turns is the probability \(p_0\). Then, its measurement: an interferometer turns it into a probability, and the qang angle of that probability is the phase (§84).
If a state \(|\psi(\mathbf R)\rangle\) depends on parameters \(\mathbf R\) and is carried slowly around a closed path, besides the dynamical phase it picks up a phase that depends only on the geometry of the path. Its density is the Berry connection, \(\mathbf A=i\langle\psi|\nabla\psi\rangle\), and its curl is the curvature. For a qubit, with the state described by its qg vector on the sphere, the curvature is a monopole of strength \(\tfrac12\) at the centre: on the unit sphere its normal component is \(\tfrac12\) everywhere.
crumbs: II. Local geometry, quantum optics and geometric phases
7  Geometric phases and Stokes' theorem on the sphere

title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
text:
7.2 Stokes on the sphere
Stokes’ theorem turns the line integral of the connection around the loop \(C\) into the flux of the curvature through the surface it encloses. Since the curvature is uniform, the flux is \(\tfrac12\) times the area, that is, the solid angle \(\Omega(C)\):
\[
\gamma(C)=-\frac{\Omega(C)}{2}\pmod{2\pi}.
\]
The phase is gauge invariant (it does not depend on the phase chosen for each state along the path) and changes sign when the loop is run backwards.

title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
section: 7.3 Loops at constant height: the phase is the probability
text:
7.3 Loops at constant height: the phase is the probability
A loop around the \(Z\) axis at constant polar bias \(qg_Z\) encloses the cap above it, of solid angle \(\Omega=2\pi(1-qg_Z)\). In turns, the library’s \(qg_\Phi\) unit,
\[
\varphi=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}=\frac{qg_Z-1}{2}=-p_1\equiv p_0\pmod 1 ,
\qquad \varphi=\frac{1000+m}{2000}\ \text{turns}.
\]
The geometric phase of a loop at constant height, measured in turns, is the probability \(p_0\) of its height, and with the milli-qang it is a linear function of the reading. The reason is the same that made the Haar distribution uniform in Chapter 4 (Section 4.2): by Archimedes’ theorem, the fraction of the sphere in the cap above the height \(qg_Z\) is \((1-qg_Z)/2=p_1\). The solid angle is \(4\pi p_1\) and the phase \(-2\pi p_1\).
Some values: a loop at \(+500\) m-qg (\(p_0=0.75\)) picks up \(0.75\) turns, that is, \(-\tfrac14\) of a turn; one on the equator picks up half a turn, \(\pi\); one hugging the pole \(|0\rangle\), nothing. Figure 7.1 shows the line together with the three independent computations of the next section.






Figure 7.1: The geometric phase of a loop at constant height against its milli-qang reading (bottom) and its probability (top). The line is \(\varphi=p_0\); the symbols are the three independent computations.



The equator deserves a note. There the phase is \(\pi\), and \(+\pi\) and \(-\pi\) are the same angle. A numerical computation can return either one depending on rounding, and a comparison that ignores this fails although the result is right. That is exactly what happened to one of the library’s tests, now fixed to compare on the circle.

7  Geometric phases and Stokes' theorem on the sphere

title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
text:
7.4 Three independent computations
The library computes the phase in three ways that share no code and checks that they agree (14 tests):

Overlap product (Pancharatnam): \(\gamma=-\arg\prod_k\langle\psi_k|\psi_{k+1}\rangle\) over the discretized loop, gauge invariant.
Solid angle, as a fan of spherical triangles (Van Oosterom and Strackee’s formula). It agrees with the overlap product to \(10^{-10}\).
Curvature flux through the cap, integrated numerically. It agrees with the line integral to \(10^{-5}\): Stokes’ theorem checked in numbers.
