title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
section: 7.5 Measuring the phase: the interferometer and the probability equation
text:
7.5 Measuring the phase: the interferometer and the probability equation
A \(Z\) measurement does not see the phase. Measuring it takes an interferometer: a control qubit in \(|+\rangle\) decides whether the system runs the loop, and at the end the control is measured in the \(X\) basis (Hadamard test). With the dynamical phase cancelled, for instance by an echo, the probability of reading 0 on the control is
\[
p_0=\frac{1+\cos\gamma}{2}=\cos^2\frac{\gamma}{2}:
\]
Born’s rule of Chapter 1 with \(\gamma\) in place of \(\theta\). Therefore the qang angle of the measured probability is the geometric phase, \(\hat\gamma=2\arccos\sqrt{\hat p_0}\), and its milli-qang reading is \(m=1000\cos\gamma\).
Everything the base says about that angle applies to the phase. In particular, being the arcsine transformation (Section 1.8), its uncertainty is \(1/\sqrt N\) for any value of the phase. Figure 7.2 checks it with a simulation from this chapter: with 1000 shots per point, the standard deviation of \(\hat\gamma\) stays around 32 mrad (about \(1.8^\circ\)) from \(10^\circ\) to \(170^\circ\). At \(0\) and \(\pi\) it is zero because the outcome is deterministic, always 0 or always 1, and there the exact intervals of Chapter 4 are needed.






Figure 7.2: Interferometric measurement of the geometric phase with the probability equation. Left: the phase estimated as the qang angle of the measured probability, against the true one. Right: its standard deviation, equal to \(1/\sqrt N\) over the whole range.



There is a limit, the same as in Chapter 1. Since \(\cos\gamma\) is even, a single probability gives \(|\gamma|\) in \([0,\pi]\), not its sign. The remedy is the branch sign (Section 1.5): measure the other quadrature too, shifting the reference phase by a quarter turn, which gives \(\sin\gamma\). The two probabilities together fix the phase on the whole circle.

title: 7  Geometric phases and Stokes’ theorem on the sphere
text:
7.6 Pancharatnam’s phase and the octant
For polarized light the same phase is Pancharatnam’s on the Poincaré sphere, and Chapter 6 already set up the coordinates (Section 6.1). The circuit H → D → R → H runs around an octant of the sphere: three quarter arcs of great circles enclosing one eighth of its area, \(\Omega=4\pi/8=\pi/2\). The phase is \(\gamma=-\pi/4\), one eighth of a turn backwards (\(0.875\) turns mod 1), and the library reproduces it from the three qg vectors.

7.9 Summary

The geometric phase of a closed loop is minus half the solid angle it encloses: Stokes’ theorem with the Berry curvature, a monopole of strength \(\tfrac12\).
For a loop at constant height, the phase in turns is \(p_0\) (mod 1), that is, \((1000+m)/2000\): the same Archimedean reason that makes the Haar measure uniform in m-qg.

The polarization circuit H → D → R → H encloses an octant and picks up \(-\pi/4\).

title: 8  Fisher information, clocks, gravity and metrology
text:
8.1 From the base: the information in one shot
Metrology is the discipline of measuring a parameter with the smallest possible uncertainty, and its central tool is the Fisher information: how much each shot teaches about the parameter. This chapter writes it on the base of Chapter 1. The probability equation \(p_0=\cos^2(\theta/2)\) fixes how much information each reading carries, and from it follow the resolution in milli-qang, the operating point of an interferometer, the comparison of two atomic clocks one metre apart in height, the advantage (and the limits) of entanglement, and the thermometry of a qubit.
A shot in the \(Z\) basis is a coin with probability \(p_0\). Its Fisher information about the angle is
\[
F_\theta=\frac{(dp_0/d\theta)^2}{p_0(1-p_0)}=\frac{\sin^2\theta/4}{\sin^2\theta/4}=1 ,
\]
constant over the whole sphere; about the reading \(qg_Z=\cos\theta\), by contrast, it is \(F_{qg}=1/(1-qg_Z^2)\), growing towards the poles. The qang angle is the flat coordinate of the information and \(qg_Z\) the curved one (Figure 8.1). The two descriptions are the same physics: the \(1/N\) variance of the angle in Chapter 1 is the Cramér–Rao bound in the flat coordinate (§167).
Expressed in milli-qang, the bound gives the resolution of a reading:
\[
\sigma_m=\frac{1000\,|\sin\theta|}{\sqrt N}\ \text{m-qg},\qquad N=\left(\frac{1000\sin\theta}{\delta}\right)^2
\ \text{shots to resolve } \delta\ \text{m-qg}.
\]
On the equator, resolving 10 m-qg takes \(10^4\) shots and resolving 1 m-qg, \(10^6\); at 60° from the pole, 5 m-qg cost 30 000. Near a pole the reading is more precise in m-qg, but one m-qg there corresponds to a larger angle: a state \(\delta\) m-qg from the pole is \(\arccos(1-\delta/1000)\approx\sqrt{2\delta/1000}\) radians away, 2.56° for 1 m-qg.

title: 8  Fisher information, clocks, gravity and metrology
section: 8.2 Information geometry and the natural gradient
text:
8.2 Information geometry and the natural gradient
The many-parameter version of the Fisher information is the Fubini–Study metric, and it governs the natural gradient: descent that measures its steps in distance between states, not between parameters. In a real ansatz of \(R_Y\) rotations and CZ gates, every state of the circuit is real, \(\langle Y_k\rangle=0\) before each rotation and every diagonal entry of the metric is exactly \(\tfrac14\): the angles are flat one by one, and all the curvature sits in the off-diagonal terms, which within a layer are correlators \(\langle Y_iY_j\rangle/4\), measurable with one circuit per layer (§159).
Two practical consequences, checked on a 4-qubit Ising chain with 20 seeds: descent in qg coordinates never converges (0 of 20), because the curved coordinate distorts the steps; and the natural gradient with the qg\(_{YY}\) block metric is 1.3 times faster than descent in the angle, and 4.6 times with the full metric. The gain comes from the metric, not from changing coordinates: the natural gradient in qg is Euclidean descent in \(\theta\). The rule is to optimize in the angle and read out in qg.

title: 8  Fisher information, clocks, gravity and metrology
text:
8.3 Two clocks and gravity
An atomic clock measures a phase, and two clocks at different heights tick at different rates: the gravitational redshift. Read with the same laser, they give \(qg_{Z,1}=\cos(\varphi+\delta)\) and \(qg_{Z,2}=\cos(\varphi-\delta)\), where \(\varphi\) is a random common phase (the laser noise) and \(2\delta\) the difference sought. Even with \(\varphi\) unknown, the pairs of readings lie on the ellipse
\[
x^2+y^2-2xy\,c=1-c^2,\qquad c=\cos2\delta ,
\]
so the difference is read from the shape of the cloud, without controlling the common phase (Figure 8.2). For two strontium clocks 1 m apart, \(2\delta=2\pi\nu\,gh\,t/c^2=0.294\) rad in one second.






Figure 8.2: Readings of two clocks with a random common phase. The height difference opens the diagonal into an ellipse; its shape gives the phase difference without knowing the common phase.



Fitting the ellipse needs the squares of the readings, and there the unbiased estimator of \(qg^2\) from Chapter 4 comes in: without the correction, the shot-noise bias flattens the ellipse. All four recorded predictions passed (§126):

title: 8  Fisher information, clocks, gravity and metrology
text:
8.4 Ramsey sensing: where to operate
A Ramsey interferometer turns a phase into a probability: \(qg=a+bV\cos(\varphi-\alpha)\), with visibility \(V\), operating point \(\alpha\) and the read-out map \((a,b)\) of Chapter 27. With ideal read-out, the information per shot about the phase is
\[
F=\frac{V^2-qg^2}{1-qg^2}.
\]
With \(V=1\) it is flat, \(F=1\) everywhere: the \(1/(1-qg^2)\) gain at the poles is exactly cancelled by the Jacobian. With \(V<1\) the optimum is the middle of the fringe, \(qg=0\), and the information vanishes at the bright fringe (Figure 8.1). This is the known practice of operating at quadrature, written in qg (§36). Three measured nuances:

Read-out asymmetry moves the optimum, but it does not matter: moving to the new optimum gains 0.17% with the calibrated read-out, and 1.6% even with a 10% read-out error.
With few shots a prior helps: with 10 shots, the Bayesian posterior mean is about 2 times better than direct inversion, because the prior range of the phase carries information.
With visibility 0.9, operating at the pole gets worse with more shots (the scaled error goes from 1.09 to 2.50 between 10 and 1000 shots): small phases become invisible there. The middle of the fringe tracks its bound (1.11–1.24, with bound 1.12).

text:
8.5 GHZ metrology: when entanglement wins
With \(N\) qubits a frequency \(\omega\) can be measured in two ways: \(N\) independent Ramsey clocks, or a GHZ state, whose parity \(X_1\cdots X_N\) is a single qg value of the whole register, \(qg_P=V_N\cos(N\omega t)\), oscillating \(N\) times faster. The advantage is paid for in visibility, which falls as the \(N\)-th power of that of one qubit. At mid-fringe the information per shot is \(V^2\), and per unit time (§58):
\[
\text{independent: } N\,t\,e^{-2t/T_2}(1-2e)^2,\qquad \text{GHZ: } N^2\,t\,e^{-2Nt/T_2}(1-2e)^{2N},
\]
with \(e\) the read-out error per qubit. Optimizing the interrogation time:

The table sums up three known results, here in a single qg reading. With Markovian dephasing there is no gain for any \(N\) (Huelga et al. 1997), and with read-out error independent qubits are strictly better. With Gaussian, slow dephasing the gain grows as \(\sqrt N\), the Zeno-type limit (Matsuzaki et al. 2011; Chin et al. 2012). And the read-out caps it: the parity carries \((1-2e)^N\), so there is an optimal size of the GHZ state, beyond which adding qubits makes the measurement worse (Figure 8.3).

8.6 Thermal states: \(qg_Z=\tanh(\beta h)\)
A qubit with \(H=-hZ\) in equilibrium at temperature \(T\) (with \(k_B=1\)) is in the Gibbs state, and its polar bias is
\[
qg_Z=\tanh(\beta h),\qquad \beta=1/T .
\]
The whole thermodynamics of the qubit is then a function of a single reading (§25):

Thermometry. A \(Z\) measurement is an energy measurement, and therefore the optimal one on a Gibbs state; its Fisher information about \(T\) is \(C/T^2\). The best relative precision is at the maximum of the heat capacity:
\[
qg\cdot\operatorname{artanh}(qg)=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad qg^\ast=0.8336,\qquad \beta h=1.1997 ,
\]
the peak of the Schottky anomaly, the known optimal operating point of a two-level thermometer (Correa et al. 2015), here as a one-line condition on the reading. The section is an exact rewriting of textbook thermodynamics, checked against \(e^{-\beta H}\) to \(5\cdot10^{-12}\); no advantage was expected or found.

8.9 Summary

Per shot, the information is 1 in the angle and \(1/(1-qg_Z^2)\) in \(qg_Z\); the resolution in m-qg is \(1000|\sin\theta|/\sqrt N\), the Cramér–Rao bound.
The natural-gradient metric in a real ansatz has diagonal \(\tfrac14\) and \(qg_{YY}\) correlators; optimizing in qg coordinates does not converge, and the gain comes from the metric.
Two clocks with a random common phase trace an ellipse; its shape gives the gravitational redshift at 1 m with 68σ in the model, if the bias of the squares is corrected.
A Ramsey interferometer with visibility \(V<1\) is operated at mid-fringe; its information is \((V^2-qg^2)/(1-qg^2)\).
The GHZ state gains nothing with Markovian dephasing, gains \(\sqrt N\) with slow dephasing and loses it to the read-out error raised to the \(N\).
A thermal qubit has \(qg_Z=\tanh(\beta h)\); its best thermometry point is \(qg^\ast=0.8336\), the Schottky peak.

title: 9  Quantum kinematics of flavour oscillation in vacuum
text:
9.1 From the base: the oscillation probability in m-qg
A neutrino is born and detected in a flavour state (\(\nu_e\), \(\nu_\mu\) or \(\nu_\tau\)), but it travels in mass states. Since the mass states pick up different phases, the flavour changes on the way: this is flavour oscillation, and in vacuum it is exactly a two- or three-level rotation. This chapter writes it on the base of Chapter 1. An oscillation probability is a qang probability like any other, with its angle, its milli-qang reading and its error bar; two-flavour oscillation is a precession on a cone of the sphere; and three flavours fit on three qubits with a circuit that conserves the weight, so the qg filter applies. The chapter ends with the project’s first real-hardware data point, taken on IQM Garnet.
Everything in this chapter is in vacuum. A 1300 km baseline crosses the Earth and has sizeable matter effects; those are the subject of Chapter 10.
With two flavours on one qubit, \(|0\rangle=\nu_e\) and \(|1\rangle=\nu_\mu\), the survival probability is \(p_0=1-P\), with \(P=P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)\). The probability equation of Chapter 1 gives all its readings:
\[
qg_Z=1-2P,\qquad m=1000\,(1-2P)\ \text{m-qg},\qquad \vartheta=\arccos qg_Z=2\arcsin\sqrt P ,
\]
and its shot resolution, \(\sigma_m=1000\,|\sin\vartheta|/\sqrt N=2000\sqrt{P(1-P)}/\sqrt N\) m-qg. A 1% appearance probability is 20 m-qg; a probability difference of 0.025 is 50 m-qg. With three flavours on three qubits (below) each qubit carries the probability of one flavour and is read the same way: \(m_\beta=1000\,(1-2P_\beta)\).
The scale adds no physics: it is the same probability. What it adds is a common ruler for comparing the signal with shot noise and, as shown next, a coordinate in which the mixing angle is read directly.

title: 9  Quantum kinematics of flavour oscillation in vacuum
section: 9.2 Oscillation as a rotation on a cone
text:
9.2 Oscillation as a rotation on a cone
In the flavour basis, going to the mass basis is a rotation \(R_Y(-2\theta)\), with \(\theta\) the mixing angle; in the mass basis the two states acquire the relative phase
\[
\Delta=\frac{\Delta m^2L}{2E}=2\times1.267\,\frac{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV}^2]\,L[\mathrm{km}]}{E[\mathrm{GeV}]},
\]
which is an \(R_Z(\Delta)\); and returning to flavour is \(R_Y(2\theta)\). The one-qubit circuit is then \(R_Y(2\theta)\,R_Z(\Delta)\,R_Y(-2\theta)\), and its reading is (§151)
\[
qg_Z=\cos^2 2\theta+\sin^2 2\theta\,\cos\Delta,\qquad P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)=\sin^2 2\theta\,\sin^2\frac{\Delta}{2}.
\]
The first formula is the spherical law of cosines. The mass axis is \(2\theta\) from the pole; the Bloch vector, which starts at the pole, precesses about that axis on a cone of half-angle \(2\theta\), and after turning by \(\Delta\) it is an arc distance \(\vartheta=\arccos qg_Z\) from the pole. It is the spherical triangle with two sides \(2\theta\) and included angle \(\Delta\). The qang angle of the reading is the distance travelled on the sphere (Figure 9.1).






Figure 9.1: Two flavours on one qubit. Left, the m-qg reading as a function of the phase, with the shot-noise band for 1000 shots. Right, the qang angle \(\vartheta=\arccos qg_Z\): at the oscillation maximum (\(\Delta=\pi\)) it is exactly \(4\theta\).

title: 9  Quantum kinematics of flavour oscillation in vacuum
section: 9.3 The mixing angle is a quarter of the qang angle
text:
9.3 The mixing angle is a quarter of the qang angle
At the oscillation maximum, \(\Delta=\pi\), the law of cosines reduces to \(qg_Z=\cos^2 2\theta-\sin^2 2\theta=\cos4\theta\), and therefore
\[
\theta_{\text{mix}}=\frac{\vartheta}{4}=\frac{\arccos qg_Z}{4}\qquad(\theta\le\pi/4).
\]
The mixing angle is read as a quarter of a qang angle, without inverting any \(\sin^2\). It must be said precisely what this is and what it is not. It is exact only at the maximum: at any other phase the relation between \(\vartheta\) and \(\theta\) is not linear, and the trigonometry is still there. And it is not new physics: it is the arcsine transformation of a proportion from Chapter 4 (§125), which at the maximum coincides with the geometry of the cone.
The condition \(\theta\le\pi/4\) is not a detail either. For \(\theta>\pi/4\) the angle \(4\theta\) exceeds \(\pi\) and \(\arccos\) returns \(2\pi-4\theta\), that is, \(\pi/2-\theta\). Since \(\sin^22\theta\) is symmetric under \(\theta\to\pi/2-\theta\), no two-flavour measurement can tell the two values apart: this is the octant degeneracy, the same one the atmospheric angle \(\theta_{23}\) has (49° in the values used here; the reading at the maximum would give 41°). The qg scale makes it visible; it does not resolve it.

9.4 Error bars that do not depend on the angle
The qang angle inherits the stabilized variance of the arcsine transformation: its shot-noise standard deviation is \(1/\sqrt{N+\frac12}\), the same over the whole sphere (Chapter 4, §125). Divided by four:
\[

Read in milli-qang, the same measurement does depend on the point: for \(\theta=0.1\) the maximum is at \(m=1000\cos0.4=921\) m-qg with \(\sigma_m=12\) m-qg. title: 9  Quantum kinematics of flavour oscillation in vacuum
text:
9.5 Three flavours on three qubits
With three flavours, flavour state \(k\) is the weight-1 state with only qubit \(k\) excited: \(\nu_e=|100\rangle\), \(\nu_\mu=|010\rangle\), \(\nu_\tau=|001\rangle\) (in qubit order 0, 1, 2). The PMNS matrix in its standard form,
\[
U=R_{23}\,U_\delta\,R_{13}\,U_\delta^\dagger\,R_{12},\qquad U_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,e^{i\delta_{CP}}),
\]
is three real rotations and two phases. Each rotation \(R_{ij}\) is an RBS gate (an \(XX+YY\)) between qubits \(i\) and \(j\); each phase is a phase gate on one qubit; and propagation, in the mass basis, is one phase gate per qubit. Every gate conserves the Hamming weight, so a shot with weight other than 1 is an error and can be discarded: this is the qg symmetry filter of Chapter 21 (§77). For antineutrinos, \(\delta_{CP}\to-\delta_{CP}\) is enough. The circuit reproduces the analytic vacuum probabilities to \(10^{-15}\).
Figure 9.2 shows the case of the prediction: an initial \(\nu_\mu\), \(L=1300\) km (a DUNE-like baseline), \(\delta_{CP}=-\pi/2\) and NuFIT-like mixing values in normal ordering. The first oscillation maximum is at 2.63 GeV, where survival drops to \(P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)=0.013\), that is, \(m_\mu=974\) m-qg.






Figure 9.2: Three-flavour probabilities for an initial \(\nu_\mu\) at 1300 km, in vacuum; on the right, the m-qg reading of each flavour’s qubit. Dashed lines are antineutrinos: \(\nu_\mu\) survival is identical (CPT), \(\nu_e\) appearance is not (CP).

title: 9  Quantum kinematics of flavour oscillation in vacuum
text:
9.7 The CP asymmetry in vacuum
CP violation shows up as a difference between neutrinos and antineutrinos:
\[
A_{CP}=P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_e)-P(\bar\nu_\mu\to\bar\nu_e) .
\]
At 2.6 GeV with \(\delta_{CP}=-\pi/2\) it is 0.0250 (0.0630 against 0.0380), that is, 50 m-qg on the \(\nu_e\) qubit. With 20 000 shots per circuit, the shot noise of the difference is about 4.4 m-qg: the signal is about 11σ. Survival, on the other hand, cannot tell them apart: in vacuum CPT imposes \(P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)=P(\bar\nu_\mu\to\bar\nu_\mu)\) (the orange curves of Figure 9.2 coincide).

The asymmetry survives even without the filter. It is the difference of two nearly identical circuits (only the sign of two phases changes), so the shift that noise produces in common cancels in the subtraction, as in the fidelity classifier of §149. What does not cancel is the contraction, which shrinks both probabilities and the difference with them: that is why FakeTorino’s raw value reads 35 m-qg and not 50. The filter halves the error on the CZ devices.

9.8 What the link between neutrinos and qang is, and is not
It is modelling: the oscillation is a rotation, and the qang angle reads the mixing angle directly at the maximum, with a known error bar. It does not remove the trigonometry in general, and it does not speed up variational methods for dense neutrino gases: those are many-body problems (Chapter 10). The limits are stated: vacuum only, fixed parameters, simulated device noise except for the single IQM Garnet run.

9.11 Summary

An oscillation probability \(P\) is read as \(m=1000(1-2P)\) m-qg, with angle \(2\arcsin\sqrt P\) and resolution \(2000\sqrt{P(1-P)/N}\) m-qg.
With two flavours, \(qg_Z=\cos^22\theta+\sin^22\theta\cos\Delta\) is the spherical law of cosines of the precession on a cone of half-angle \(2\theta\).
At the maximum, \(\theta=\arccos(qg_Z)/4\) with standard deviation \(1/(4\sqrt{N+\frac12})\), independent of \(\theta\); for \(\theta>\pi/4\) the reading returns \(\pi/2-\theta\) (octant degeneracy).
Three flavours are three qubits in the weight-1 sector; PMNS is three RBS gates and two phases, and the qg filter lowers the error 3.0–3.8 times on simulated models.
On IQM Garnet the filter gains 1.6× and puts the oscillation maximum back at 2.6 GeV; the error that remains is inside the sector.
The CP asymmetry at 2.6 GeV is 50 m-qg and survives without the filter, because the common shift cancels in the subtraction.

title: 10  Matter effects, solar neutrinos and collective oscillations
text:
10.1 From the base: the medium as a shift in m-qg
Chapter 9 left the neutrino in vacuum. But a 1300 km beam crosses the Earth, solar neutrinos are born at the centre of the Sun, and in a supernova neutrinos are so dense that they interact with each other. In all three cases the medium adds a term to the flavour Hamiltonian, and the chapter’s question is the same in all three: which number is still conserved, because that decides whether the qg filter applies, and in which basis. On the base of Chapter 1, each effect of the medium is read as a shift in milli-qang, on the same scale as shot noise.
Each flavour (or mass) qubit is read as in Chapter 9, \(m=1000\,(1-2P)\) m-qg, so an effect of the medium that changes a probability by \(\delta P\) is a shift of \(2000\,\delta P\) m-qg, directly comparable with the resolution \(\sigma_m=2000\sqrt{P(1-P)/N}\). Three examples from this chapter, on that scale:
With 1000 shots and \(P\approx0.07\) the resolution is about 16 m-qg: the Earth’s effect shows at 3σ in a single circuit, and the solar drop spans most of the scale.

section: 10.2 The MSW effect in the Earth
text:
10.2 The MSW effect in the Earth
Electrons in the Earth forward-scatter \(\nu_e\) and add to the flavour Hamiltonian a potential \(A=2\sqrt2\,G_FN_eE\), which in oscillation units is
\[
A=1.52\times10^{-4}\,Y_e\,\rho[\mathrm{g/cm^3}]\,E[\mathrm{GeV}]\ \mathrm{eV}^2 ,
\]
with the opposite sign for antineutrinos (Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein). In the crust (\(\rho=2.85\) g/cm³, \(Y_e=0.5\)) and at 2.6 GeV, \(A=5.6\times10^{-4}\) eV², 22% of \(\Delta m^2_{31}\): not a small correction.
The potential acts on \(\nu_e\) only, that is, it is a phase on qubit 0. The circuit alternates the exact vacuum step of Chapter 9 with that phase (second-order, or Strang, Trotter), and every gate still conserves the weight: the qg filter applies just as in vacuum (§152). With \(L=1300\) km and between 0.8 and 5 GeV:

Three lessons. Matter fakes CP violation: at \(\delta_{CP}=0\), where vacuum gives no asymmetry at all, the Earth produces 84 m-qg of difference between \(\nu\) and \(\bar\nu\), more than the 50 m-qg of Chapter 9’s CP signal; that is why long-baseline experiments must model matter, and the filtered circuit sees it. There is no depth trade-off: a single Trotter step already has less error (0.012) than the noise, so \(r^\ast=1\) with or without the filter, and M4 holds only because both are 1. And M5’s gap to the exact value is Trotter error, not noise: the filtered values sit within 0.004 of the \(r=2\) Trotter value.

title: 10  Matter effects, solar neutrinos and collective oscillations
section: 10.4 Solar neutrinos: the whole Sun is one rotation
text:
10.4 Solar neutrinos: the whole Sun is one rotation
A \(\nu_e\) is born at the solar core, where \((\rho Y_e)\approx100\) g/cm³, and travels out to vacuum. At low energy matter barely matters and it reaches the Earth with the averaged vacuum probability; above the resonance (about 2 MeV at the core), the central density turns the matter mixing angle \(\theta_m\) almost to 90°, the neutrino adiabatically follows the heavy eigenstate and leaves the Sun as \(\nu_2\). The phases are lost on the way to the Earth, so what arrives is a population in the mass basis, and the survival probability (§156)
\[
P_{ee}=c_{13}^4\left(\cos^2\theta_{12}\,p_1+\sin^2\theta_{12}\,p_2\right)+s_{13}^4
\]
is linear in \(qg_Z\) of the \(\nu_2\) qubit. It falls from 0.54 to 0.30 between 0.5 and 15 MeV (Figure 10.2); on the \(\nu_2\) qubit that is going from \(+304\) to \(-868\) m-qg, more than half of the scale.






Figure 10.2: Survival probability of solar \(\nu_e\). The curve is the adiabatic conversion from the core; the squares, the exact reference of the scaled Sun the circuit uses; the circles, the 8-slab circuit on the FakeFez noise model with the filter. On the right, the same reading in m-qg of the \(\nu_2\) qubit.



The circuit uses two effective flavours (\(\nu_3\) decoupled; it agrees with three flavours to 0.001) and a scaled Sun: an exponential profile with a 100 km scale height, cut into \(r\) slabs uniform in \(\theta_m\). Each slab is one exact \(2\times2\) propagator, \(R_Z\cdot\mathrm{RBS}\cdot R_Z\) on two qubits in the weight-1 sector, and the filter applies. All six pre-registered predictions held:

The filter gains 1.9–2.3× on the slab circuit, as in the Earth. But the important result is another one: the physics makes the circuit unnecessary. Because the phases are lost before detection, the observable is a single population, and the compiled circuit (the whole Sun in the one RBS that loads \(p_2\)) beats every slab circuit even without the filter; with two flavours, one qubit with readout correction is as good as anything. The adiabatic answer is classical, \(\sin^2\theta_m\) at the core. A quantum computer could add something only where coherence survives: day–night regeneration in the Earth, or the collective effects of the next section.
Open: the real Sun. The profile is scaled (the real one has a scale height of about \(6\times10^4\) km and is far more adiabatic, with the same adiabatic answer), and the slab discretization error (0.009 at \(r=8\)) is of the size of the filtered noise. The comparison with a Standard Solar Model density profile has not been done: it stays a proposal, not a result.

title: 10  Matter effects, solar neutrinos and collective oscillations
section: 10.5 Collective oscillations: what is conserved is the mass number
text:
10.5 Collective oscillations: what is conserved is the mass number
In a supernova the neutrino density is so high that neutrinos scatter off each other. With \(N\) two-flavour neutrinos, one qubit each, in the single-angle approximation, the Hamiltonian in the mass basis is
\[
H_m=-\sum_i\frac{\omega_i}{2}Z_i+\frac{\mu}{2N}\sum_{i<j}\boldsymbol\sigma_i\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_j ,
\]
with \(\omega_i=\Delta m^2/2E_i\) and \(\mu\) the neutrino–neutrino coupling. Section §151 had named these gases a natural target for the filter because “the total flavour number is conserved”. That holds only for the neutrino–neutrino term. The product \(\boldsymbol\sigma_i\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_j\) is the same in every basis, but the vacuum term is diagonal only in the mass basis: what is conserved is the number of \(\nu_2\), not the flavour number (§154). Figure 10.3 shows it with the exact evolution of four neutrinos: the number of \(\nu_2\) is constant and the number of \(\nu_x\) moves, a little at the experiment’s angle and more at a large angle.






Figure 10.3: Left: exact evolution of four neutrinos (\(\omega\) = 0.25–1, \(\mu\) = 4, initial \(\nu_e\nu_e\nu_x\nu_x\)). The number of \(\nu_2\) is conserved; the flavour number is not. Right: the error of the three read-outs on simulated noise models (post hoc analysis, not pre-registered), raw in light and corrected in dark.



A flavour initial state is a superposition of mass sectors with known, conserved probabilities (for \(\nu_e\nu_e\nu_x\nu_x\) at \(\theta=0.195\): 0.863 in the two-\(\nu_2\) sector and 0.067 in each neighbour). The function reweight_sectors rescales each sector to its probability; when the distribution is a delta, it is the filter.
All seven pre-registered predictions failed, for one reason: the noiseless Trotter error (0.095) was larger than the whole noisy error against the exact evolution (0.074–0.088), so every read-out was scored mostly on Trotter error. A post hoc analysis, not pre-registered, scored against the noiseless circuit, gives what the predictions meant to measure:

The lesson for the next pre-registration is on record: score against the noiseless circuit when the Trotter error is not known to be small, or measure that error before fixing the predictions.

text:
10.8 Summary

An effect of the medium that changes a probability by \(\delta P\) is a shift of \(2000\,\delta P\) m-qg, comparable with shot noise on the same scale.
The Earth adds a phase on the \(\nu_e\) qubit; the Trotter circuit conserves the weight, the filter gains 2.8× in the median, and a single step is enough.
Matter fakes CP violation (84 m-qg at \(\delta_{CP}=0\)) and reveals the mass ordering: the sign of the shift flips between normal and inverted.
In the Sun, \(P_{ee}\) is linear in \(qg_Z\) of the \(\nu_2\) qubit and falls by 1173 m-qg; since the phases are lost, the whole Sun is one rotation, and the answer is classical.
In collective oscillations the number of \(\nu_2\) is conserved, not the flavour number: the filter works in the mass basis (2.2–2.8×, post hoc) and not in the flavour basis; all seven pre-registered predictions failed on Trotter error.
The comparison with a realistic solar density profile is still open.

title: 11  Majorana phases, neutrinoless double beta decay and sterile neutrinos
text:
11.1 From the base: what changes no probability changes no reading
Chapters 9 and 10 read what an oscillation circuit sees: mixing angles, the CP phase, the mass ordering through matter. This chapter takes two open questions of neutrino physics that have a clear answer in qg terms, one negative and one positive. Majorana phases change no oscillation probability, and therefore no qang reading: the compiler deletes them. A sterile neutrino, on the other hand, is one more qubit in the weight-1 sector, and the filter treats it like any other flavour. At the end, closing Part III, the four quantum numbers of the atom written with the same rule.
All the readings of Chapter 1 are functions of probabilities: \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\), \(m=1000\,qg_Z\), the angle \(\arccos qg_Z\) and the entropy \(qg_S\). So a physical parameter that changes no measurement probability is invisible to all of them at once, without exception and with any number of shots. The question “does a circuit see it?” reduces to “does it change any probability?”, and is answered before running anything.
Conversely, a parameter that does change a probability by \(\delta P\) shows up as \(2000\,\delta P\) m-qg on the qubit of the corresponding flavour, as in Chapters 9 and 10. The sterile neutrino of this chapter is of that kind: with the hypothetical parameters used below, it lowers \(\nu_\mu\) survival by 0.085, that is, 171 m-qg.

11  Majorana phases, neutrinoless double beta decay and sterile neutrinos

title: 11  Majorana phases, neutrinoless double beta decay and sterile neutrinos
section: 11.2 Majorana phases are invisible to oscillations
text:
11.2 Majorana phases are invisible to oscillations
If the neutrino is its own antiparticle (a Majorana particle), the mixing matrix has two more phases,
\[
U_M=U\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\ e^{i\alpha_{21}/2},\ e^{i\alpha_{31}/2}\right).
\]
The added matrix is diagonal in the mass basis, and so is propagation. The two commute, and in the evolution operator \(U_M\,D\,U_M^\dagger\) the phase cancels against its inverse: \(U_M D U_M^\dagger=U D U^\dagger\). No oscillation probability depends on \(\alpha_{21}\) or \(\alpha_{31}\), in vacuum or in matter (in matter the Hamiltonian is \(U_M\,\mathrm{diag}(0,\Delta m^2_{21},\Delta m^2_{31})\,U_M^\dagger+V\), and the cancellation already happens in the first term, before the potential is added). Numerically the largest difference among the nine probabilities with and without the phases is \(4\times10^{-16}\), machine rounding (§163).
In the three-flavour circuit of Chapter 9 the phases are phase gates in the mass basis, inserted on either side of propagation (majorana_circuit). What is instructive is what the transpiler does: on all three simulated devices, the circuit compiled with phases \((\alpha_{21},\alpha_{31})=(\pi/2,\,3\pi/4)\) is identical to the one compiled without them (on FakeFez, 18 CZ, 48 \(R_Z\) and 47 \(\sqrt X\) in both). The optimizer merges each phase gate with its inverse and deletes them. It is not an “analytic elimination” designed by anyone, but the direct consequence of the operator not changing: a compiler that simplifies consecutive phases finds the identity on its own.

11.3 Majorana phases in neutrinoless double beta decay
Where the phases do show is in a process that violates lepton number: neutrinoless double beta decay, \((A,Z)\to(A,Z+2)+2e^-\), possible only if the neutrino is Majorana. Its rate is proportional to the square of the effective mass
\[
m_{\beta\beta}=\left|\sum_i U_{ei}^2\,m_i\right| ,
\]
and since \(U_{ei}^2\) enters and not \(|U_{ei}|^2\), the phases do not cancel: they can add the three contributions or make them interfere destructively. With a massless lightest neutrino, scanning the two phases gives (§163)

Figure 11.1 shows both bands as a function of the lightest mass. In inverted ordering the band has a floor of about 19 meV, which is the target of the next generation of experiments. In normal ordering, for a lightest mass between about 2 and 7 meV, the phases can make \(m_{\beta\beta}\) vanish completely: a cancellation that no double beta experiment could tell apart from a Dirac neutrino.






Figure 11.1: The effective mass \(m_{\beta\beta}\) as a function of the lightest neutrino mass, scanning the two Majorana phases (bands), and with zero phases (lines). In normal ordering the phases can cancel it between about 2 and 7 meV.



The qg reading of this section is just the previous section said the other way round: an oscillation circuit cannot measure what this figure plots. What the scale does do is separate the two questions cleanly, the oscillation one (probabilities, qang readings) and the mass one (an amplitude with phases, outside any reading of a flavour qubit).

section: 11.4 The sterile neutrino: a fourth qubit in the weight-1 sector
text:
11.4 The sterile neutrino: a fourth qubit in the weight-1 sector
A sterile neutrino \(\nu_s\) is a fourth flavour that does not interact through the weak force, but mixes with the other three. In the 3+1 model there is a fourth mass state with \(\Delta m^2_{41}\sim1\) eV², much larger than the other two, and the real mixing is a sequence of six rotations,
\[
U=R_{34}\,R_{24}\,R_{14}\,R_{23}\,R_{13}\,R_{12}
\]
(without CP phases, to keep it simple). In the circuit each flavour is a qubit with a single 1: the sterile one is simply one more qubit in the weight-1 sector (sterile_circuit). Each rotation is an RBS and propagation is one phase gate per qubit; everything conserves the weight and the filter applies unchanged.
At short distances, where the three-flavour oscillations have not started yet, survival is effectively two-level,
\[
P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)\approx1-4|U_{\mu4}|^2\left(1-|U_{\mu4}|^2\right)\sin^2\frac{\Delta_{41}}{2} .
\]
With the hypothetical values \(\theta_{14}=\theta_{24}=0.15\) and \(\Delta m^2_{41}=1\) eV², \(|U_{\mu4}|^2=0.022\) and the amplitude is 0.085; at \(L=0.5\) km the first minimum falls at 0.40 GeV (Figure 11.2). It is the same case as Chapter 9, with the same geometry: a precession cone with an effective mixing angle, now between \(\nu_\mu\) and \(\nu_s\).
On the simulated noise models, all three pre-registered predictions for the sterile neutrino held:

At the minimum (exact 0.915), FakeBrisbane reads 0.678 raw and 0.879 filtered; FakeTorino, 0.749 and 0.890; FakeFez, 0.792 and 0.890. The gain is larger than with three flavours (5.5× against 3.0–3.8×) because the circuit has four qubits: there are more ways for a shot to leave the weight-1 sector, and the filter discards them all.

What remains is, again, inside the sector: the filtered values still sit 0.025 to 0.036 below the exact value at the minimum, because noise that moves a 1 from one qubit to another conserves the weight and the filter cannot see it.
Open: the data. The mixing angles in this section are hypothetical, chosen so that the signal is visible; they are not a fit. Phenomenological limits and the comparison of 3+1 models with short-baseline experiments have not been done: they stay a proposal.

section: 11.5 The four quantum numbers in qg terms
text:
11.5 The four quantum numbers in qg terms
Chapter 10 ended on the question of which number is conserved. The same question, applied to the atom, gives a qg reading of the four quantum numbers (§155). It is a translation, not new physics.

The magnetic number. A register of \(n\) qubits in its symmetric subspace is a spin \(j=n/2\), and in each shot the magnetic number is read from the Hamming weight: \(m=n/2-w\). The weight filter is the projection onto one value of \(m\), and \(qg_Z=\langle J_z\rangle/j\) for any angular momentum.
\(m_s\) is one qubit, with \(qg_Z=2m_s\). \(m_l\) of an \(l\) orbital is the weight of a symmetric register of \(2l\) qubits: the three complex \(p\) orbitals are \(|00\rangle\), \((|01\rangle+|10\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|11\rangle\). The real \(p_x\) and \(p_y\) mix \(m_l=\pm1\), which is why they have \(qg_Z=0\) like \(p_z\), but with entropy 0.63 instead of zero.
\(l\) is the permutation symmetry, and is read with qg values of SWAP: for two qubits, \(\langle J^2\rangle=1+qg_{\text{SWAP}}\).
\(n\): by hydrogen’s hidden SO(4) symmetry, shell \(n\) is two spins \((n-1)/2\), that is, two symmetric registers of \(n-1\) qubits; \(m_l\) is \((n-1)\) minus the total weight of the \(2(n-1)\) qubits, and the weight filter fixes it.

The qang angle of an eigenstate \(|l,m\rangle\) is \(\arccos(m/l)\). The textbook vector-model angle is \(\arccos\!\big(m/\sqrt{l(l+1)}\big)\), and always lies closer to the equator (Figure 11.3), because \(|l,m\rangle\) has a transverse spread \(\langle J_x^2+J_y^2\rangle=l(l+1)-m^2>0\):

title: 11  Majorana phases, neutrinoless double beta decay and sterile neutrinos
text:
11.8 Summary

Every qang reading is a function of probabilities: a parameter that changes no probability is invisible to all of them at once.
Majorana phases cancel in \(U_MDU_M^\dagger\) (difference \(4\times10^{-16}\)); the transpiler outputs the same circuit with and without them.
Neutrinoless double beta decay does see them: \(m_{\beta\beta}\) ranges from 1.4 to 3.7 meV (normal) and from 18.7 to 48.3 meV (inverted) with a massless lightest neutrino, and can vanish in normal ordering.
A sterile neutrino is a fourth qubit in the weight-1 sector; with hypothetical mixing, the filter gains 5.5× and places the minimum at 0.4 GeV. Limits from real data are still open.
The four quantum numbers are read in qg: \(m\) from the Hamming weight, \(l\) from SWAP, \(n\) from the register size; the qang angle \(\arccos(m/l)\) is not the vector-model one.

title: 12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit
text:
12.1 From the base: the fidelity is a probability
Part IV takes the qang scale to quantum communication networks. This chapter deals with teleporting a qubit through a passive optical network: a central office shares an entangled state with a user through a fibre and a passive \(1{:}N\) splitter, and the photon arrives with low probability. The question is which state to share. The usual answer, a Bell pair, stops being optimal as soon as the channel loses photons, and the optimal state is fixed by a single number: the \(qg_Z\) reading of one of its qubits. The chapter closes with the qg reading of Bell pairs in a network, which is what Chapter 13 uses as a predictor of the fidelity.
The fidelity of teleporting an input state is the probability that Bob, after undoing the preparation, measures 0: it is a \(p_0\) of Chapter 1, with its reading \(m=1000(2p_0-1)\) m-qg and its error bar. The average fidelity over the Bloch sphere is obtained exactly with six inputs, the cardinal states \(|0\rangle\), \(|1\rangle\), \(|\pm\rangle\), \(|\pm i\rangle\), because they form a spherical 3-design.
The shared state is \(\cos\alpha|00\rangle+\sin\alpha|11\rangle\), and each of its qubits has
\[
qg_Z=\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha=\cos2\alpha,\qquad \alpha=\frac{\arccos qg_Z}{2}.
\]
The resource angle is half the qang angle of either of its qubits. The Bell pair, \(\alpha=\pi/4\), is the equator: \(qg_Z=0\), \(m=0\). A less entangled resource leans toward \(|00\rangle\) (\(m>0\)); a “more than maximally entangled” one, in the sense of this section, leans toward \(|11\rangle\) (\(m<0\)). The whole design rule of this chapter is an m-qg reading of a single qubit.

12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit

title: 12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit
text:
12.2 Teleportation with a Bell pair
In the protocol of Bennett et al. (1993), Alice measures her input qubit and her half of the resource in the Bell basis, sends Bob two classical bits, and Bob applies one of four Pauli corrections. With a perfect Bell pair the fidelity is 1. With an imperfect resource, the average fidelity depends only on its singlet fraction \(f=\langle\Phi^+|\rho|\Phi^+\rangle\):
\[
F=\frac{2f+1}{3},
\]
and teleportation beats every classical strategy (measure and resend) only if \(F>2/3\), that is, \(f>1/2\). In the circuit the Bell measurement is in deferred form (CX, H, CX, CZ), with no mid-circuit measurements.

12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit

title: 12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit
text:
12.3 A channel that loses photons
In a downlink passive optical network (§157) the resource’s second qubit is a photon present or absent (single rail) that travels through a fibre of transmission \(T=10^{-0.02L}\) (\(L\) in km, 0.2 dB/km) and reaches a \(1{:}N\) splitter. For Bob’s mode both are beam splitters, that is, RBS gates that conserve the photon number, and the photon arrives with probability
\[
\eta=\frac{T}{N}.
\]
A lost photon leaves Bob in \(|0\rangle\): the channel is amplitude damping, which does not treat the two branches of the resource alike. The \(|00\rangle\) branch has nothing to lose; the \(|11\rangle\) branch loses its photon with probability \(1-\eta\). So it pays to put less weight on the fragile branch, and the optimum moves away from \(\alpha=\pi/4\).

title: 12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit
text:
12.4 The design rule
The singlet fraction of the resource after the channel is
\[
f=\frac{(\cos\alpha+\sqrt\eta\,\sin\alpha)^2}{2\,(\cos^2\alpha+\kappa\sin^2\alpha)} ,
\]
with \(\kappa=1\) in the non-assisted protocol, in which only Alice and Bob act. In the assisted protocol the other \(N-1\) users report whether the photon reached them, and those shots are discarded: it is a sector filter on the other users’ register, and the only loss left unheralded is the fibre loss, with \(\kappa=\eta+1-T\). Maximizing \(f\) gives
\[
\tan\alpha^\ast=\frac{\sqrt\eta}{\kappa},\qquad F^\ast=\frac{2+\eta/\kappa}{3},\qquad
qg_Z^\ast=\cos2\alpha^\ast=\frac{\kappa^2-\eta}{\kappa^2+\eta} .
\]
The original master index wrote the rule as \(\sqrt{\eta/\kappa}\); the correct form is \(\sqrt\eta/\kappa\), which is what the code verifies. The whole rule is the third formula: one resource qubit measured in \(Z\) fixes \(\alpha\). On the four links of the experiment:

text:
12.6 Bell pairs in a network, read in qg
Before teleporting it pays to know how good the shared pair is. A pair meant to be \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) is described by five qg readings: three two-qubit correlators, \(qg_{XX}\), \(qg_{YY}\), \(qg_{ZZ}\), and the polar biases of each side, \(m_A=\langle Z_A\rangle\) and \(m_B=\langle Z_B\rangle\). Three measurement settings are enough (§57). The fidelity with \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) is exact for any state,
\[
F_{\Phi^+}=\frac{1+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ}}{4},
\]
and with it the teleportation fidelity the pair will give, \(F=(2F_{\Phi^+}+1)/3=(3+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ})/6\), without running the teleportation (Chapter 13 puts it to the test). Figure 12.3: The signatures of the table: each Pauli noise leaves one correlator at its ideal value (the dotted line), and only amplitude damping moves the local polar biases.



Each Pauli noise leaves one correlator untouched, and only damping (the T1 relaxation of a memory) moves the local biases (Figure 12.3). That reading decides how to distil. The DEJMPS protocol combines the \(\Phi^+\) weight with the error sitting in a fixed slot, and local rotations choose which error goes there. The textbook order can make things worse: with Y-flip noise, one round lowers the fidelity from 0.820 to 0.705, and with damping it gains almost nothing (0.828). The rule “smallest estimated error in that slot”, read from the three correlators with 200 shots per setting, reaches the best output in all three cases: 0.954, 0.954 and 0.915 (against an optimum of 0.920).

title: 12  Optical teleportation and the Bell-pair limit
text:
12.9 Summary

The teleportation fidelity is a probability; the resource \(\cos\alpha|00\rangle+\sin\alpha|11\rangle\) has \(qg_Z=\cos2\alpha\) on each qubit, and the Bell pair is \(m=0\).
On a channel that loses photons (\(\eta=T/N\)) the optimum is not the Bell pair: \(\tan\alpha^\ast=\sqrt\eta/\kappa\), \(F^\ast=(2+\eta/\kappa)/3\), \(qg_Z^\ast=(\kappa^2-\eta)/(\kappa^2+\eta)\).
Without assistance, on a 1:8 splitter or at 20 km the Bell pair falls below 2/3 and the optimal resource stays above; with assistance and no fibre, \(F^\ast=1\) with a resource on the \(|11\rangle\) side.
The rule survives simulated noise (five of six predictions); the qg filter does not help here because teleportation does not conserve the weight.
A Bell pair is read with three correlators and two biases; each Pauli noise leaves one untouched, and that signature picks the right distillation round.

title: 13  Dual rail, the sector filter and long-distance fidelity
text:
13.1 From the base: three qg readings predict a fidelity
Chapter 12 ended on a limitation: the qg filter did not help against device noise, because the teleportation circuit does not conserve the weight. This chapter asks the two questions that follow. The first is whether the fidelity a resource will give can be read before teleporting, with few measurements; the answer is yes, with three qg correlators. The second is what happens if every gate conserves the photon number; the answer is dual rail, in which the filter heralds every loss, and which at 20 km beats the noiseless single-rail optimum until false heralds set a floor. The chapter closes Part IV with entanglement swapping along a chain, read with the same correlators.
Each two-qubit correlator is a qg reading like those of Chapter 1: the parity of two bits measured in a basis, \(qg_{PP}=1-2P(\text{odd parity})\), with its m-qg reading and its error bar \(\sqrt{(1-qg^2)/N}\). Chapter 12 showed that the fidelity with \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) is linear in three of them; so is the average teleportation fidelity (§158):
\[
F=\frac{3+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ}}{6}.
\]
It is a linear read-out of the resource alone, without the Bell measurement: three circuits with 4–5 two-qubit gates, against 10–11 for the teleportation. Being linear, its error bar combines the three: with \(N\) shots per correlator, \(\sigma_F=\sqrt{\sum(1-qg^2)/N}/6\), about 0.0025 with \(N=10\,000\) near \(F\approx0.7\).

title: 13  Dual rail, the sector filter and long-distance fidelity
text:
13.2 The fidelity from three correlators
On the four links of Chapter 12, with both protocols and on three simulated noise models, the fidelity predicted by the correlators was compared with the teleported one. In all 24 combinations the difference is at most 0.029 (Figure 13.1): three short circuits predict the teleported fidelity.






Figure 13.1: Measured teleported fidelity against the one predicted by three correlators, 4 links × 2 protocols × 3 simulated noise models. All 24 fall within ±0.03 of the diagonal.



The pre-registered predictions wanted more: that the difference would isolate the noise of the Bell measurement. That failed. The prediction fell below the noiseless optimum in 5 of 24 cases (A1), was not always above the teleported one (A2, 3 of 24, all within two shot errors), and the difference was not always larger with assistance (A3, 2 of 12). The reason is that the three correlator circuits read two data qubits and the herald, so they carry almost all the noise the teleportation sees. They work as a predictor, not as a decomposition.

title: 13  Dual rail, the sector filter and long-distance fidelity
section: 13.3 Dual rail: every loss is heralded
text:
13.3 Dual rail: every loss is heralded
In single rail a qubit is a photon present or absent, and losing the photon turns a \(|1\rangle\) into a valid \(|0\rangle\): the loss is invisible. In dual rail each qubit is one photon in two modes, \(|0_L\rangle=|10\rangle\) and \(|1_L\rangle=|01\rangle\). The logical gates are built to conserve the photon number: the logical CNOT is a controlled SWAP of the target’s modes, the logical CZ a CZ between modes, and one-qubit gates act on the subspace \(\{|10\rangle,|01\rangle\}\). Every loss leaves Bob’s pair with weight 0, and the qg filter (weight 1 on each pair) heralds every loss, fibre included, without help from the other users.
Without gate noise, the result is clean:
\[
F_{\text{filtered}}=1\ \text{at any distance},\qquad \text{kept}=\eta,\qquad
F_{\text{raw}}=\frac{1+\eta}{2},
\]
where the raw value assumes Bob guesses when no photon arrives, and falls below the single-rail optimum \((2+\eta)/3\). The filter turns loss into rate: the fidelity does not fall with distance; the number of useful pairs does. The price is the circuit: 65–66 two-qubit gates, six times those of single rail.

False heralds set a floor (B1, B2 and B5 failed). When the photon is lost, a gate or readout error can still leave Bob’s pair with weight 1: at 20 km, \((\text{kept}-\eta)/(1-\eta)\) is 3 to 6%. Those shots carry a fidelity of about 1/2, and as \(\eta\) falls they weigh more among the kept ones. With a false-herald probability \(p_f\), the filtered fidelity is
\[
F_{\text{filtered}}=\frac{\eta\,F_0+(1-\eta)\,p_f/2}{\eta+(1-\eta)\,p_f},
\]
which falls with distance even though the channel adds no error (Figure 13.2). It is the dark-count floor of a real heralded link, produced here by gate and readout errors.






Figure 13.2: Filtered dual-rail fidelity as a function of the arrival probability, on three simulated noise models, against the noiseless single-rail optimum (grey line; the diamonds are the assisted one at 20 km). The black curves are the false-herald model with \(F_0=0.87\), an illustration, not a fit.



Heralding still wins at 20 km. In a post hoc analysis, not pre-registered, on FakeTorino and FakeFez the filtered dual rail beats the noiseless single-rail optimum on both splitters: 0.783 and 0.791 against 0.714 at 1:4; 0.727 and 0.710 against 0.692 at 1:8. It does so with six times the two-qubit gates. The raw value loses everywhere (B4), so the gain is the filter’s. B3, the pre-registered version of that comparison (against the noisy teleported fidelity), failed only on FakeBrisbane at (20 km, 1:8).
The comparison with the continuous-variable work is qualitative: there the fidelity is deterministic and falls with distance and with \(N\); here the filter keeps the fidelity high and pays in rate (kept \(\approx\eta\)), until false heralds, not loss, set the limit.

title: 13  Dual rail, the sector filter and long-distance fidelity
text:
13.5 Entanglement swapping along a chain
To go further than one link, a network chains pairs: an intermediate node makes a Bell measurement between its two halves, and the ends become entangled (entanglement swapping). This section is new in the book: it is exact density-matrix algebra, verified in the figure script, with no device run.
For pairs diagonal in the Bell basis, which are what the Pauli noises of Chapter 12 leave, the result in qg is a one-line rule: the correlators multiply. After swapping two pairs, with the Pauli correction that belongs to each outcome,
\[
qg_{PP}^{(1\to3)}=qg_{PP}^{(1\to2)}\cdot qg_{PP}^{(2\to3)},\qquad P\in\{X,Y,Z\},
\]
and along a chain of \(n\) equal links each correlator is raised to the \(n\)-th power. With depolarized pairs of parameter \(w\) (\(qg_{XX}=qg_{ZZ}=w\), \(qg_{YY}=-w\)), the teleportation fidelity of the final pair is \(F=(1+w^n)/2\), and it beats the classical limit while \(w^n>1/3\), that is, up to \(n\le\ln3/\ln(1/w)\): 21 links at \(w=0.95\), 10 at \(w=0.9\) and 4 at \(w=0.8\) (Figure 13.3).






Figure 13.3: Teleportation fidelity of the final pair of a chain of \(n\) links without distillation. With depolarizing noise it falls as \((1+w^n)/2\) and crosses the classical limit; with dephasing, \(qg_{ZZ}\) stays at 1 and the fidelity tends to 2/3 without crossing it.



The correlator reading also says which error accumulates. With dephasing, \(qg_{ZZ}=1\) on every link and therefore along the whole chain, while \(qg_{XX}\) and \(qg_{YY}\) decay as \(0.64^n\): the final pair keeps its \(Z\) correlations and loses its phase ones, and its fidelity tends to 2/3 from above. It is the same signature as in the noise table of Chapter 12, propagated along the chain, and it is what decides where to distil.
The link with dual rail is direct: in a chain of dual-rail pairs, every intermediate Bell measurement also conserves the photon number, and the filter heralds the losses of all links at once. That experiment has not been done.

13.9 Summary

The teleportation fidelity is linear in three qg correlators of the resource, \(F=(3+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ})/6\); in 24 simulated cases it predicts the teleported one to 0.029, although it does not isolate the noise of the Bell measurement.

Along a chain of swaps, the correlators of Bell-diagonal pairs multiply; with depolarization \(F=(1+w^n)/2\), and with dephasing \(qg_{ZZ}\) survives whole.
Routing, repeaters on devices and gate teleportation remain open.

title: 14  Postselected closed timelike curves (P-CTC) and the resolution of paradoxes
text:
14.1 From the base: the success probability has qang angle \(\varphi\)
Part V deals with two information-theory models that use the vocabulary of relativity: time loops and black-hole evaporation. It is worth saying from the start: they are models of information theory, not statements about spacetime (§164). Both are teleportation with postselection on a Bell outcome, that is, a filter on the Bell sector, and that is why they belong in this book. This chapter treats the time loop in its two known formulations, the postselected one (P-CTC) and Deutsch’s (D-CTC), and what a qg reading tells apart between them.
In the simplest model the qubit that “travels to the past” undergoes a rotation \(R_X(\varphi)\), and the postselection succeeds with probability
\[
P_{\text{success}}=\cos^2\frac{\varphi}{2}.
\]
It is the probability equation of Chapter 1 with \(p_0=P_{\text{success}}\), so its qang angle is exactly the rotation, \(\arccos(2P-1)=\varphi\), its reading is \(m=1000\cos\varphi\), and the success rate measured over \(N\) attempts gives \(\varphi\) with uncertainty \(1/\sqrt N\). The grandfather paradox, \(\varphi=\pi\), sits at the south pole: \(P=0\), \(m=-1000\).

14  Postselected closed timelike curves (P-CTC) and the resolution of paradoxes

title: 14  Postselected closed timelike curves (P-CTC) and the resolution of paradoxes
section: 14.2 Two ways to close a time loop
text:
14.2 Two ways to close a time loop
Deutsch (D-CTC, 1991). (Deutsch 1991) The system in the loop must be self-consistent: its state \(\rho_C\) is a fixed point of the evolution, \(\rho_C=\operatorname{Tr}_S[U(\rho_S\otimes\rho_C)U^\dagger]\). At least one fixed point always exists, so there is never a paradox, but there may be several, and an extra rule is needed to choose; the usual one takes the maximum-entropy fixed point.
Postselection (P-CTC; Bennett and Svetlichny, Lloyd and co-workers, 2011). (Svetlichny 2011; Lloyd et al. 2011) The qubit sent to the past, \(C\), is half of a Bell pair \((C,A)\). After \(C\) interacts with the system \(S\), \((C,A)\) is projected back onto the Bell state: it is a teleportation of \(C\) to its own past, with the Bell measurement forced to its trivial outcome. The effective evolution of \(S\) is
\[
\rho_S\mapsto\frac{\operatorname{Tr}_C(U)\,\rho_S\,\operatorname{Tr}_C(U)^\dagger}{\operatorname{Tr}[\ldots]},
\]
which is not linear because of the normalization. In the circuit the projection is a Bell measurement keeping the shots that read 00: a filter on the Bell sector.

text:
14.3 The success law and the grandfather paradox
With \(R_X(\varphi)\) on \(C\) alone, \(\operatorname{Tr}_C(U)=\operatorname{Tr}R_X(\varphi)/2=\cos(\varphi/2)\), and the success is \(\cos^2(\varphi/2)\). At \(\varphi=\pi\) the qubit flips its own past: it is the grandfather paradox, and in P-CTC it has probability zero. It is not resolved: it does not happen. In D-CTC the same case has the maximally mixed state as its fixed point, and it happens with probability 1, like a coin.
On three simulated noise models, with 8000 shots (§164), the success law holds within 0.05 except at \(\varphi=0\) on two devices (C1 failed: 0.950 and 0.931 against 1), and the paradox is suppressed to the noise floor on two of three (C2 failed on FakeTorino):

section: 14.4 The rotation controlled by the system
text:
14.4 The rotation controlled by the system
If it is the system \(S\) that controls the rotation of \(C\), the partial trace is an operator on \(S\):
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_C(U)=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\ \cos\tfrac{\varphi}{2}\right),
\]
and the branch of \(S\) that would produce the paradox is damped by \(c=\cos(\varphi/2)\). From \(|+\rangle\), the postselected state of \(S\) has
\[
qg_Z(S)=\frac{1-c^2}{1+c^2},\qquad qg_X(S)=\frac{2c}{1+c^2},
\]
with success \((1+c^2)/2\). At \(\varphi=\pi\), \(qg_Z(S)=1\): the system is forced into the branch that does not flip the past. On the simulated models FakeFez follows the curve within 0.061 over the whole range, FakeBrisbane reads 0.903 at \(\varphi=\pi\), and FakeTorino loses most of the suppression (0.600): prediction C3 failed.

section: 14.5 What a qg reading tells apart between D-CTC and P-CTC
text:
14.5 What a qg reading tells apart between D-CTC and P-CTC
This section is new in the book: it is exact density-matrix algebra, computed in the figure script, with no device run. The same controlled circuit is taken, with \(S\) in \(|+\rangle\), and the output of \(S\) is computed in both formulations.
In D-CTC the channel on \(C\) is \(\rho_C\mapsto\tfrac12\rho_C+\tfrac12R_X\rho_CR_X^\dagger\), and every state that commutes with \(R_X(\varphi)\) is a fixed point. With the maximum-entropy rule, \(\rho_C=I/2\), and the output of \(S\) is
\[
qg_Z(S)=0,\qquad qg_X(S)=\cos\frac{\varphi}{2},\qquad r=\cos\frac{\varphi}{2}.

title: 14  Postselected closed timelike curves (P-CTC) and the resolution of paradoxes
text:
14.6 The cost of postselection
“Time travel” in this model costs shots. Each useful shot needs, on average, \(1/P_{\text{success}}\) shots: 2 at \(\varphi=\pi/2\), 4 at \(2\pi/3\), 400 at a tenth of a radian from the paradox (Figure 14.3). With the controlled rotation the cost never exceeds 2, because half of the superposition of \(S\) pays nothing. It is the same accounting as the sector filter of the previous chapters, with one difference: here the discarded fraction is not noise but the model’s physics, and it cannot be reduced.






Figure 14.3: Shots needed per useful postselected shot, uncontrolled and with the rotation controlled by S.

title: 14  Postselected closed timelike curves (P-CTC) and the resolution of paradoxes
text:
14.10 Summary

The time loops of this chapter are information models: teleportation with postselection on a Bell outcome.
In P-CTC the success probability is \(\cos^2(\varphi/2)\) and its qang angle is \(\varphi\); the grandfather paradox has probability zero and, on two of three simulated models, sits at the noise floor.
With the controlled rotation, \(qg_Z(S)=(1-c^2)/(1+c^2)\): the paradoxical branch is suppressed; FakeTorino loses most of the suppression.
D-CTC does not change the populations of S and only removes coherence; a \(Z\) reading separates the two models, and the local radius separates Deutsch’s fixed points.
Postselection costs \(1/P\) shots per useful shot; it is the model’s physics, not noise, and it cannot be reduced.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.1 From the base: success 1/4 and the equator of the fidelity
This is the second model of Part V, and the warning of chapter 14 holds again: it is an information-theoretic model, not a statement about real black holes (§164). A black hole of a few qubits, a unitary that scrambles information, and a teleportation postselected on a Bell outcome: the same filter on the Bell sector as in the previous chapter, now set to recover a message that fell into the horizon.
The protocol produces two numbers, and both are probabilities, so the probability equation of chapter 1 reads them directly. The postselection succeeds with probability \(P=1/4\): its reading is \(m_P=1000(2P-1)=-500\) and its qang angle \(\arccos(-1/2)=2\pi/3\). The fidelity \(F\) of the recovered pair with a Bell pair is the probability that the Bell measurement gives its trivial outcome, and it reads the same way, \(m_F=1000(2F-1)\).
The scale has a concrete virtue here: the threshold that matters falls on the equator. A Bell fidelity above \(1/2\) certifies entanglement, and \(F=1/2\) is \(m_F=0\). Without scrambling the pair comes out maximally mixed, \(F=1/4\), and reads \(-500\); with scrambling, \(F=1\), and it reads \(1000\). Decoding is crossing the equator.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.2 The information paradox and complementarity
Hawking (1976) showed that a black hole radiates with a thermal spectrum, and that the radiation does not seem to depend on what fell in. If the hole evaporates completely, a pure state would end as a mixed one: evolution would not be unitary. Complementarity (Susskind et al. 1993) and, above all, Page’s argument (1993) led to the opposite position, the majority one today: the information comes out in the radiation, encoded in fine correlations.
Hayden and Preskill (2007) asked when it comes out. Their answer, for a black hole past the middle of its life whose dynamics scrambles information fast, is “almost at once”: a message of a few qubits thrown into the hole can be rebuilt from just a few more qubits of radiation, given the early radiation. Yoshida and Kitaev (2017) gave an explicit decoder, and it is the one run in this chapter.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.3 Scrambling: a 3-qubit micro black hole
The toy black hole has 3 qubits: the message \(A\) and two qubits \(B_1,B_2\) that were already inside. Its dynamics is a unitary \(U\) on the three, and “\(U\) scrambles information” has an operational definition: every single-qubit Pauli operator ends up, after \(U\), acting on all three qubits. For a Clifford this is checked with no approximation, by evolving the 9 Paulis \(X,Y,Z\) of each qubit. find_scrambler takes the first random Clifford (seed 164) that meets the condition, and its 9 Paulis have weight 3.
Scrambling is the quantum version of chaos: a local error (a Pauli) becomes, after the dynamics, an error of the whole system, and no measurement of one qubit detects it. So it is no surprise that a black hole “hides” the message, and it is a surprise that the message can be recovered.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
section: 15.4 The Hayden–Preskill protocol and the decoder
text:
15.4 The Hayden–Preskill protocol and the decoder
The circuit has 8 qubits. The message \(A\) is entangled with a reference \(R\), the one who throws it; the black hole \(B\) is entangled with the early radiation \(B'\), held by the outside observer. After \(U\) on \((A,B_1,B_2)\), one qubit \(D\) (the output of \(B_2\)) is radiated. The observer holds \(D\) and \(B'\), and prepares a copy of the experiment: a pair \((A',R')\) and the conjugate unitary \(U^*\) on \((A',B'_1,B'_2)\). Then \((D,D')\) is postselected on the Bell state. On success, the entanglement of \(A\) with \(R\) has moved to \(R'\): the message was teleported out of the interior.
For a scrambler, the postselection succeeds with probability \(1/d_A^2=1/4\) and the fidelity of the pair \((R,R')\) is 1. Without scrambling (\(U=I\)), the postselection almost always succeeds, because \(D\) carries nothing of \(A\), and the fidelity is that of a random pair, \(1/4\). The postselection is, as in chapter 14, a filter on the Bell sector of \((D,D')\).

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.5 The exact law \(P\cdot F=1/4\)
This section is new in the book. In Yoshida and Kitaev’s probabilistic decoder, the success and the fidelity are not independent:
\[
P\,F=\frac{1}{d_A^{2}}=\frac14 .
\]
The figure script checks it on exact states over 60 random Cliffords and 25 Haar unitaries of 3 qubits, and at every size of the next section: on 3 qubits the largest deviation is \(3\times10^{-16}\). On the chapter 1 scale the law is a hyperbola,
\[
(1000+m_P)(1000+m_F)=10^{6},\qquad\text{or}\qquad \cos\frac{\theta_P}{2}\,\cos\frac{\theta_F}{2}=\frac12 ,
\]
with a practical consequence: without noise, the success already tells the fidelity. A success of \(1/4\) (\(m_P=-500\)) forces \(F=1\); a success of 1 (\(m_P=1000\)) forces \(F=1/4\). Among random 3-qubit Cliffords, 27 of 60 decode perfectly.
With noise the law breaks, and the direction in which it breaks is what makes it useful. Full noise takes \((D,D')\) to the mixed state, whose success is also \(1/4\), with \(F=1/4\): the success alone does not tell a perfect decoder from one destroyed by noise. The product does: \(4PF\) is 1 for the first and \(1/4\) for the second.

text:
15.7 Larger black holes
This section is new as well: exact states, gate counts and a simulation with the FakeFez noise model, no device run. The circuit is generalised to an \(n\)-qubit black hole with \(k\) radiated qubits: \(2n+2\) qubits in all, 16 for \(n=7\).
Two results organise the topic. The first: with a single radiated qubit, a generic black hole is not enough. For a Haar unitary the average success is \(P\approx\tfrac14+4^{-k}-4^{-k-1}\), and by the law \(F=1/(4P)\): with \(k=1\), \(F\approx4/7=0.57\), barely above the equator, whether \(n=3\), 5 or 7. One has to radiate a little more than the message: with \(k=2\), \(F\approx0.84\); with \(k=3\), \(F\approx0.95\) (Figure 15.2, left). It is the quantitative version of Hayden and Preskill’s “a few more qubits”. The 3-qubit Clifford scrambler, with \(F=1\) at \(k=1\), is a special case, not the typical one.
The second: the gate cost separates the two kinds of scrambler. A Clifford scrambler is transpiled as a Clifford circuit: 35, 126 and 252 two-qubit gates for \(n=3\), 5 and 7. A Haar unitary is synthesised as a generic unitary, and its cost grows as \(4^n\): 92, 1908 and 32 680 (Figure 15.2, right). There is also a lesson for the §164 run: the same 3-qubit scrambler, handed to the transpiler as a matrix, was synthesised with 90 gates; handed over as a Clifford, with 35, and on the FakeFez model the fidelity rises from 0.742 to 0.887 (a new simulation with another seed, not the saved run).

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.8 A toy Page curve
Page (1993) predicted how the entanglement of the radiation of a unitarily evaporating black hole grows: it rises while the radiation is the smaller part, peaks when half has been radiated, and falls to zero at the end, because the total state is pure. An exact toy: a Haar state of 8 qubits, with the first \(k\) as the radiation.
The index proposed reading this curve with \(qg_S\). It does not work, and it is worth saying why. \(qg_S\) is the Shannon entropy of a \(Z\) reading, and a random state looks random in any basis: the joint reading of the \(k\) radiated qubits has entropy close to \(k\) through the whole evaporation, including when the radiation is already nearly pure (Figure 15.3, triangles). It is the limit qang.circuits already documents with graph states as the counterexample: \(qg_S\) depends on the basis and does not measure entanglement.
What does work uses the same qg readings, squared. The purity of the radiation is the sum of the squares of its Pauli correlators,
\[
\operatorname{Tr}\rho^{2}=\frac{1}{2^{k}}\sum_{P\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{k}}qg_P^{\,2},
\]
and \(S_2=-\log_2\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2\), the Rényi entropy of order 2, is a lower bound on the von Neumann entropy that follows the Page curve: at \(k=4\), the half, \(S_2=2.98\) bits against \(S=3.24\), and both return to zero at \(k=8\), while the Shannon entropy of the \(Z\) reading reaches 7.46. The cost is the unfavourable side: \(4^k-1\) correlators, 255 for \(k=4\). (The script computes it from the correlators up to \(k=4\); beyond that it uses \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2\) directly, the same quantity.)






Figure 15.3: A toy Page curve, 8 qubits. The von Neumann entropy of the radiation and the Rényi-2 entropy computed from the qg correlators rise and fall; the Shannon entropy of the \(Z\) reading keeps rising and does not see the curve.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.9 Traversable wormholes
The Yoshida–Kitaev decoder is, as a circuit, the same protocol that the holographic literature calls teleportation through a traversable wormhole (Gao et al. 2017; Maldacena et al. 2017): two entangled systems, a scrambling dynamics on each (one side conjugated) and a coupling between them that lets a qubit through. The ER = EPR conjecture (Maldacena and Susskind 2013) proposes that such entangled pairs are, in a dual gravitational theory, an Einstein–Rosen bridge. The circuit decides none of that; it does let the result be read with the tools of this book.
The fidelity of the recovered pair is linear in three qg correlators, as in chapter 13:
\[
F=\frac{1+qg_{XX}-qg_{YY}+qg_{ZZ}}{4}.
\]
On the exact state, with the scrambler, \((qg_{XX},qg_{YY},qg_{ZZ})=(1,-1,1)\) and \(F=1\); without scrambling, \((0,0,0)\) and \(F=1/4\). The experiment of Jafferis et al. (2022) on a Google processor used a learned 7-qubit model to mimic this physics, and its reading as a wormhole was disputed (Kobrin et al. 2023). This book does not run that experiment; the correlator reading stays a tool, not evidence.

None of the new results of this chapter (the law \(PF=1/4\) as a diagnostic, the 5- and 7-qubit black holes, the Page curve from correlators) has a device run. A real-hardware run of the 3-qubit decoder, with 90 two-qubit gates, would be the next step and costs credits; it stays outside this book for now.

title: 15  Black-hole thermodynamics, quantum chaos and the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder
text:
15.13 Summary

The Yoshida–Kitaev decoder is teleportation postselected on the Bell sector of a radiated qubit and its copy: a model of information, not of gravity.
On the chapter 1 scale, the success \(1/4\) is \(m_P=-500\) and the fidelity that certifies recovery, \(F>1/2\), is \(m_F>0\): decoding is crossing the equator.
The exact law \(PF=1/4\) is a hyperbola in m-qg; with noise, the success stays at \(1/4\) but the fidelity drops, and \(4PF\) (0.57–0.73 on three simulated models) measures the quality of the decoder.
With a single radiated qubit, a generic black hole gives \(F\approx0.57\); 2 or 3 radiated qubits are needed for \(F\approx0.84\)–\(0.95\).
A Clifford scrambler costs 35, 126 and 252 two-qubit gates on 3, 5 and 7 qubits; with 7, the fidelity on FakeFez stays at 0.88 but the success falls to 0.105 and \(4PF\) to 0.37: the filter keeps the quality and charges in rate.
\(qg_S\) does not see the Page curve; the Rényi-2 entropy from the qg correlators does, at the cost of \(4^k-1\) readings.

title: 16  Demarcation: quantum cryptography against post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
text:
16.1 From the base: which probabilities exist on each side
Part VI is about security. Before reading quantum key distribution (Chapter 17) and certified random numbers (Chapter 18) in qg, it is worth drawing the border. There are two answers to the quantum computer that share the word “quantum” and little else. Quantum cryptography (QKD, QRNG) uses qubits: its security rests on a physical measurement, and so it enters the probability equation of Chapter 1. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is classical software that runs on ordinary computers: its security rests on the hardness of a mathematical problem, and there is no qubit to read. This chapter says where the line runs, with numbers, and what qang reads on each side.
Any probability \(p_0\) enters the equation of Chapter 1: it has qang angle \(\theta=2\arccos\sqrt{p_0}\) and reading \(m=1000(1-2p_1)\) m-qg. The question is not whether it can be written down, but whether the reading says anything.
The security of PQC, moreover, is not that probability: it is the hardness of a lattice problem (module learning with errors, MLWE), which is not the frequency of anything. That is the demarcation in one line: qang reads probabilities of measurements; PQC has no measurements.

title: 16  Demarcation: quantum cryptography against post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
text:
In QKD, the probability that decides security is the quantum bit error rate (QBER) of a measurement in one basis. It is the probability of a qubit, and its reading is the one of Chapter 17: \(Q=(1-|qg|)/2\), that is, \(m=1000\,|qg|=1000(1-2Q)\).
In PQC, the only probability in the scheme is that decryption fails, \(\delta\). For ML-KEM, the FIPS 203 standard bounds it by \(2^{-138.8}\), \(2^{-164.8}\) and \(2^{-174.8}\) for the three levels. Written in m-qg it is \(m=1000-3.3\times10^{-39}\) at best: it sits against the pole, and there is no Hermitian operator, measurement basis or Bloch sphere behind that number.

title: 16  Demarcation: quantum cryptography against post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
text:
16.2 The nature of PQC
NIST’s standards of August 2024 are three: ML-KEM (FIPS 203, formerly Kyber), a lattice key-encapsulation mechanism; ML-DSA (FIPS 204, formerly Dilithium), lattice signatures; and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, formerly SPHINCS+), signatures built only on hash functions. In 2025 HQC, based on error-correcting codes, was also chosen as a second key mechanism. All of them are integer arithmetic: polynomials modulo \(q=3329\) in ML-KEM, hash trees in SLH-DSA. None of them prepares a state, applies a gate or measures.
In ML-KEM, decrypting is subtracting and rounding: the message survives if an accumulated noise (the sum of many products of small coefficients) stays within \(\pm q/4\). If not, decryption fails. That is the \(\delta\) above.

The count agrees with the exact sum, and qang.probability.analyze reads it in m-qg with its interval. But that reading is the Wilson proportion in another unit: there is no angle of a state behind it. And no count reaches where real PQC lives (Figure 16.1, right). Seeing a single ML-KEM-512 failure takes on the order of \(1/\delta\approx6\times10^{41}\) decryptions; with \(10^{12}\) trials, about the most one can count, the floor sits 30 orders of magnitude above. The shot rule of Chapter 1 says the same in m-qg: next to the pole, \(\sigma_m\approx2000\sqrt{\delta/N}\), and to bring it below the offset \(2000\,\delta\) one needs \(N>1/\delta\). PQC’s \(\delta\) is proved, not measured.






Figure 16.1: Left: the security frontier of BB84 is a line in m-qg; the Shor–Preskill asymptotic key rate vanishes at 780 m-qg (Q = 11%), and with 2000 shots the reading has ±2σ of 14–24 m-qg. Right: the decryption failure of a toy ML-KEM-like scheme (n = 256, no compression), exact, Gaussian and counted; the orange lines are the FIPS 203 bounds, 30 to 41 orders of magnitude below what can be counted.



On the other side of the line (Figure 16.1, left), the quantity that decides BB84’s security sits in the middle of the scale. The Shor–Preskill asymptotic rate, \(1-2h(Q)\), vanishes at \(Q=11.0\%\), which is \(m=780\) m-qg; intercept-resend gives \(Q=25\%\), \(m=500\). With 2000 shots, \(\sigma_m\) is 11.8, 9.7 and 7.0 m-qg at 850, 900 and 950 m-qg: the margin to the threshold is resolved comfortably. It is the probability of a qubit, readable and with an error bar; Chapter 17 uses it to separate the eavesdropper from the noise.

text:
16.4 The quantum attack vector: Grover
The quantum computer is quantum, and its attacks do enter the base. Grover’s attack on an \(n\)-bit key has, after \(k\) iterations, failure probability
\[
p_{\text{fail}}=\cos^2\!\big((2k+1)\,\beta\big),\qquad \beta=\arcsin 2^{-n/2},
\]
which is the probability equation with qang angle \(2(2k+1)\beta\): each iteration advances the qang angle by \(4\beta\), in a straight line. This was checked with the circuits of qang.algorithms for \(n=4\), 6, 8 and 10: the angle of the exact probability matches the law to \(10^{-10}\) rad (Figure 16.2). In m-qg, the failure goes from +1000 to −1000 along a cosine and crosses the equator (success 1/2) halfway.






Figure 16.2: Left: the qang angle of the probability that Grover fails grows linearly with the iterations, \(4\arcsin 2^{-n/2}\) per step (dots: exact circuits; lines: the law). Right: the same probability in m-qg against the fraction of the optimal iterations.



For AES-128 the step is \(4\arcsin2^{-64}=2.2\times10^{-19}\) rad per iteration, and reaching the pole takes \(1.4\times10^{19}\) serial iterations, each a full AES circuit; for AES-256, \(2.7\times10^{38}\). PQC’s answer to this attack is to double the symmetric key length, and the geometry explains it: the angle advances as \(2^{-n/2}\), so Grover halves the security bits and nothing more.

16.5 The quantum attack vector: Shor and phase estimation
The attack that breaks RSA and elliptic curves, and that PQC sidesteps, is Shor’s algorithm: phase estimation (QPE) on modular multiplication. The notes (§13) show that QPE recovers exact phases, and the book’s index said that “the eigenstate register projects onto \(qg_Z=-1\) without resolving the phase”. That holds for the QPE of an eigenstate, and the exact computation of this chapter says how far a qg reading goes in Shor’s case (Figure 16.3).
QPE of an eigenstate. With the \(T\) gate on \(|1\rangle\) (\(\varphi=1/8\)), the target register stays at \(m_Z=-1000\) and carries no information: the phase lives in the counting register. There, before the inverse QFT, qubit \(k\) has \(m_X=1000\cos(2\pi2^k\varphi)\): 707, 0 and −1000 m-qg. Each qubit carries one bit of the phase in its qang angle, which is Kitaev’s iterative phase estimation.
Shor for \(N=15\). The work register is not in an eigenstate but in a superposition of the \(r\) eigenstates, and the counting qubits end up entangled with it. With four counting qubits:
