text:
26.4 The surface code and the T1-aware decoder
In the rotated distance-3 surface code (9 data qubits), each averaged stabilizer is the qg readout of a parity. The script recomputes at code capacity, enumerating the 512 patterns: \(p_L=1.79\cdot10^{-5}\), \(1.73\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(1.44\cdot10^{-2}\) at \(p=0.001\), 0.01 and 0.03, and a pseudo-threshold of 0.0753 (notes §59).
The syndromes barely see T1. Under damping, a weight-\(w\) syndrome reads exactly \((1-\gamma)^w+\gamma^w\), against \((1-\gamma)^w\) for the equivalent Pauli model: at \(\gamma=0.01\) and \(w=2\), 0.98020 against 0.98010, a difference that would need about \(10^8\) shots. The register’s mean readout does see it: it is \(\gamma\) under T1 and 0 for symmetric flips, and it comes from the same bits.
Decoding knowing that T1 leaves zeros. A decay only turns a 1 into a 0, so a decoder that places errors only on bits read 0 lowers the logical error:

A qg witness (final mean readout over detector rate) chooses the decoder without labels: 1.3–2.6 where the T1-aware decoder wins and 0.34–0.54 where it loses, although the threshold of 1 was chosen after seeing the cases.

title: 26  Error correction and continuous syndromes
text:
26.5 Qutrits and erasure qubits
Before extending qang beyond the qubit, the notes asked whether a three-level readout gives it an advantage (§70–§74), with criteria committed before each run:

If the leaked qubit keeps its value, the \(|2\rangle\) flag is useless (§70): all the gain was the T1 reweighting, and adding the flag made it worse. Recorded verdict: no qutrit advantage.
If the leak scrambles the qubit, it helps (§70b): reweighting plus flag give 1.78 times over standard, more than the product of the two parts (1.55).
A rule for the flag (§71): weighting it by where the leak came from (posterior \(1/(1+a)\)) is never worse than standard, and the qutrit-plus-qg gain grows with distance (1.48 times at \(d=3\), 1.77 at \(d=5\)). One of the four predictions failed, so it stands as a partly confirmed rule.
A real transmon (§72, coherent three-level CZ): leakage comes only from \(|11\rangle\), the asymmetry is zero and the flag is nearly useless; the qg reweighting is not (1.8–2.0 times).
Erasure qubits (§73, §74): if the device heralds decays with probability \(h\), naively combining the herald with the reweighting makes things worse (0.46 times at \(h=0.99\)). The \((1-h)\) rule, committed before running, fixes it: qg still gives 1.4–1.9 times at \(h=0.25\)–\(0.5\) and fades towards 1 when heralding is nearly perfect.

section: 26.6 Cutting circuits: where and at what cost
text:
26.6 Cutting circuits: where and at what cost
Cutting a two-qubit gate to run a large circuit in pieces multiplies the shots needed by \(\gamma^2\). For a Pauli rotation such as RZZ\((\theta)\), in qg (notes §15.2):
\[
\gamma=1+2|\sin\theta|=1+2\sqrt{1-qg^2},\qquad qg=\cos\theta .
\]
Cutting is free at the poles (\(qg=\pm1\)) and costs 9 times at the equator. A shortcut that circulates, \(\gamma^2=1+\sqrt{1-qg^2}\), underestimates the cost by up to 4.5 times (2 instead of 9 at \(qg=0\)).
Where to cut? An 8-qubit circuit with 12 RZZ couplings must run in blocks of at most 4 qubits (§26). The script compares three rules on 200 instances per regime, choosing among the 3795 partitions:

With small angles, “cut the weakest bonds” nearly matches the qg rule. With large angles it is the worst rule: RZZ\((\theta\approx\pi)\) is almost a local \(Z\otimes Z\) and nearly free to cut. The reference tool already does this: qiskit-addon-cutting’s find_cuts reaches the optimum on all 400 of the notes’ instances (it is not installed in this environment, so the script does not run it). What qg adds is the closed form: scoring the 3795 partitions takes 1–2 ms per instance. In the notes’ end-to-end run, the qg choice lowers the error 2.9 times with shots proportional to the weights, and raises it with equal shots per subexperiment: the \(\gamma^2\) law assumes importance sampling.

section: 26.7 Randomized benchmarking, ZNE and \(qg_S\) as a signal
text:
26.7 Randomized benchmarking, ZNE and \(qg_S\) as a signal

Randomized benchmarking (§11.1): with per-gate depolarizing noise, the survival is exactly \(qg_Z(m)=(1-p)^{m+1}\), the same for any Clifford sequence. The script confirms it on four seeds (0.95, 0.7351 and 0.5688 at \(m=0\), 5 and 10).
ZNE: which space to extrapolate in (§11.2): if the noise shrinks the readout, extrapolating in qg is exact (\(10^{-16}\)) and in the angle it is not (\(10^{-4}\)); if the noise rotates the angle, the other way round. Rule: extrapolate where the noise is linear, and the \(\theta\leftrightarrow qg\) change makes trying both cheap.
\(qg_S\) as a signal (§10): the output entropy follows the heavy-output probability without ideal simulation (correlation −0.926 under depolarizing noise), but under T1 it stops being monotone: on a fake brisbane model with a 200 µs idle it falls below the noiseless value, and would rank the most damaged point as the least noisy. With the register’s mean readout alongside, which rises at every step, the pair is no longer fooled.

title: 26  Error correction and continuous syndromes
text:
26.11 Summary

Each syndrome is the qg readout of a parity; \(qg_Z\) of \(|1\rangle\) and \(qg_X\) of \(|+\rangle\) read T1 and dephasing.
No repetition code corrects T1; the Leung code does. Rule: Leung if \(T_2>T_1\), no code if \(0.4\,T_1<T_2<T_1\), phase code if \(T_2<0.4\,T_1\).
The Leung syndromes track drift without probe shots, and read the product mean of the dephasing.
In the surface code the syndromes do not see T1 and the mean readout does; placing errors only on bits read 0 lowers the logical error 2–3 times when T1 dominates.
With qutrits and erasure qubits, qg adds up if the flag is weighted by its origin and the herald by \((1-h)\).
Cutting an RZZ costs \((1+2\sqrt{1-qg^2})^2\): free at the poles, 9 times at the equator.

title: 27  Hardware characterization in qg
text:
27.1 From the base: an idle qubit is a readout
Before running any algorithm one has to know what the device is like: how long it takes to decay (T1), how long to lose its phase (T2), how hot it is and how often it misreads. This chapter reads those quantities on the Chapter 1 scale. Each one shows up as a qg readout, and the scale helps in three concrete cases: separating temperature from readout error, telling T1 from unital noise with the mean readout, and choosing the grid with which the electronics sets the angles. All three are recomputed with code. The results on IBM device models are those of the notes’ committed runs.
A real qubit is never completely cold: at rest it has a residual excited population \(p\), and its equilibrium readout is \(qg_{eq}=1-2p\), in m-qg \(m_{eq}=1000(1-2p)\). For a qubit of frequency \(f\) in thermal equilibrium,
\[
qg_{eq}=\tanh\!\left(\frac{hf}{2k_BT_{\text{eff}}}\right),
\]
so the equilibrium readout is a thermometer. The instrument’s readout is also affine in qg: if it confuses 0→1 with probability \(e_{01}\) and 1→0 with \(e_{10}\), the measured readout is \(a+b\,qg\), with \(a=e_{10}-e_{01}\) and \(b=1-e_{01}-e_{10}\) (notes §31). The problem is that in the Z basis only \(a+b\,qg_{eq}\) is seen: temperature and readout error are mixed.

section: 27.2 T1, T2, temperature and readout in one sweep
text:
27.2 T1, T2, temperature and readout in one sweep
The standard calibration measures “\(|0\rangle\)” and “\(|1\rangle\)”, which are really the thermal state and X applied to it, and counts the thermal population as readout error. The qg protocol adds a herald: measure, apply I, X or \(R_y(\pi/2)\), wait and measure again. The pairs at zero delay give, in closed form, the mean \(m\), the readout covariance \(V=b^2(1-qg_{eq}^2)\) and \(C_X=a^2-b^2\), from which \(a\), \(b\) and \(qg_{eq}\) follow. The delays add T1 (after X) and T2 (the decay of \(qg_X\)). The script repeats the notes’ experiment with 40 repetitions of 16 circuits of 2000 shots (T1 = 100 µs, T2 = 70 µs, \(e_{01}=0.015\), \(e_{10}=0.04\), 5 GHz):

27.3 Which noise is it? The mean readout against XEB and HOP
With \(N\) shots of a 4-qubit quantum-volume circuit, can one decide whether the noise is dissipative (T1) or unital (dephasing or depolarizing)? The notes (§18) set it up with 24 circuits, three channels and 10 strengths, and each measure is turned into a classifier with a single threshold fitted on 16 circuits and scored on 8 it has not seen. XEB and HOP need the ideal distribution (a classical simulation); the mean readout and \(qg_S\) only need counts. The script recomputes it:

With strong noise, the mean readout identifies T1 much better than the standard measures, from only 100 shots and without the ideal distribution: 0.88 with 100 shots and 0.91 with 1000 or more. Its accuracy grows with the strength (0.75 below 10% per gate, 0.98 above 25%). XEB and HOP measure how much noise there is, not which kind.
At realistic strengths everything is at chance, even with 100,000 shots. The limit is not shot noise: the ideal mean readout already varies from circuit to circuit (spread 0.139, from −0.325 to +0.334), more than the T1 shift.

The practical consequence: the mean readout is a T1 detector on circuits whose ideal value is known, such as an idle wait before measurement, not a passive detector on any circuit.

title: 27  Hardware characterization in qg
section: 27.4 Coherent errors and the always-on ZZ
text:
27.4 Coherent errors and the always-on ZZ
A conditional-phase error (an extra ZZ) conserves the weight, so one might expect it to pass the weight filter unnoticed. The notes tested this twice with committed predictions, and both times the prediction failed in an informative way:

A coherent RZZ after every native gate (§145): the kept fraction fell by 0.009–0.020 at \(\varepsilon=0.10\) rad, and the filtered error grew only 4% on the ECR devices but 62% on FakeTorino (CZ). The error acts inside the decomposition of the logical gate, where the qubits are not in the computational basis, and part of it leaves the sector.
Always-on ZZ between neighbours (§150, 5 and 15 kHz): the filter removed 32–60% of the added error; the filtered error grew 14–38% at 15 kHz and stayed 4–5 times below raw. Short circuits suffer least.

On these devices coherent errors are filtered in proportion to the time the qubits spend outside the computational basis.

title: 27  Hardware characterization in qg
section: 27.5 Control quantization: an even grid in the angle or in qg
text:
27.5 Control quantization: an even grid in the angle or in qg
The electronics sets each angle from a grid of \(2^b\) values. The usual choice is a grid even in \(\theta\); a grid even in \(qg=\cos\theta\) is even in the Born probability and, on the Bloch sphere, is made of equal-area bands (notes §17). The script recomputes it:

One qubit, random targets: the qg grid’s worst probability error is exactly \(\pi/2\) times smaller (1.568, 1.570 and 1.570 with 4, 8 and 10 bits; it saves \(\log_2(\pi/2)\approx0.65\) bits). But its worst infidelity is worse, by a factor that grows like \(2^b\) (from 2.7·10⁻³ to 1.7·10⁻² with 4 bits), because it is coarse near the poles.
Loading a distribution with a tree of \(R_y\) rotations (the state-preparation step of quantum Monte Carlo): in qg each rotation is set directly by a conditional probability, \(qg=2p-1\). In the 45 cases (4, 6 and 8 qubits; 4, 6 and 8 bits; five distributions), the qg grid lowers the total variation distance in 43 of 45 (median 1.56 times, up to 2.9).
For smooth distributions the infidelity is also lower with the qg grid (25 of 27, median 1.98 times); for sparse or sharply peaked ones the \(\theta\) grid wins (15 of 18, median 3.3 times, up to 56).

Design rule: a grid even in qg when the task is to reproduce probabilities (sampling, Monte Carlo, smooth distributions); a grid even in \(\theta\) when state fidelity matters and the targets sit near the poles.






Figure 27.2: Left: accuracy in telling T1 from unital noise with four measures, at 100 and 10,000 shots and strong noise. Right: ratio between the total variation distance with a \(\theta\) grid and with a qg grid in the 45 loading cases; above 1 the qg grid wins.

27.6 What remains open
The heralded sweep (§86, 32 one-qubit circuits) is ready for a real IBM device and is the first thing worth running: the thermal population, its central point, does not exist in the simulators. T1 detection at realistic strengths needs circuits with a known ideal value.

Balance. This is the chapter where the qang scale contributes most on its own, without depending on the weight filter: the equilibrium readout is a thermometer, the instrument’s readout is affine in qg and separates from the temperature in closed form, the mean readout tells dissipation from unital noise, and a grid even in qg is the right grid for probabilities. The limits are written down: with realistic noise the mean readout does not classify arbitrary circuits, and the qg grid loses in fidelity near the poles.

title: 27  Hardware characterization in qg
text:
27.9 Summary

The equilibrium readout \(qg_{eq}=\tanh(hf/2k_BT_{\text{eff}})\) is a thermometer, and the instrument’s readout is affine in qg.
The standard calibration counts temperature as readout error; the heralded sweep separates the two without bias and measures the temperature to 1 mK.
The mean readout tells T1 from unital noise with 100 shots when the noise is strong (0.88 against 0.70–0.72); with realistic noise nothing manages it on arbitrary circuits.
Coherent ZZ errors are not invisible to the filter: they are filtered according to the time spent outside the computational basis.
A grid even in qg improves 43 of 45 distribution loads; one even in \(\theta\) is better for fidelity near the poles.

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
text:
28.1 From the base: a prediction is a readout that can be wrong
The previous chapters quoted “predictions committed before running” again and again. This chapter explains what that means, how many held and how many failed, and something a book about a new scale owes its reader: an audit of whether that “before” can be checked. There is no new physics here. The chapter’s script simulates nothing: it inspects the repository itself, its git history and the files the runs stored.
On the Chapter 1 scale, nearly every claim in the notes is a number in m-qg or a ratio between two errors. That the filter “helps” says nothing; that it lowers the readout error from 104 to 23 m-qg on three devices does, and it can fail. The discipline is to write that number and the threshold that would make it false before running, to pin it in a way that cannot be changed later, and to publish the outcome whatever it is.

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
section: 28.2 Two ways of pinning a prediction
text:
28.2 Two ways of pinning a prediction
The notes used two:

By commit: the predictions are written and pushed to the repository before the run, and the section cites that commit (for instance, “committed before the run (77700bd)”). It is the method of §71 to §165.
By sha256: the script that does the run is frozen, the sha256 of its bytes is computed and stored in examples/data/*.prereg with a timestamp. If the script changes, the hash stops matching. It is the method of the neutrino, kernel, VarQTE, IQM and other sections.
crumbs: X. Experimental evidence, real hardware and the falsification audit

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
section: 28.3 The tally of hits and misses
text:
28.3 The tally of hits and misses
What the code stored. 33 runs leave in their results file a dictionary of verdicts computed by the script itself. The chapter’s script counts them: 143 predictions, 89 passed (62%) and 54 failed. Three runs failed all their predictions (the IBM fleet, the coherent ZZ and collective neutrinos) and six passed all of theirs.
The QML line. For §75–§123, the repository’s README keeps another tally: 176 predictions judged, 123 passed and 53 failed, with 4 more waiting for the IonQ hardware run. The two counts are separate bookkeeping that partly overlap, and must not be added.
What cannot be recounted automatically. The sections before §71 barely use pre-registration, and many later ones record their verdicts only in prose (“Four passed; V1 failed”), with varied wording. A full count over §1–§168 would have to be done by hand, section by section. This book does not do it: it gives the two counts that can be checked.
A 62% hit rate is not a weakness. A rate near 100% would signal thresholds that are too soft. Several failures were the most informative results in the notes: the coherent ZZ that the filter does see (Chapter 27), the erasure rule that had to be fixed with \((1-h)\) (Chapter 26), the qg_YY metric that helps less than predicted (Chapter 23).
crumbs: X. Experimental evidence, real hardware and the falsification audit
28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
text:
28.4 Audit of the “before”
That a prediction was written “before” has to be checkable. The script checks it with git:

By commit (54 citations, §71–§165): every cited commit exists in the history and, at that commit, the notes do not yet contain the section’s results. All 54 are consistent.
By sha256 (15 files): no script matches its hash today, as expected, because after the run the findings are added to its opening comment. The question is whether any stored version matches.

In 7 of 15, the hash matches the script at the commit that added the .prereg, and that commit is earlier than the results’. The “before” is checked.
In 8 of 15, the .prereg and the results came in the same commit, and no version of the script stored in git matches the hash: the script was frozen, run and edited before anything was pushed. For those eight the “before” rests only on the file’s own timestamp, which the author could have written at any time.


The eight are: neutrino matter and oscillation, mass ordering and steriles, solar neutrinos, post-selection and CTCs, pulse area, the quantum kernel and VarQTE. Their results are not false because of this; their pre-registration cannot be checked by a third party. The fix for what comes next is simple: push the .prereg and the frozen script in a commit of their own before running.






Figure 28.1: Left: predictions passed and failed in the 33 runs that store their verdicts. Right: audit of the “before”: the 54 predictions pinned by commit are consistent; of the 15 sha256 pre-registrations, 7 can be checked in git and 8 only have their own timestamp.

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
text:
28.5 Testbeds
Nearly all the book’s results come from simulations with calibrated noise models, not from hardware:

IBM: qiskit-ibm-runtime’s models with real published calibrations (Brisbane, Sherbrooke, Torino, Fez and a fleet of 21), run locally in Aer or in IBM Runtime’s local mode (§137, §144).
IonQ: the cloud simulator with the Aria-1 and Forte-1 noise models, free (§20, §38). Without dominant T1: the mean readout does not move (+0.004 and +0.007, consistent with zero), the opposite of the IBM model.
IQM: the simulated Apollo and Garnet models, used as a free rehearsal before every real run.

A calibrated noise model is not a device: it has no thermal population (Chapter 27), no drift, and none of the ways the vendor’s software batches circuits. That is why the book calls “simulated” everything that did not run on hardware.

title: 28  Methodology: the pre-registered falsification protocol
text:
28.6 Real hardware

IonQ Forte-1 (§128): the predictions for H\(_2\) with the filter were pinned by commit and the simulator rehearsal met them, but the vendor refused the first submission before accepting the job (the project did not have that QPU enabled). Nothing was charged and there is no data.
IQM Garnet, three-flavour neutrinos (§165, 8 circuits of 300 shots): the script rescores the four checks from the stored run, and all four hold. The error falls from 0.0615 to 0.0386 (1.59 times) and 88% of the shots are kept. With the filter the survival minimum sits at 2.6 GeV (exact 2.63); without it, at 0.8 GeV.
IQM Garnet, the milli-qang (§168, 26 circuits of 4000 shots on one qubit): three of four predictions held. The script recomputes the X-gate cost with a single slope: 1.64 m-qg per gate (\(\chi^2/\text{dof}=0.81\)). Prediction M2 failed: the ten equator copies scatter half as much as binomial noise allows (ratio 0.50). It remains open.

The two IQM runs are the project’s first real-hardware data, and Chapter 31 treats them in detail. A replication of §168 on five qubits and two days is prepared but not pushed to the repository, because at full size it would cost about 80 credits and 12.50 are left.
The \(\mathrm{Var}_\theta(F_{\text{echo}})\) criterion. The index announced a QPU falsification criterion based on the variance of the inversion echo over continuous trajectories. It is not defined anywhere in the repository, so the book does not use it. It remains an unwritten proposal.

title: 29  The confirmed empirical advantages
text:
29.1 From the base: where the advantages come from
After twenty-eight chapters of “without qang and with qang” comparisons, this one gathers those that gave a measurable benefit, with their size, their limits and where each figure comes from. The bar for entry is strict: a gain measured in code or in a pre-registered run, against the same action without the scale or without the filter, with the case where it stops holding written next to it. Every factor is recomputed here, device by device, from the runs’ stored files. Nothing is simulated again. What did not pass the bar goes to Chapter 30.
The book’s advantages have two origins, and they should not be mixed:
crumbs: X. Experimental evidence, real hardware and the falsification audit
29  The confirmed empirical advantages

title: 29  The confirmed empirical advantages
text:
The weight filter (Chapters 20–25): if the circuit conserves the number of excitations, every shot with the wrong weight had an error and is discarded. It is symmetry verification, a known technique. The qang scale contributes the witness (the register’s mean readout, whose ideal value is known before running) and the rule for when it pays (Chapter 21).
The scale itself (Chapters 18, 23, 26, 27): readouts that separate things the raw readout mixes. Temperature from readout error, T1 from unital noise, thermal drift from an attack.

title: 29  The confirmed empirical advantages
text:
29.4 In-sector errors: the echo
What the filter does not see, the echo measures (Chapter 22). With the weight-1 network on 189 inputs and 1000 shots, on five simulated devices, the decisions that differ from the noiseless network are 15 without qang, 7 with the filter and 3 with the filter plus the echo, over 945 readouts (§106). The echo removes 43 to 56% of the decision-value error the filter leaves. It does not help with narrow-margin inputs, when the filtered error is already close to its shot noise (§108).
crumbs: X. Experimental evidence, real hardware and the falsification audit
29  The confirmed empirical advantages

title: 29  The confirmed empirical advantages
text:
29.5 Characterization and control
These advantages belong to the scale itself, without the filter (Chapter 27):

Temperature and readout: the heralded sweep measures the readout error without bias and the effective temperature to 1 mK, where the standard calibration inflates the error by \(p\cdot b\) and sees the qubit at 0 mK.
T1 diagnosis without classical simulation: the mean readout tells T1 from unital noise with 88% accuracy from 100 shots under strong noise, against 70–76% for XEB and HOP, which also need the ideal distribution. With realistic noise nothing tells the two apart on arbitrary circuits.
Control quantization: a grid even in qg lowers the total variation distance when loading a distribution in 43 of 45 cases (median 1.56 times), and the worst probability error by an exact factor \(\pi/2\). It loses in fidelity near the poles.
crumbs: X. Experimental evidence, real hardware and the falsification audit
29  The confirmed empirical advantages

title: 29  The confirmed empirical advantages
text:
29.6 Neutrinos: mitigation without extra circuits
Neutrino oscillations in a circuit conserve the weight, so the filter applies without adding any circuit. With three flavours (§151), the error falls 3.4 times in the median of three simulated devices (the index said 3 times); with a sterile neutrino (§163), 5.6 times, and the survival dip appears at the right energy on all three. On IQM Garnet (§165), on real hardware, the filter cuts the error 1.59 times and puts the oscillation maximum back at 2.6 GeV (exact 2.63), where the raw readout placed it at 0.8 GeV. It is the only one of these advantages confirmed on hardware.

title: 30  Structural limits, equivalences and negative results
text:
30.1 From the base: what the scale cannot see
Chapter 29 gathered what gave a measurable benefit. This one gathers what did not: the blind spots that come from the definition of the scale itself, the equivalences that were offered as advantages, and the predictions that failed. A limit gets in if it can be shown in code or is in a stored run, with the same action without qang next to it. The new checks are in tools/make_cap30_figures.py; the rest is quoted from the notes and from the chapters where it was measured.
The equation of Chapter 1 makes qg a function of a single probability, \(p_0\), measured in the Z basis. Two kinds of limits follow:
Neither is an implementation defect: both follow from the definition.

What lives outside the Z populations. Relative phases and coherences do not change \(p_0\), so no Z-basis qg readout sees them. They only show up when measuring in another basis, and that is no longer the Z-basis qg readout.
What the filter cannot reach. The filter discards shots outside the right weight sector. An error that leaves the shot in the sector, or a circuit that does not conserve the weight, is out of its reach.

title: 30  Structural limits, equivalences and negative results
text:
30.3 \(qg_S\) is not monotonic under T1
Under depolarizing noise, \(qg_S\) (the entropy of the Z distribution divided by \(n\)) rises towards 1 as the noise grows, so it can rank devices. Under amplitude damping (T1) it cannot: it first rises, because the noise mixes, and then falls, because T1 pushes everything to \(|0\ldots0\rangle\), which has entropy 0.
The script runs 24 four-qubit quantum-volume circuits with amplitude damping on every qubit after every two-qubit block, with exact density matrices:

\(qg_S\) rises and falls in all 24. In circuit 0 it starts at 0.919, reaches 0.981 at \(\gamma=0.06\) and comes back to 0.923 at \(\gamma=0.28\). On its own it cannot tell an almost noiseless device from one with a lot of T1.
The pair (\(qg_S\), mean \(qg_Z\)) can. At those two points the mean \(qg_Z\) is −0.029 and +0.209. T1 pushes the mean \(qg_Z\) towards +1 and depolarizing noise leaves it at 0 (it goes from −0.029 to 0.000).
The fix is not a theorem. In this model the mean \(qg_Z\) rises monotonically in 21 of the 24 circuits. The notes, with their mid-circuit T1 model, found it in 23 of 24 (§10.4 D). The others have small downward steps.







Figure 30.1: Left: under T1 (blue, band over 24 circuits) \(qg_S\) rises and falls back; under depolarizing noise (grey) it only rises. Right: the mean \(qg_Z\) rises under T1 and stays at 0 under depolarizing noise.

title: 30  Structural limits, equivalences and negative results
text:
30.4 The natural-gradient equivalence
Chapter 23 measured it, and here it is written down as a limit. A change of coordinate does not speed up an optimizer. The natural gradient written in qg is plain descent in \(\theta\), up to terms of order \(\eta^2\) (notes §15.1). Claims that it “converges in qg where \(\theta\) does not” came from clipping \(\theta\) to \([0,\pi]\). That hides the minima at \(\theta<0\), and without the clip descent in \(\theta\) converges.
In the pre-registered run of §159, with 20 seeds of the 4-qubit Ising model:

descent in \(\theta\) got there in 103 steps (median);
descent in qg never got there;
the natural gradient with the full metric took 22.5 steps.

That gain belongs to the natural gradient, not to qang: the full metric is not read in qg. The version that is read from qg correlators (\(qg_{YY}\) blocks) took 79.5 steps. It improved 1.3 times on \(\theta\), not the 1.5 that had been predicted (G2 failed).

The qg remedy for the X/Y groups fails. Rescaling them by the depolarizing strength read from the kept fraction overcorrects, by 2 to 3 times (from +97 to −124 mHa). Local gate noise is not global depolarizing noise.
Hubbard hits the same wall (§29). On fake_brisbane, from 4 Trotter steps on (188 ECR or more, 18 % of the shots kept), every method sits on the noise floor: the double occupancy tends to 1/4 and the charge imbalance to 0.

title: 30  Structural limits, equivalences and negative results
text:
30.6 The weight-1 network is classical
The filter protects a weight-conserving quantum neural network exactly against T1 (Chapter 20). The same reason makes it simulable. In the weight-1 sector the network is an orthogonal matrix \(O\) acting on the loaded data \(v\), and each readout is \(qg_Z^{(i)} = 1 - 2\,(Ov)_i^2\). It is a quadratic form in \(v\), computable in \(O(n^2)\) (notes §76, F2). The script checks it on 5-qubit circuits with a unary loader and a random RBS network: the largest error is \(7.8\cdot10^{-16}\).

§75: the best classical model ties or beats the best quantum network on all four datasets (on digits, an RBF-kernel SVM 0.963 against 0.933). There is no quantum advantage.
§76: prediction Q3 said the network would not beat its quadratic twin by more than 1 point, and it failed, but because of the baseline. The twin used the default regularization. Rerun after the result with \(C=100\), it sits 0.3 to 1.6 points from the network.
With weight 2 the output is quartic and no longer trivial. Even so, the ceiling of the encoding is bounded by a quadratic form on the products of amplitudes (§87).

The filter gives small networks robustness on noisy hardware. It does not give supremacy.

Phase estimation and everything built on it (Shor, HHL) start with Hadamards, which mix every weight. There the scale gives a closed-form reading of the phase, \(qg_\Phi = e^{i2\pi\varphi}\), invertible on its whole domain (notes §13). That is the reading QPE computes with a circuit, but it does not lower QPE’s error. Post-quantum cryptography (Chapter 16) is classical arithmetic: there are no qubits or operators, so qang has nothing to read.

text:
30.8 The failed predictions of §157–§164
In the eight pre-registered runs of §157–§164, 26 of 45 predictions passed, by the verdicts the code stored. The 19 that failed:

Teleportation over a passive optical network (§157, Q5): 5 of 24 cases far from the optimum, all where the ideal fidelity is 1 (measured 0.897 to 0.957). The circuit does not conserve the weight, so the only filter is the loss herald.
Dual rail (§158, seven failed): the fidelity read from three correlators predicts the teleported one within 0.029, but does not decompose it (A1–A3). False heralds set a floor (B1, B2, B5).
Natural gradient (§159, G2): 1.3 times against the 1.5 predicted.
Pulse area (§160, P4): the period-\(\pi\) wrap of RZZ saves 1.14 times in error against the 1.5 predicted.
Kernels (§161, K2–K4): accuracy hardly changes with the repair and target alignment does not see the shrink; K4 failed on its thresholds, not on its direction.
VarQTE (§162, V1): the ansatz is not expressive enough at late times (noiseless fidelity 0.934 at \(t=2\)).
Neutrinos (§163, O3): the filtered values sit 0.010 to 0.033 high, because of the error inside the sector.
Time loops and black holes (§164, four failed). On FakeTorino the paradox is not fully suppressed: the success at \(\varphi=\pi\) is 0.056 where the prediction asked for close to 0 (C2), and the controlled rotation gives 0.600 where the exact value is 1 (C3). The decoder worked on all three devices (H2, H3); H1 missed by 0.001.

title: 30  Structural limits, equivalences and negative results
text:
30.9 Consolidated list of limitations
The notes’ list (§14), with what the book added:

Jacobian singularity at \(\theta\in\{0,\pi\}\): regularizing it costs exactness near the poles (Chapter 23).
arccos range trap: qg-space updates cannot reach \(\theta<0\); on H₂ they lose all of the correlation energy (§8.2).
Z-basis blindness: graph-state entanglement and readout dephasing are invisible to \(qg_Z\), \(qg_S\) and the qg correlation.
The qg correlation is not an entanglement measure: it is positive for classical mixtures and 0 for graph states (§7.2).
\(qg_S\) is not monotonic under T1: read it together with the mean \(qg_Z\), a pair that is monotone in 21 to 23 of 24 circuits, not in all of them.
Finite-shot bias of \(qg_S\): corrected with Miller–Madow (§10.2).
Pole damping costs 3 to 20 times more iterations when the optimum sits on a pole (§9).
No speed or energy advantage: qg does not change how many shots a given precision needs (§14, item 9; §15.3).
Reach of the filter: it only acts on weight-conserving circuits and on what is measured in Z; it does not see the error inside the sector.
The networks that admit the filter are simulable at weight 1.
On real hardware the filter gained less than in simulation (1.59 times against 2.2 on IQM’s model, Chapter 31).

text:
30.12 Summary

The entanglement of a graph state is invisible in Z: its distribution matches that of \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\) exactly.
\(qg_S\) rises and falls under T1 in all 24 circuits tested; the pair with the mean \(qg_Z\) separates them, without being a theorem.
The natural gradient in qg is descent in \(\theta\): a change of coordinate does not speed things up.
In LiH the error is in the X/Y groups, out of the filter’s reach; Hubbard hits the same wall from 4 steps on.
The weight-1 network the filter protects is a classical quadratic form.
In the runs of §157–§164, 19 of 45 predictions failed.

title: 31  First real-hardware experiment: IQM Resonance
text:
31.1 From the base: what goes to the chip
Up to here, almost the whole book was measured on simulators with device noise models. This chapter tells how qang was taken to a real superconducting chip, IQM’s Garnet (20 qubits), on trial credits: why that machine, how it was rehearsed for free, what it cost and what came out. The figures are recomputed from the runs’ stored files with tools/make_cap31_figures.py. Nothing is sent to IQM, and checking them does not need iqm-client.
The readout of a real qubit is the same as in Chapter 1: zeros and ones are counted, and \(qg_Z = 2p_0 - 1\). What changes is everything around that count: the circuit is compiled to the chip’s native gates, the readout has errors of its own and every shot costs credits. qang brings three things, all in post-processing:

title: 31  First real-hardware experiment: IQM Resonance
text:
31.3 The qang.iqm module
The index announced a module qang/iqm.py, the analogue of qang/ibm.py. The two runs of this chapter were done without it: the scripts examples/iqm_neutrino_qg.py and examples/iqm_milliqang_qg.py read the counts with qang.interop (canonical_counts, qg_z_profile, filtered_qg_z_profile, weight_filter). The module was written afterwards, with what those runs left pending:

Readout correction. §165 had none: IQM’s simulated models do not publish their readout errors in the Qiskit target, where qang.ibm looks for them, but in an error profile of their own. qang.iqm.readout_errors reads them there. For a real device, pole_circuits and readout_from_poles measure them with two circuits, every qubit in \(|0
angle\) and every qubit in \(|1
angle\), as §168 did. On the stored counts of §168 it gives \(e_0=0.0055\) and \(e_1=0.029\). iqm_qg applies the inversion of qang.ibm and gives the four readings: raw, corrected, filtered, and filtered after correction.
Chain choice. best_chain compares the default layout with chains of the square lattice and keeps the one with the highest predicted kept fraction (predict_kept_fraction, with IQM’s gates and units).
The weight-preservation pass. IQM’s native single-qubit gate does not conserve the weight gate by gate, so check_weight checks the circuit before compiling.

The free rehearsal on the Garnet model (examples/iqm_readout_chain_qg.py, the eight circuits of §165, 4000 shots) gives a raw error of 0.124, filtered 0.055 and filtered after readout correction 0.047: the correction §165 lacked removes another 15%. The simulated kept fraction is 0.689 and the prediction brackets it between 0.640 and 0.775, less tightly than on IBM. The chain choice barely tells chains apart (0.777 against 0.775), because the model’s qubits are nearly identical. None of this has been tried on the real chip yet.

section: 31.7 What came next, and what remains

31.7 What came next, and what remains

The milli-qang on Garnet (§168, Chapter 28) used most of the credits. Three of four predictions passed: one X gate costs 1.64 m-qg and the cost grows in a straight line with the number of gates. The equator copies scattered half as much as expected (M2 failed), and that is still open.
The replication on five qubits and two days is prepared in examples/iqm_milliqang_replication_qg.py, not yet pre-registered or run. At full size (130 circuits × 4000 shots per day) it would cost about 80 credits per day, far more than is left: it has to be shrunk before use.
The index’s candidates are still pending: the one-qubit P-CTC (§164), the Yoshida–Kitaev decoder (8 qubits and 90 two-qubit gates on the IBM models, probably too deep) and H₂ (§20, §128). The H₂ run on IonQ was refused before any job was accepted, and nothing was charged.

With 12.50 credits at about 0.15 per 1000 shots, some 80,000 shots are left, minus the per-job floors.

text:
31.11 Summary

On Garnet, real hardware, the filter cut the error 1.59 times and moved the oscillation maximum from 0.8 to 2.6 GeV (exact 2.63). All four pre-registered predictions passed.
The chip did better than its simulated model, and the filter gained less (1.59 times against 2.16).
IQM’s compilation advantage (12 against 18) came from the optimization level: at the same level IBM also gives 12.
17.50 of 30 credits were spent, at about 0.15 per 1000 shots with a floor of 0.50 per job.
qang.iqm, written after the runs, adds readout correction and chain choice. On the Garnet model the correction removes another 15% of the filtered error; it has not been tried on the real chip.

title: 32  Software architecture, the multi-SDK ecosystem and physical execution
text:
32.1 From the base: one count, many paths
A qg readout is only useful if it travels intact from the device to the number that gets reported. In between there is an SDK that orders bits its own way, primitives that return expectation values instead of counts, a compiler that picks qubits and a chip with errors no filter sees. This chapter walks that chain as the library solved it. The new checks and the rescoring of the stored IBM runs are in tools/make_cap32_figures.py.
The equation of Chapter 1 needs one thing: how many zeros each qubit gave. Everything else is plumbing, and every pipe can break the readout without anyone noticing:

text:
32.2 One qubit order
Qiskit writes qubit 0 at the right of the bitstring; Cirq, PennyLane, Braket and pytket write it first. qang.interop.canonical_counts brings everything to \(\{(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}):\text{count}\}\), qubit 0 first. The script checks it with the two SDKs installed here:

the same outcome (only qubit 0 excited), written 001 by Qiskit and 100 by PennyLane, gives (1, 0, 0) in both;
a 3-qubit W state sampled 20,000 times in each SDK gives \(qg_Z\) between 0.328 and 0.343 (ideal 1/3), every shot in weight 1 and register \(qg_S\) 0.528 (ideal \(\log_2 3/3 = 0.528\)), the same in Qiskit and in PennyLane.

Cirq, Braket and pytket are not installed on this machine. Their order is pinned by the library’s tests (notes §130) and was not run again.

title: 32  Software architecture, the multi-SDK ecosystem and physical execution
text:
32.3 V2 primitives and filtered observables
Qiskit’s V2 primitives come in two forms, and qang reads both (notes §131):

Sampler. interop.sampler_qg takes a SamplerV2 result and gives each qubit’s \(qg_Z\), with its error, for every parameter set at once. Given the weight, it also gives the filtered profile and the kept fraction.
Estimator. It returns no shots, so none can be discarded. But the filtered \(qg_Z\) is a ratio of two expectation values, \(\langle P_w Z_i\rangle / \langle P_w\rangle\), where \(P_w\) projects on weight \(w\). Both operators are diagonal, so they are sums of Z strings. interop.filtered_observables builds those sums.

The script checks that it is exact: on 20 random 4-qubit states, the values of filtered_observables(4, 2) give the kept fraction and the filtered \(qg_Z\) with a largest error of \(3.3\cdot10^{-16}\). It has a cost: the largest observable has \(2^{n-1}\) Z strings (8 with 4 qubits, 2048 with 12). They all commute and are measured in the same basis, so the cost is classical bookkeeping, not circuits. It still limits the method to registers of about a dozen qubits.

Choosing qubits from the calibration (§138). predict_kept_fraction multiplies the survival of the weight under each calibrated channel, and best_chain picks the chain with the best prediction:

the prediction comes out too low: the mean error is 0.08 to 0.13 (L1 failed);

title: 32  Software architecture, the multi-SDK ecosystem and physical execution
text:
32.5 Static ZZ: simulated, not mitigated
Coupled transmons pick up a ZZ phase all the time. ibm.add_static_zz adds it to the compiled circuit, after every layer and on every edge in use, with the layer’s calibrated duration. It is there to measure how much of that error the filter sees. It does not correct it. In §150, at 0, 5 and 15 kHz:

The filter sees part of the ZZ, not all of it. Between logical gates ZZ is diagonal and passes the filter. Inside the native decomposition of the XX+YY gates it moves excitations out of the sector: the kept fraction fell by 0.019 to 0.022 on the two ECR devices, and by 0.001 on FakeTorino.
The filter removed 32 to 60 % of the added error. The filtered error grew by 0.0025 to 0.0086 (14 to 38 %) at 15 kHz and stayed 3.6 to 5.1 times below raw. The notes said “4 to 5 times”; the rescoring gives 3.6–5.1.
Short circuits suffer least: FakeTorino runs for 2.1 µs against 9 to 10 µs on the others.

Predictions Z2 and Z3 failed, because they assumed the filter would see none of the ZZ.






Figure 32.1: Mean raw (dashed) and filtered (solid) \(qg_Z\) error against the simulated static ZZ, on three devices (§150).

section: 32.6 ZNE with the filter, and shot planning
text:
32.6 ZNE with the filter, and shot planning
In local mode, IBM Runtime’s mitigation options do nothing. That is why ibm.zne_qg folds every two-qubit gate (scale 3), runs both scales and extrapolates linearly. Folding conserves the weight, so the extrapolation (ZNE) combines with the filter (§142):

The filter does more than the extrapolation, 2 to 7 times more: filter + ZNE gives 0.012, 0.011 and 0.015 against 0.053, 0.034 and 0.085 for ZNE alone (Z2 passed).
ZNE does not always help. On FakeTorino, adding it to filter + readout makes the error worse, from 0.013 to 0.014 (Z1 failed), and the best combination there is filter + readout (Z3 failed).

ibm.plan_shots turns a target precision of the filtered \(qg_Z\) into shots and QPU seconds, from the predicted kept fraction (§143). For an error of 0.02 it planned 3000 to 3400 shots, and over 30 repetitions the worst qubit landed at 0.021–0.023 (P1 passed). The per-qubit prediction was 1.4 to 1.6 times too small (P2 failed). The misses are the qubits near a pole, where the noise pulls \(qg_Z\) away from ±1. That is why the plan uses the worst case.






Figure 32.2: Ten weight-1 circuits on three devices (§142): raw, readout correction and ZNE without qang; filter, filter + readout and filter + ZNE with qang.

title: 32  Software architecture, the multi-SDK ecosystem and physical execution
text:
32.7 Guidelines by hardware type
Superconductors (IBM, IQM).

Compile with weight-conserving gates (XX+YY, RBS) and check it with the analysis before running.
Compare two-qubit gate counts at the same optimization level (Chapter 31).
Choose the chain by the predicted kept fraction, and correct the readout from the calibration, or from the two poles where the calibration is not available (IQM).
Prefer short circuits: ZZ and dephasing inside the gates are filtered in proportion to the time the qubits spend outside the computational frame.

Ions (IonQ, through its cloud or AWS Braket). Connectivity is all-to-all and the native gate is Mølmer–Sørensen. The H₂ rehearsal on IonQ’s simulator with the Forte-1 noise model (§128) gave:

witness +0.0003;
97.9 % of the shots kept;
the error falls from 29.9 to 15.0 mHa with the filter.

The run on the real machine was refused before any job was accepted, because the project did not have Forte-1 enabled, and nothing was charged. Through Braket, interop handles the bit order.
On any platform.

Rehearse for free on the simulated model.
Measure the cost with a small probe.
Pre-register before the main job.
Read the token from an environment variable, and spend nothing without an explicit flag.

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
text:
33.1 From the base: one probability per experiment
At the nanometre scale many measurable quantities are a probability: that an electron crosses a barrier, that a level is occupied, that a spin is up. This chapter reads them with the equation of Chapter 1. There is no notes section and no qang module for these topics, so every figure comes from a closed form or from a Monte Carlo written in tools/make_cap33_figures.py. Next to each reading with qang goes the usual form, and the text says when the scale adds something and when it only changes the notation.
The equation of Chapter 1 takes a probability \(p_0\) and gives four exact readings:
\[
\theta = 2\arccos\sqrt{p_0},\qquad qg_Z = 2p_0-1,\qquad qg_S = H(p_0),\qquad m = 2000\,p_0 - 1000\ \text{m-qg}.
\]
In this chapter \(p_0\) is, case by case, the transmission \(T\) of a channel, the occupation of a level or the population of a spin state. Two properties from Chapter 1 do all the work:

the angle stabilizes binomial noise: with \(N\) counts, \(\sigma_\theta = 1/\sqrt N\) for any \(p_0\), while \(\sigma_{p_0} = \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/N}\) changes with \(p_0\).

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.2 Tunnelling transmission as a qang probability
text:
33.2 Tunnelling transmission as a qang probability
An electron reaches a rectangular barrier and crosses it with probability \(T\). With \(p_0 = T\):
\[
\theta_T = 2\arccos\sqrt T,\qquad \cos(\theta_T/2) = \sqrt T = |t|.
\]
The qang half-angle is the modulus of the transmission amplitude \(t\). It is not an analogy: it is the same definition, and the script checks it to \(10^{-16}\). With a 1 eV barrier, a 0.5 eV electron (\(\kappa = 3.62\) nm⁻¹) and the exact rectangular barrier formula:

Without qang one plots \(\ln T\), which falls with slope \(-2\kappa\).
With qang, the angular distance to the pole, \(\pi - \theta_T \approx 2|t|\), falls with slope \(-\kappa\): the script measures −3.620 nm⁻¹ against −3.623. It is the amplitude instead of the probability, the same information.
Thick barriers live right at the pole. One nanometre leaves the reading 5.7 m-qg from the pole, and one and a half nanometres, 0.15 m-qg. Reading that difference with the error of an electron count needs the exact angle near the pole (Chapter 1), not the linear approximation.

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.3 The Landauer formula: one channel, one reading
text:
33.3 The Landauer formula: one channel, one reading
The conductance of a ballistic conductor is \(G = G_0\sum_n T_n\), with \(G_0 = 2e^2/h\). Written in qg:
\[
\frac{G}{G_0} = \frac{N}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N} qg_n .
\]
The script uses the saddle-point model of a quantum point contact, \(T_n = 1/(1+e^{-2\pi(V-n-1/2)/w})\), and checks the identity to \(9\cdot10^{-16}\):

Each plateau is a set of channels at the poles: open at +1000 m-qg, closed at −1000. At \(V = 1, 2, 3\) the conductance is exactly 1, 2 and 3.
Each step is one channel crossing the equator. The midpoint of the step is that channel’s 0 m-qg reading.
Conductance alone does not separate channels that open together: it gives \(\sum T_n\) and nothing else. Shot noise (next section) gives \(\sum T_n(1-T_n)\). With both, two partly open channels are recovered exactly: the script starts from \(T = 0.4031\) and \(0.9716\) and gets them back. It is the known technique for measuring the transmissions of an atomic contact. In qg, the conductance reads the channels’ mean \(qg\) and the noise reads their mean \(qg^2\).







Figure 33.1: Left: the conductance staircase of a quantum point contact with four channels. Right: each channel’s reading in m-qg; each step is one channel going from −1000 to +1000 m-qg and crossing the equator halfway.
crumbs: XI. Nanoquantum
33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.4 Partition noise: the binomial variance, stabilized
text:
33.4 Partition noise: the binomial variance, stabilized
Every electron that reaches the channel either passes or bounces back: a Bernoulli trial with probability \(T\). That gives the partition noise, \(S = 2eI(1-T)\), with Fano factor \(F = 1-T\). In qg, \(T(1-T) = (1-qg^2)/4 = \sin^2\theta/4\): it is the binomial variance of Chapter 1. The script counts 1000 electrons per window, over 20,000 windows:

The Fano factor, measured as variance over mean of the transmitted electrons, matches \(1-T\) to within 0.02.
Without qang, the spread of \(\hat T\) times \(\sqrt N\) runs from 0.14 to 0.50: it depends on what is being measured, and near the poles the error bar shrinks so much that it misleads.
With qang, the spread of the angle \(\hat\theta\) times \(\sqrt N\) stays between 0.985 and 1.009 for \(T\) between 0.05 and 0.95, and is still 1.01–1.02 at 0.02 and 0.98. The error bar is the same over the whole range.

It is the arcsine transform, known in statistics for a long time. qang does not invent it. What it adds is that the stabilized angle is the natural coordinate of the state.






Figure 33.2: Spread of the estimated transmission and of the estimated qang angle, times \(\sqrt N\), with 1000 electrons per window: the first follows \(\sqrt{T(1-T)}\); the second stays at 1.

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.5 Coulomb blockade: the occupation of a level
text:
33.5 Coulomb blockade: the occupation of a level
In a quantum dot in Coulomb blockade, a level at energy \(\varepsilon\) from the leads’ chemical potential is occupied with the Fermi probability \(f = 1/(1+e^{x})\), with \(x = \varepsilon/k_BT\). With \(p_0 = f\):
\[
qg_Z = 2f - 1 = -\tanh(x/2).
\]
It is the same thermal state as \(qg_Z = \tanh(\beta h)\) of Chapter 8, with the sign of the convention. The script checks it to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\). The slope at the centre, \(-1/(2k_BT)\), is a thermometer: a charge sensor reads the occupation and its width gives the electron temperature. With 25 values of \(\varepsilon\), 200 readouts per point and 400 repetitions (\(k_BT = 1\)):



Table 33.2: Thermometry from the occupation of a level.









method
estimated \(k_BT\)




maximum-likelihood Fermi fit (without qang)
0.9986 ± 0.0294


straight line through \(\operatorname{artanh}(qg_Z)\) (with qang)
1.0294 ± 0.0305






qang loses here. The straight line is closed-form and needs no non-linear fit, but it is biased by +2.9 %. In the tails, \(\operatorname{artanh}\) amplifies the noise of readings close to ±1 (visible in the figure), and points where every readout agrees have to be dropped. The Fermi fit uses the same information without bias. The qg reading is for seeing the thermometer, not for estimating with it.






Figure 33.3: Left: a level’s \(qg_Z\) against \(\varepsilon/k_BT\), exact and with 200 readouts per point. Right: \(\operatorname{artanh}(qg_Z)\) is a straight line of slope \(-1/2k_BT\), but in the tails the noise bends it.

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.6 Charge and spin qubits in quantum dots
text:
33.6 Charge and spin qubits in quantum dots
A spin qubit in a quantum dot is read with a charge sensor: the spin is converted into charge and the sensor decides 0 or 1, with errors \(e_0 = P(1\,|\,0)\) and \(e_1 = P(0\,|\,1)\). It is the same readout as a transmon’s, and the rule of Chapter 28 describes it in m-qg:
\[
m_{\text{read}} = (1 - e_0 - e_1)\,m + 1000\,(e_1 - e_0).
\]
The script simulates a Rabi oscillation with \(e_0 = 0.02\) and \(e_1 = 0.08\) (illustrative values) and 2000 readouts per point:

the affine identity holds to \(2\cdot10^{-13}\);
uncorrected, the oscillation has an amplitude of 898 m-qg instead of 1000 and is shifted by +60 m-qg. Its rms error is 95.5 m-qg;
corrected from the two poles (2000 readouts on each), the error falls to 19.4 m-qg. The price is that the noise grows \(1/(1-e_0-e_1) = 1.11\) times;
the usual readout fidelity, \(1-(e_0+e_1)/2 = 0.95\), is in m-qg a visibility of 900 m-qg and a shift of 60.

The correction is the standard one. Writing it in m-qg makes it a linear account: each point of readout error costs 10 m-qg of visibility.

title: 33  Nanoquantum: transmission, partition noise and nanoscale qubits
section: 33.7 NV centres: contrast as an m-qg budget
text:
33.7 NV centres: contrast as an m-qg budget
An NV centre in diamond is read through fluorescence: the \(m_s = 0\) state is brighter than \(m_s = \pm1\), with a contrast \(C\). If \(p_0\) is the population of \(m_s = 0\) and \(N_b\) the photons the bright state would give, the count is Poisson with mean \(N_b\,[1 - C(1-p_0)]\), and the m-qg reading of \(p_0\) has
\[
\sigma_m \approx \frac{2000}{C\sqrt{N_b}}\ \text{m-qg}.
\]

With \(C = 0.3\) and 444,444 photons the formula gives 10.00 m-qg. The Monte Carlo gives 9.22, the same as the formula without the approximation (the factor \(\sqrt{1-C/2}\) at \(p_0 = 1/2\)).
Resolving 10 m-qg costs about 444,000 photons. A contrast of 0.3 makes every m-qg cost eleven times more photons than a contrast of 1 would. It is the same budget as in Chapter 1 with a factor \(1/C^2\).
ODMR magnetometry. A 1 MHz wide line, contrast 0.2, 61 frequencies and 1.16 million photons in total. Fitting the line gives its centre with a spread of 8.3 kHz, equal to the Cramér–Rao bound (8.3 kHz). That is 296 nT with \(\gamma = 28\) GHz/T.

The line fit does not change with qang. What the scale adds is the account beforehand: how many photons a given resolution needs, in a unit that is linear in the spin population.

text:
33.10 Summary

Tunnelling transmission is a qang probability, and its half-angle is the modulus of the amplitude: \(\cos(\theta_T/2) = |t|\).
In the Landauer formula each channel is a qg reading: plateaus are channels at the poles and steps are channels crossing the equator. Conductance and noise together recover two channels opening at once.
Partition noise is the binomial variance; the qang angle stabilizes it at \(1/\sqrt N\) over the whole range.
A level’s occupation is \(qg_Z = -\tanh(x/2)\); as a thermometer, the line in artanh has a +2.9 % bias the Fermi fit does not.
Spin readout through a charge sensor and NV readout through fluorescence are written as linear m-qg budgets; their estimators do not change.

text:
34.1 From the base: readings, not cycles
This chapter answers a proposal: thirteen phenomena from five fields, each with an equation, a “qg mapping” and an analytic test with its pass criterion. The proposal uses a currency the Chapter 1 base does not have: it speaks of “qg cycles” and “qg periods”. Before anything is run, those criteria have to be translated into readings. Then each test is run in tools/make_cap34_figures.py, which takes about 25 seconds. There is no notes section and no qang module for these topics, so every figure comes from a closed form, an exact diagonalization or a Monte Carlo written there. None comes from an experiment. The verdict on each test is in Table 34.3: some hold as written, others hold only once corrected, and two fail.
The Chapter 1 equation starts from a probability \(p_0\) and gives four exact readings:
\[
\theta = 2\arccos\sqrt{p_0},\qquad qg_Z = 2p_0-1 = \cos\theta,\qquad qg_S = H(p_0),\qquad m = 1000\,qg_Z\ \text{m-qg}.
\]
This has three consequences for the proposal:
crumbs: XII. Cross-domain applications

title: 34  Angular architecture: chemistry, condensed matter, relativistic optics, thermodynamics and geometry
text:
qg has no period. \(qg_Z\) lives in \([-1,1]\) and the qang angle in \([0,\pi]\). A criterion such as “phase \(=\pi\equiv
0.5\) qg cycle” cannot be checked as it stands. It has to be rewritten as a reading: for instance, \(qg_X=-1\), which is \(-1000\) m-qg.
A phase does not change \(qg_Z\). A rotation about \(Z\) (Larmor precession, Aharonov–Bohm phase, the sign of an exchange) leaves the populations alone. It is read with an interferometer, in \(qg_X\) or \(qg_Y\), like the Berry phase of Chapter 7.
Where there is a probability, there is a reading. A reflectance, the weight of a determinant, the vacuum occupation or a transition probability is a \(p_0\), so everything from Chapter 1 applies: the linear scale and the angle that stabilizes the noise.

title: 34  Angular architecture: chemistry, condensed matter, relativistic optics, thermodynamics and geometry
text:
34.2 Quantum chemistry

34.2.1 Jordan–Wigner: the exchange sign is a reading
The mapping is \(a_j^\dagger=\big(\prod_{k<j}(-Z_k)\big)\,\sigma_j^+\). The script builds the operators of four modes and checks the anticommutation relations \(\{a_i,a_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}\) and \(\{a_i,a_j\}=0\) with exactly zero error. It also checks that \(a_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger|0\rangle + a_2^\dagger a_1^\dagger|0\rangle = 0\). The proposal asks for the exchange to be “a half-period qg phase shift”. On the Chapter 1 base that is not a reading. To make it one, the exchange has to act inside a Hadamard test: an ancilla controls the exchange of the two occupied modes and is read in \(X\).

With the fermionic exchange, the ancilla reads \(qg_X=-1\), that is \(-1000\) m-qg.
With a qubit SWAP, the same circuit reads \(+1000\) m-qg.

The Pauli sign is the difference between the two poles of \(qg_X\). The \(Z\) gates of the parity string are exact, so there is no “phase loss from accumulated gates”. The error of a real circuit comes from noise, not from the mapping.


34.2.2 UCC for H\(_2\): the amplitude is half a qang angle
For H\(_2\) in STO-3G at 0.735 Å, with the four-qubit Hamiltonian of Chapter 25, UCCSD reduces to a single double excitation. The state is \(|\Psi(t)\rangle=\cos t\,|\text{HF}\rangle+\sin t\,|\text{double}\rangle\), and the energy has the closed form \(E(t)=A+B\cos 2t+C\sin 2t\):

the minimum is at \(t^\ast=-0.1118\) rad, where the energy is \(-1.1373060\) Ha, the FCI energy to within \(5\cdot10^{-14}\) Ha; Hartree–Fock gives \(-1.1169990\);
the Hartree–Fock weight is a reading: \(p_0=\cos^2 t^\ast=0.9876\), that is \(+975.1\) m-qg, and its qang angle is \(\theta=2|t^\ast|=0.2235\) rad. The UCC amplitude is half a qang angle, the same relation Chapter 33 finds for tunnelling;
a sweep with step \(\pi/200\) gets within \(5.4\cdot10^{-6}\) Ha of the minimum.

The proposal asks for “sub-millihartree precision, \(<1.6\cdot10^{-3}\) Ha”. That threshold is chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol), not a sub-millihartree, and in an exact simulator it is beaten by eleven orders of magnitude: it discriminates nothing. The dissociation curve is not redone because the environment has no PySCF; the stored runs of Chapter 25 cover it. The gradient vanishes at the minimum in both \(t\) and \(m\), because \(dm/dt=-2000\sin 2t\neq 0\) there. At Hartree–Fock (\(t=0\), the pole) the \(m\) coordinate is singular, as Chapter 23 shows.


34.2.3 Larmor and the Hahn echo
Free precession \(\Delta\varphi=\gamma B_0t\) is a rotation about \(Z\). With the proton (\(\gamma/2\pi=42.577\) MHz/T) and a spin on the equator, the script gives \(qg_Z=0\) at all times and \(qg_X=\cos\Delta\varphi\). The precession does not show in the \(Z\) reading.
For the echo, the script takes 20,000 spins with Gaussian detuning (\(\sigma=2\pi\cdot50\) kHz), \(\tau=20\) µs, the sequence \(\pi/2-\tau-\pi-\tau\), and reads the magnetization in \(qg_X\):

34.3.1 Transverse-field Ising: the peak moves with size

The proposal asks to find it with 2 to 4 spins, at the peak of the derivative of the entanglement entropy. The script diagonalizes with \(N=2\) to \(12\) (in the even sector of the parity \(\prod X\), so that the cat state below the transition is well defined):

The test fails with 2 to 4 spins. The peak is at \(g/J=0.33\) and \(0.65\), that is at \(\theta=18^\circ\) and \(33^\circ\), not at \(45^\circ\). With two spins there is no transition: the curve is smooth. The peak approaches 1 as \(N\) grows, and the entropy converges faster than the \(qg_X\) reading (Figure 34.1). The transverse reading at \(g=J\), \(m_X\), also falls towards the exact value \(1000\cdot 2/\pi=636.6\) m-qg (Pfeuty 1970), but with 12 spins it is still 84 m-qg above it. What gives \(\theta=\pi/4\) is the limit, not the scale.






Figure 34.1: Left: \(-dS/dg\) of the half-chain entropy for \(N=2\) to \(12\). Right: the susceptibility of the transverse reading, \(d\,qg_X/dg\). Both peaks approach \(g/J=1\) as the chain grows; with 2 to 4 spins they are far from it.





34.3.2 Kitaev chain: the protection is in the Hamiltonian, not in the angle
The parity \(P=\prod_j(-i\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j})\) takes the values \(\pm1\), that is \(\pm1000\) m-qg. The script separates two questions:

Does the chain protect? With \(t=\Delta=1\) and \(\mu=0.5\), the energy difference between the two parity sectors halves with each site: 0.207 with 2 sites and 0.0029 with 8. With \(\mu=0\) and local disorder \(\pm0.3\) it falls from \(1.5\cdot10^{-2}\) to \(3\cdot10^{-7}\), though not monotonically. That is topological protection: exponential in the length.
Does the gate protect? The braid \(B=e^{\pi\gamma_2\gamma_3/4}=(1+\gamma_2\gamma_3)/\sqrt2\) holds to \(10^{-16}\), with exact eigenphases \(\pm\pi/4\) and \(B^2=\gamma_2\gamma_3\). But applied as a gate with a relative angle error \(\epsilon\), the infidelity is \(6.2\cdot10^{-5}\) at 1 %, \(1.5\cdot10^{-3}\) at 5 % and \(6.2\cdot10^{-3}\) at 10 %, quadratic in \(\epsilon\), like any rotation.

Writing the braid in “quarter qg cycles” does not protect it. Invariance under local perturbations comes from the Hamiltonian with separated Majorana modes (Kitaev 2001; Ivanov 2001). A gate that imitates the braid has the error of any gate.


34.3.3 Aharonov–Bohm: one fringe per flux quantum
In a two-path ring, the output has \(p_0=\cos^2(\pi\Phi/\Phi_0)\), so
\[
qg_Z=\cos\!\left(2\pi\,\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_0}\right),\qquad \theta = 2\pi\,\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_0}\ \ (\text{folded into }[0,\pi]).
\]
The qang angle is the Aharonov–Bohm phase. The reading returns to its value every \(\Phi_0=h/e\) (the script checks it to \(10^{-15}\)). What is periodic is the flux, not qg. With 2000 electrons per measurement and 4000 repetitions, the flux estimated from the angle has a spread times \(\sqrt N\) of between 0.156 and 0.163 for \(\Phi/\Phi_0\) from 0.05 to 0.45. The bound is \(1/2\pi=0.159\), the same over the whole range (Figure 34.2). It is the Chapter 1 arcsine transformation applied to an interferometer. What the reading does not give is the sign: \(\Phi\) and \(-\Phi\) (and \(\Phi_0-\Phi\)) read the same. Telling them apart needs the second quadrature, \(qg_Y\), as in Chapter 7.






Figure 34.2: Left: the ring’s reading in m-qg against flux; one fringe per quantum. Right: spread of the flux estimated from the qang angle, times \(\sqrt N\), with 2000 electrons per measurement: it stays at \(1/2\pi\) over the whole range.

title: 34  Angular architecture: chemistry, condensed matter, relativistic optics, thermodynamics and geometry
text:
34.4 Relativity and optics

34.4.1 Wigner rotation
Two non-collinear boosts, \(v_1=0.6c\,\hat x\) and \(v_2=0.8c\,\hat y\), compose into a boost followed by a rotation. The script multiplies them as \(4\times4\) matrices, splits off the resulting boost and reads the angle: \(\Omega_W=0.3303\) rad (\(18.92^\circ\)). The proposal’s formula gives the same to \(1.5\cdot10^{-15}\). With spinors, the same product in \(SL(2,\mathbb C)\) splits into a Hermitian part (the boost) and a unitary part (the rotation), and gives the same angle to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\). The proposal’s checks pass: \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\) to \(9\cdot10^{-16}\), the rotation is orthogonal and the spinor part is unitary. A spin that pointed along \(x\) afterwards reads \(qg_X=\cos\Omega_W\), that is \(+945.9\) m-qg. With collinear boosts, \(\Omega_W=0\). All of this is structure of the Lorentz group: the scale only translates the angle into a spin reading. With Dirac spinors the result is the same, because a Dirac spinor is two \(SL(2,\mathbb C)\) spinors.


34.4.2 Fresnel: Brewster is a zero of probability, total reflection is a phase
From air into glass with \(n=1.5\):

Brewster, at \(56.31^\circ\): \(r_p=0\) exactly. \(s\) light reflects \(R_s=0.148\), which as a “reflected” reading is \(-704\) m-qg. At normal incidence, \(R=0.04\), that is \(-920\) m-qg.
Total reflection, from inside the glass and above \(41.81^\circ\): \(|r_s|=|r_p|=1\) to \(4\cdot10^{-16}\). The reflectance always reads \(+1000\) m-qg and says nothing. All the information is in the phases. Their difference \(\delta_p-\delta_s\) reaches a maximum of \(45.24^\circ\) at \(51.67^\circ\) and passes through \(45^\circ\) at \(50.23^\circ\) and \(53.26^\circ\): the Fresnel rhomb. Linear light at \(45^\circ\) incident at \(45^\circ\) leaves with \(qg_Y=S_3/S_0=\sin(\delta_p-\delta_s)=0.600\), that is \(+600\) m-qg, a Stokes reading like those of Chapter 6.
Goos–Hänchen is not a “phase shift”. It is a lateral displacement that comes from the derivative of the phase: with Artmann’s formula, \(D=-(\lambda/2\pi n)\,d\delta/d\theta_i\), it is 0.64 \(\lambda\) for \(s\) at \(45^\circ\) (Goos and Hänchen 1947; Artmann 1948).

The total-reflection phase as a “single-qubit phase gate” works: it acts on the polarization and is read in \(qg_Y\).


34.4.3 Bogoliubov and Unruh: the half angle is the Gudermannian
The Minkowski vacuum seen by an accelerated observer is a two-mode squeezed state. Each reduced mode is thermal, with \(\bar n=\sinh^2r\) and Boltzmann factor \(\tanh^2r=e^{-2\pi\omega c/a}\) (Unruh 1976; Crispino et al. 2008). The script checks the closed-form entropy, \(S=\cosh^2r\ln\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r\ln\sinh^2r\), against the sum over occupation numbers: they agree to \(10^{-16}\) up to \(r=1\), and to \(2\cdot10^{-6}\) at \(r=1.5\) because of the 80-level cutoff. The hyperbolic matrix preserves the form \(\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)\) to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\). The proposal calls it a “pseudo-unitary rotation parametrized in qg”. An \(SU(1,1)\) transformation is not a rotation, but the vacuum weight is a probability, \(p_0=1/\cosh^2r\), and it gives an exact identity:
\[
\frac{\theta}{2}=\operatorname{gd}(r)=\arctan(\sinh r).
\]
The qang half-angle of the vacuum weight is the Gudermannian function of the squeezing parameter. It maps the hyperbolic line onto a circle angle, and the script checks it to \(10^{-16}\). The vacuum readings are \(+880.0\), \(+572.9\), \(-160.1\) and \(-638.6\) m-qg for \(r=0.25\), \(0.5\), \(1\) and \(1.5\). As \(r\to\infty\) (huge acceleration or zero frequency), \(\theta\to\pi\).

title: 34  Angular architecture: chemistry, condensed matter, relativistic optics, thermodynamics and geometry
text:
34.5 Thermodynamics and metrology

34.5.1 Jarzynski with two measurements
A qubit with \(H=-\tfrac h2(\cos\varphi\,Z+\sin\varphi\,X)\) is driven from \(h=1\), \(\varphi=0\) to \(h=2\), \(\varphi=1\) rad in a time \(1.5\) (400 steps), with \(\beta=1\). Work is measured with two projective measurements (Talkner et al. 2007). The transition probabilities \(|\langle n_f|U|m_i\rangle|^2\) are readings: the two “stay” probabilities are \(qg=0.707\), that is \(707.4\) m-qg.

Exact: \(\langle e^{-\beta W}\rangle=1.3684330=Z_f/Z_i\), with error \(3.8\cdot10^{-15}\). \(\Delta F=-0.3137\) and \(\langle W\rangle=-0.0958\ge\Delta F\).
With sampled trajectories (2000 repetitions), the estimator \(-\ln\overline{e^{-\beta W}}/\beta\) has a bias of \(+0.021\) with 10 trajectories, \(+0.0016\) with 100 and \(+1.5\cdot10^{-4}\) with 1000. With 10,000 trajectories the bias is within the noise.

The equality holds (Jarzynski 1997), and the scale changes nothing in the thermodynamics. What it adds is that each transition probability is a reading with the Chapter 1 error bar.


34.5.2 Fisher information of a GHZ state
For \(N=1\) to \(8\) qubits and the phase generated by \(\sum Z/2\), the script gives a quantum Fisher information of \(N^2\) for the GHZ state and \(N\) for the product state, with \(10^{-15}\) error. The step that connects to Chapter 1 is the parity reading. Its mean is \(qg=\cos N\varphi\), and the single-shot Fisher information of a \(\pm1\) reading is \((dqg/d\varphi)^2/(1-qg^2)\). That gives exactly \(N^2\) at any \(\varphi\): the parity reading reaches the quantum bound (Bollinger et al. 1996; Giovannetti et al. 2006). The proposal asks to use “qg as a continuous differentiable parameter”. If the parameter were the reading itself, the information would be divided by \((dqg/d\varphi)^2\) and diverge at the poles. The scale reads, and the parameter is still the phase. The cost of read-out noise, \((1-2e)^N\), is in Chapter 8.

title: 34  Angular architecture: chemistry, condensed matter, relativistic optics, thermodynamics and geometry
text:
34.6 Geometry and chaos

34.6.1 Fubini–Study: pole to pole, half the qang angle
The script sums, in 20,000 steps, the distances \(\arccos|\langle\psi_k|\psi_{k+1}\rangle|\) along a meridian and gets \(1.5707963=\pi/2\). With \(\sqrt{1-|\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle|^2}\) it gets the same, and also with the qg coordinate, \(ds=dqg/\big(2\sqrt{1-qg^2}\big)\), although that integrand is singular at the poles. The Gaussian curvature of \(ds^2=\tfrac14(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)\) comes out as \(4.000\): a sphere of radius 1/2 (Provost and Vallee 1980). The proposal speaks of “half a qg metric period”. Translated to the base, the Fubini–Study distance is half the qang angle, \(d_{FS}=\theta/2\), the Wootters distance of Chapter 1.


34.6.2 OTOC: integrable against chaotic
On an 8-spin chain, with \(W=Z_1\), \(V=Z_8\) and infinite temperature, the script compares the transverse Ising model (\(g=1.05\), integrable) with the same model plus a longitudinal field of 0.5 (chaotic):

The front arrives at the same time: \(F(t)=\mathrm{Re}\langle W(t)VW(t)V\rangle\) drops below 0.5 at \(t=4.0\) and \(4.2\).
What separates them is what comes after: the chaotic one stays at \(0.036\) on average (\(+36\) m-qg) for \(t\) between 10 and 30, and the integrable one revives, with mean \(0.839\) (Figure 34.3).
The usual diagnostic agrees: the mean level-spacing ratio (10 spins, reflection-even sector) is \(0.532\) for the chaotic chain (GOE: 0.531) and \(0.387\) for the integrable one (Poisson: 0.386) (Oganesyan and Huse 2007; Atas et al. 2013).

The proposal’s test cannot be done here. With 8 spins there is no exponential window separate from the front, and the bound \(\lambda_L\le2\pi k_BT/\hbar\) (Maldacena et al. 2016) is empty at infinite temperature. That bound has content in large-\(N\) models at low temperature, such as SYK (Sachdev and Ye 1993; Maldacena and Stanford 2016), not in an 8-spin chain. For Paulis, \(F(t)\) is the \(qg_X\) reading of an ancilla in an interferometric protocol (Swingle et al. 2016), the same kind of reading as the decoder of Chapter 15.






Figure 34.3: OTOC \(F(t)\) of \(Z_1\) and \(Z_8\) on an 8-spin chain at infinite temperature. The front arrives at the same time in both; the chaotic chain stays near zero and the integrable one revives.

Verdict. The proposal is right in its intuition: almost everything it looks at has an angle or a probability inside. It goes wrong in the currency, because “qg cycle” and “qg period” do not exist in the base. Translated into readings, the scale contributes four concrete things: the UCC amplitude as half an angle, the constant error bar of the flux, the Gudermannian of the squeezed vacuum, and the GHZ parity at the quantum bound from the single-shot formula. For the echo and Jarzynski it changes only the unit. For Wigner, Kitaev and the OTOC it contributes nothing: the physics is in the group, the Hamiltonian or the spectrum. Two criteria fail as written: Ising with 2 to 4 spins and the braid as a protected gate. Everything is exact computation or simulation, and there is no qang module for these topics yet.

text:
34.10 Summary

The base has no “qg cycles”: qg is a reading in \([-1,1]\). Phases are read in \(qg_X\) or \(qg_Y\) with an interferometer, and probabilities directly.
The sign of a fermionic exchange is \(-1000\) m-qg in a Hadamard test; the UCC amplitude of H\(_2\) is half a qang angle (\(+975.1\) m-qg at the FCI minimum).
The Hahn echo recovers \(+1000\) m-qg only with static detuning; Ising with 2 to 4 spins does not show the transition at \(\theta=\pi/4\), and the Majorana braid written as a gate is not protected.
The qang angle of an Aharonov–Bohm ring is the phase, with a constant \(1/2\pi\sqrt N\) error bar; the half-angle of the squeezed vacuum is \(\operatorname{gd}(r)\).
GHZ parity reaches the quantum information \(N^2\) with Chapter 1’s single-shot formula, and the Fubini–Study distance is half the qang angle.
Wigner, Jarzynski and the OTOC hold or are diagnosed with the usual tools; the scale only translates them.

Bibliographic notes
The Jordan–Wigner mapping is Jordan and Wigner (1928), and UCC for VQE, Romero et al. (2018); the H\(_2\) energy follows O’Malley et al. (2016). The echo is Hahn (1950), and precession, Bloch (1946). The solved transverse Ising model is Pfeuty (1970), and entanglement entropy at criticality, Calabrese and Cardy (2004). The Kitaev chain is Kitaev (2001), and Majorana braiding, Ivanov (2001). The Aharonov–Bohm effect is Aharonov and Bohm (1959). Thomas precession is Thomas (1926); Wigner’s representations, Wigner (1939), and the composition of boosts, O’Donnell and Visser (2011). Fresnel and Brewster follow Born et al. (1999); the lateral shift is Goos and Hänchen (1947) and Artmann (1948). The Unruh effect is Unruh (1976) (review: Crispino et al. (2008)). The Jarzynski equality is Jarzynski (1997), and work from two measurements, Talkner et al. (2007). Spectroscopy with GHZ states is Bollinger et al. (1996), and quantum metrology, Giovannetti et al. (2006) and Braunstein and Caves (1994). The Fubini–Study metric as a Riemannian structure is Provost and Vallee (1980). The chaos bound is Maldacena et al. (2016); SYK, Sachdev and Ye (1993) and Maldacena and Stanford (2016); measuring scrambling, Swingle et al. (2016), and spacing ratios, Oganesyan and Huse (2007) and Atas et al. (2013). text:
35.1 From the base: what each library gets
Every chapter of this book noted what it would ask of an existing library. This chapter delivers that list. qang 0.13.0 ships a new subpackage, qang.integrations, with one module per library: mitiq, qiskit-experiments, Qiskit Dynamics, QuTiP, Stim, scikit-learn, JAX, PyTorch, Qibo, pytket, Amazon Braket and NVIDIA’s CUDA-Q. Each module brings qang’s three things (the readings, the filter and the closed-form rules) into that library’s own terms and has its test in tests/test_integrations.py. The figures in this chapter come from tools/make_cap35_numbers.py, which runs in three environments because not every library fits in one. None comes from real hardware. The chapter separates what is done and tested inside qang from what would still have to be proposed to each project.
The Chapter 1 base is a probability \(p_0\) and its readings, \(qg_Z=2p_0-1\), \(m=1000\,qg_Z\) and \(\theta=\arccos qg_Z\). What qang adds to another library is always one of three things:

35.3 Mitigation: mitiq
mitiq can already post-select on Hamming weight: its post_select ships with that very example. There was no need to write it again. What qang adds on top is:

qg_z and filtered_qg_z, to read a MeasurementResult in qg;
qg_executor, which turns a sampler into the real-valued executor that mitiq’s techniques use;
execute_with_filter_zne, which combines the filter with zero-noise extrapolation;
filter_rule, the Chapter 21 rule.

The script runs a three-qubit weight-1 circuit (Givens rotations in Cirq), with amplitude damping of 0.05 and dephasing of 0.03 per moment, and reads qubit 1. The exact value is \(-257.3\) m-qg:

With T1 alone the filter is exact (Chapter 21, F1) and ZNE has nothing to correct. With T1 and dephasing, the filter leaves only the dephasing and ZNE removes it (F6): the error drops from 30.3 to 1.1 m-qg. ZNE on the raw reading stays at 55.9 m-qg, because T1 does not scale well under folding. 35.5 Open systems: QuTiP
qg_readings reads \((qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)\) of each qubit of a Qobj, mesolve_qg reads a mesolve evolution, and t1_collapse builds the collapse operators for equal T1. 35.7 Learning: scikit-learn, JAX and PyTorch

scikit-learn. WeightQNNClassifier and MultiClassQNNClassifier have fit, predict, decision_function and score, accept any labels and work in Pipeline, cross_val_score and GridSearchCV. On the two-moons set (120 points), with T1 of 0.15 and 5-fold cross-validation, the filtered model scores 0.833 ± 0.083 and the raw one 0.842 ± 0.081. There is no difference, as in Chapter 20: trained under the calibrated noise, the model without the filter catches up. GridSearchCV can choose qang=True/False like any other hyperparameter.
JAX. The readings and the filter written with jax.numpy go through jit, grad and vmap. The gradient of a filtered loss through a PennyLane QNode with interface="jax" matches finite differences to \(2\cdot10^{-10}\). That was what Chapter 20 left untested. Getting there turned up a conflict: PennyLane 0.45 uses jax.core.is_concrete, which JAX 0.12 removed, and it works only with JAX < 0.9.
PyTorch. WeightQNNTorch is an nn.Module: a PennyLane TorchLayer with SingleExcitation rotations, which conserve the weight, the filtered reading and a linear layer. With T1 of 0.1 per layer, the filtered reading differs from the clean one by \(1.2\cdot10^{-16}\) and the raw one by 262.5 m-qg. The gradient flows through backward().
