35.8 Pulses: Qiskit Dynamics
rabi_qg solves a resonantly driven qubit and returns \(qg_Z\). Against \(\cos A\), with \(A\) the pulse area, the error is \(1.1\cdot10^{-7}\) to \(5\cdot10^{-7}\) with a square pulse and \(5\cdot10^{-7}\) to \(1.9\cdot10^{-6}\) with a Gaussian pulse, for \(A\) equal to \(\pi/2\), \(\pi\) and 2.2. It is the basis of the §160 minimal-area rule. The conflict: Qiskit Dynamics 0.6 requires qiskit<=1.3, so it does not coexist with Qiskit 2.x and needs its own environment.

Verdict. Two integrations add something the library does not have: heralded calibration, which separates temperature and readout, and ZNE of the filtered reading with the cost rule. The learning ones open up use without improving accuracy, which is what Chapter 20 had already measured. The rest are translation: readings in m-qg and a single qubit order, which is little but prevents real errors, such as pytket’s half-turns. No figure comes from hardware. The proposals have not been sent to any project yet.

title: 35  qang as a module: changes to quantum and machine-learning libraries
text:
35.14 Summary

qang 0.13.0 has qang.integrations, with twelve libraries, one extra for each and tests that skip themselves.
mitiq: the filter with ZNE lowers the error from 55.9 to 1.1 m-qg under T1 and dephasing; post-selection already existed.
qiskit-experiments: heralded calibration gives unbiased \(e_{01}\), \(p\) and \(T_{\text{eff}}\), where the standard one sees the qubit as cold.
QuTiP, Stim, Qiskit Dynamics and the SDKs get readings in m-qg and the filter, and the four SDKs share the same qubit order.
scikit-learn, JAX and PyTorch let weight networks train like any other model, without an accuracy gain.
Three environment conflicts are documented: Qiskit Dynamics with Qiskit 2, PennyLane with JAX ≥ 0.9 and Braket with cloudpickle.

title: Appendix A — Catalogue of the 15 fundamental gates in qg representation
text:
A.1 Fixed single-qubit gates
This appendix collects the action of the gates of qang.formulation on the qg readings. A gate \(U\) transforms each Pauli reading by conjugation,
\[
qg'_P = qg_{U^\dagger P U},
\]
so it is enough to say what each local reading becomes. The tables are not written by hand: tools/make_appendices.py generates them from formulation.gate_table, is_clifford, conserves_weight and gate_radius_class. If the code changes, they are regenerated. In Pauli strings the leftmost letter is qubit 0, which is the control of CX and CZ, both controls of Toffoli and the control of Fredkin.
Why fifteen. The module defines 16 matrices: six fixed single-qubit gates, four parametric ones and six multi-qubit gates. \(R_Z(\varphi)\) and the phase gate \(P(\varphi)\) differ only by a global phase, \(P(\varphi)=e^{i\varphi/2}R_Z(\varphi)\), so they act identically on every reading and count as one in qg.
Clifford gates permute the readings with signs, and \(T\) mixes them. The diagonal gates (\(Z\), \(S\), \(T\)) leave \(qg_Z\) alone: they do not move populations, only the phase, which is read in \(qg_X\) and \(qg_Y\). Conserving the weight is what allows the filter of Chapters 21 and 22.

title: Appendix B — Transition formulas, Gell-Mann matrices and Chebyshev polynomials
text:
B.1 Single-qubit formulas
This appendix gathers in one place the closed forms used in Chapters 2 and 3: the universal gate and the reflections written in \(q=qg_Z\), the transition probability, the generalization of \(qg_Z\) to qudits with the diagonal Gell-Mann matrices, and the Grover trajectory as a Chebyshev polynomial (notes, §37 and §166). There are no new results. What it adds is the check: tools/make_appendices.py evaluates each formula of qang.algebra against direct linear algebra on 2000 random states and writes the maximal error here. If a formula were wrong, the script would stop.
With \(q=qg_Z=\cos\theta\), \(\cos\tfrac\theta2=\sqrt{(1+q)/2}\) and \(\sin\tfrac\theta2=\sqrt{(1-q)/2}\). The pure state with polar bias \(q\) and azimuth \(\varphi\) is
\[
|\psi(q,\varphi)\rangle=\sqrt{\tfrac{1+q}{2}}\,|0\rangle+e^{i\varphi}\sqrt{\tfrac{1-q}{2}}\,|1\rangle,\qquad \vec r=\big(\sqrt{1-q^2}\cos\varphi,\ \sqrt{1-q^2}\sin\varphi,\ q\big).
\]
The formulas are:
\[
U_3^{qg}(q,\varphi,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\tfrac{1+q}{2}} & -e^{i\lambda}\sqrt{\tfrac{1-q}{2}}\\ e^{i\varphi}\sqrt{\tfrac{1-q}{2}} & e^{i(\varphi+\lambda)}\sqrt{\tfrac{1+q}{2}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \big|U_{ij}\big|^2=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1+q}{2} & \tfrac{1-q}{2}\\ \tfrac{1-q}{2} & \tfrac{1+q}{2}\end{pmatrix}
\tag{B.1}\]
\[
I-2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|=-q\,Z-\sqrt{1-q^2}\,X,\qquad 2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I=q\,Z+\sqrt{1-q^2}\,X
\tag{B.2}\]
\[
|\langle\psi_1|\psi_2\rangle|^2=\frac{1+\vec r_1\cdot\vec r_2}{2}\ \xrightarrow{\ \varphi_1=\varphi_2\ }\ \frac{1+q_1q_2+\sqrt{(1-q_1^2)(1-q_2^2)}}{2}
\tag{B.3}\]
The transition matrix is doubly stochastic, rational in \(q\) and independent of the phases: the probability a gate leaves is read without trigonometry. With \((q,\varphi,\lambda)=(1,0,0)\), \((-1,0,\pi)\), \((1,0,\pi)\) and \((0,0,\pi)\), Equation B.1 gives exactly \(I\), \(X\), \(Z\) and \(H\); the script checks it. The reflector and the diffuser are the same operator with opposite sign, and both are linear combinations of \(Z\) and \(X\) with coefficients \(q\) and \(\sqrt{1-q^2}\) (Chapter 3).

title: Appendix B — Transition formulas, Gell-Mann matrices and Chebyshev polynomials
text:
B.2 Diagonal Gell-Mann matrices
A \(d\)-level qudit has \(d^2-1\) generators of \(\mathfrak{su}(d)\), the generalized Gell-Mann matrices. Only \(d-1\) of them are diagonal: they form the Cartan subalgebra and are the only ones read by measuring in the computational basis. They are
\[
\lambda_k=\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{k(k+1)}}\;\mathrm{diag}(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k},-k,0,\dots,0),\qquad k=1,\dots,d-1,\qquad \mathrm{Tr}(\lambda_j\lambda_k)=2\delta_{jk},
\tag{B.4}\]
and their expectation values are linear in the populations \(p\) and determine them:
\[
\langle\lambda_k\rangle=\sum_i p_i\,(\lambda_k)_{ii},\qquad p=\frac1d+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\langle\lambda_k\rangle\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_k).
\tag{B.5}\]

For \(d=2\) the only one is \(\lambda_1=Z\) and its value is \(qg_Z\). For \(d=3\) they are Gell-Mann’s \(\lambda_3\) and \(\lambda_8\). The script recovers the populations from the \(d-1\) values for \(d=2,\dots,6\), 200 random distributions each, with maximal error \(2.2\cdot10^{-16}\). An example: the qutrit with \(p=(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) reads \(\langle\lambda_3\rangle=0.2000\) and \(\langle\lambda_8\rangle=0.2309\).
This is a definition and an identity. Whether reading more levels gives qang any advantage was asked in §70 for leakage, and none was found (Chapter 2).

title: Appendix B — Transition formulas, Gell-Mann matrices and Chebyshev polynomials
section: B.3 Chebyshev polynomials and the Grover trajectory
text:
B.3 Chebyshev polynomials and the Grover trajectory
With amplitude \(a=\sin^2t\) and the good/bad flag read as a qubit, \(qg_0=1-2a=\cos2t\). Each Grover iteration adds \(2t\) to the angle, so after \(k\) iterations
\[
qg_k=T_{2k+1}(qg_0),\qquad T_m(\cos x)=\cos mx,
\tag{B.6}\]
with \(T_m\) the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. Since \(T_m'=m\,U_{m-1}\) and \(1-T_m^2=(1-q^2)\,U_{m-1}^2\), the one-shot Fisher information at depth \(m\) is
\[
F_m(qg_0)=\frac{m^2}{1-qg_0^2},
\tag{B.7}\]
the factor \(m^2\) over the depth-1 information, the same along the whole fringe. It is the qg form of the known \(4m^2\) for the angle (Suzuki et al. 2020).

title: Appendix C — The echo-calibration protocol and inversion in Hamming sectors (§105–§108)
text:
C.1 The protocol
Chapter 22 explains why the echo is needed: the qg filter discards the shots that left the sector, but it does not see the errors that move an excitation from one qubit to another without changing the weight. This appendix gives the protocol step by step, what it costs, an exact example generated by tools/make_appendices.py with the functions of qang.sectors, and the record of the four pre-registered runs of the notes.
crumbs: Appendices
C  The echo-calibration protocol and inversion in Hamming sectors (§105–§108)

title: Appendix C — The echo-calibration protocol and inversion in Hamming sectors (§105–§108)
text:
Sector. \(n\) qubits and weight \(w\): the sector has \(D=\binom{n}{w}\) basis states, \(|e_1\rangle,\dots,|e_D\rangle\) (sector_states).
Echoes. For each \(j\): prepare \(|e_j\rangle\) with \(X\) gates, apply the network \(W\) and then \(W^\dagger\), and measure in \(Z\). Without errors the circuit returns to \(|e_j\rangle\). The notes use 4000 shots per echo.
Matrix. Filter each echo to the sector (filter_distribution). Its distribution over the \(D\) states is column \(j\) of \(M\), with \(M_{ij}=P(e_i\text{ measured}\mid e_j\text{ prepared})\) (echo_transfer_matrix).
Root. The circuit to be read has half the gates of the echo, so it is corrected with \(A=M^{1/2}\): the principal, real, non-negative, column-normalized root (matrix_power_stochastic).
Unmixing. Filter the circuit’s distribution, \(f\), and solve \(Ax=f\) with \(x\ge0\) by non-negative least squares; normalize \(x\) (unmix_sector).
Reading. Each qubit reads \(m_Z(q)=1000\,(1-2p_q)\) with the populations of \(x\).
Before using it. Simulate without noise at the same shots to know the sampling error. The echo helps when the filtered error is well above that level, and not when it is already almost all shot noise (§108).

text:
C.3 An exact example
The script builds an in-sector channel \(K\) on 5 qubits and weight 1, with probability 0.90 of staying on the right qubit, and a T1 loss of 15% of the shots to \(|00000\rangle\), which reads \(+1000\) m-qg on every qubit. The echo applies \(K\) twice, so \(M=K^2\) (mean diagonal 0.81), and the principal root recovers \(K\) exactly. That is the assumption behind \(M^{1/2}\): that the way back has the same error as the way out. In §105 the full \(M\) did better on Forte-1, so it does not always hold.

Why non-negative least squares and not the inverse. With 1000 shots per run, in 37 of 300 runs the direct inverse \(A^{-1}f\) gives some negative population, which is not a probability. The non-negative solution never does. The mean \(qg_Z\) error is almost the same: 21.6 m-qg with the inverse and 21.5 m-qg with the non-negative solution. What is gained is that the result is always a distribution, not accuracy; that is why the usual readout mitigation also restricts the solution to the simplex.

Bibliographic notes
The echo is that of Hahn (1950); readout-error mitigation by inverting a confusion matrix, Bravyi et al. (2021). The sector filter is the symmetry verification of Bonet-Monroig et al. (2018). The numbered notes (§) and the scripts are in the repository (Monteverde 2026).

E.1 Falsification statement
The book’s plan announced a full count of §1–§164 here. Chapter 28 explains why it was not done: the sections before §71 hardly use pre-registration, and many later ones leave their verdicts only in prose, worded differently. This appendix lists what can be checked with code. tools/make_appendices.py generates it with the same functions as the Chapter 28 figure (tools/make_cap28_figures.py), so its totals are the chapter’s.
crumbs: Appendices
E  Falsification register: the predictions the repository allows one to check

title: Appendix E — Falsification register: the predictions the repository allows one to check
text:
Definitions and identities are not falsified by experiments. The qg unit, the milli-qang, the probability equation and the formulas of Appendices A and B are proven or checked to machine precision in tests/. If one fails, it is a code bug, not a result.
Empirical claims are. Each says that a reading with qang is more accurate, cheaper or more stable than without qang, and it is fixed with a threshold before running. A failed prediction is published with its number and not rewritten.
What would falsify the programme as a whole. That the advantages of Chapter 29 did not repeat on real hardware with thresholds fixed in advance. Today that test has two runs on IQM Garnet (§165 and §168), with 7 of 8 predictions passed. That is too little to decide.

title: Appendix F — Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
text:
F.1 The setting
This appendix is conceptual and adds no results. It is Appendix A of the research notes, which Chapter 4 cites: it explains why \(qg_Z\) is the canonical linear readout of a state and why \(qg_S\) cannot be one. The three numerical checks are done by tools/make_appendices.py.
For \(n\) qubits, the operators on \(\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\) form a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product
\[
\langle A,B\rangle=\mathrm{Tr}(A^\dagger B),
\]
and density matrices live in it.
crumbs: Appendices
F  Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet

title: Appendix F — Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
text:
F.2 The theorem
Riesz–Fréchet representation (Riesz 1907; Fréchet 1907). Every continuous linear functional \(f\) on a Hilbert space \(H\) has the form \(f(x)=\langle y_f,x\rangle\) for a unique \(y_f\in H\). In finite dimension continuity is automatic and the theorem reduces to linear algebra: with an orthonormal basis \(\{E_i\}\), \(y_f=\sum_i\overline{f(E_i)}\,E_i\). That is why it is a foundation and not a result.
crumbs: Appendices
F  Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet

title: Appendix F — Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
text:
F.3 Application: \(qg_Z\) has a representative
The readout \(\rho\mapsto qg_Z(\rho)=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_z)\) is linear in \(\rho\), so it has a unique Hilbert–Schmidt representative: \(\sigma_z\) on one qubit, and \(\sigma_z^{(i)}\otimes I\) on qubit \(i\) of a register. Every linear readout of a state, be it an expectation value, a population or a per-shot average such as linear XEB, has this form. \(qg_Z\) is the one whose representative is the \(Z\) observable.
The script checks it on two qubits with the normalized Pauli basis, \(E_P=P/2\). It rebuilds the representative of \(\rho\mapsto\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\,Z\otimes I)\) and gets \(Z\otimes I\) with error 0. For a population readout with random weights, \(\rho\mapsto\sum_x w_x\langle x|\rho|x\rangle\), it gets \(\mathrm{diag}(w)\) with error \(8.7\cdot10^{-18}\).

title: Appendix F — Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
text:
F.4 What has no representative: \(qg_S\)
\(qg_S(\rho)=H(\langle0|\rho|0\rangle)\) is strictly concave in \(\rho\), not linear, so no operator represents it. The shortest example: \(|0\rangle\langle0|\) and \(|1\rangle\langle1|\) both have \(qg_S=0\), and their equal mixture has \(qg_S=1\) bit; a linear readout would give the average, 0. With \(qg_Z\) the average does hold: \((+1-1)/2=0\).
The same structural fact is behind two results of the notes:

§10.3 B: linear readouts have unbiased shot-average estimators, and entropy does not (Jensen’s inequality). The table gives the exact bias, by binomial sum, of the two direct estimators.
§7.1: the identity \(qg_S=H\big((1+qg_Z)/2\big)\) writes the non-linear metric as a fixed scalar function of the linear one. \(qg_S\) carries no information about the state beyond what the representative of \(qg_Z\) already extracts.

title: Appendix F — Functional-analysis foundation: Riesz–Fréchet
text:
F.5 On Riesz’s lemma (1918)
The almost-orthogonal-vector lemma is used to show that the closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional normed space is not compact. In the finite dimensions of this book it is trivial, because an exactly orthogonal vector always exists. It plays no role in qang and should not be cited as if it did.
